图 85
Fist Beneath the Elbow: with the turning of the body the left palm moves to slightly left of the front of the body and arcs down to the left
图 86
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the settled posture with the left palm moved by the turning of the body to slightly left of the front of the body

4. The left foot comes down to the left (east), touching down heel first, and the centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg. With the turning of the body the two palms translate in an arc to the left, and the left arm rotates inward as it moves so that the two palms turn to face down. The right leg lifts, shifts slightly forward and comes down, and the centre of gravity at once moves onto the right leg. When, with the turning of the body, the left palm has moved to slightly left of the front of the body it arcs down to the left. The gaze first attends to the left palm moving left, and when the right palm is about to arrive in front of the chest, to the right palm (see the third, fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh figures on this page).

图 87
Fist Beneath the Elbow: the left palm going from the left downward and inward, passing inside the right forearm and piercing forward and up, the right palm covering and grasping outside the left palm to form a fist placed beneath the left elbow

5. The centre of gravity shifts entirely to the right leg; the left foot lifts a little, moves slightly forward and comes down, touching down on the heel with the toes slightly raised; the body continues to turn slightly left. The left palm goes from the left downward and inward, passes inside the right forearm, and turns and pierces forward and up, palm facing right, the index finger level with the eyebrows and aligned with the tip of the nose; the right palm passes to the left outside the left palm, covering and grasping to form a fist, which is placed beneath the left elbow, the eye of the fist upward, and the upper body turns slightly right. The eyes attend a little to the left palm circling down to the left; when the left palm is about to pierce out past the inside of the right arm they look level ahead, but the gaze must still attend to the piercing out of the left palm (see the eighth figure on this page).

Book page 86

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. Solid and empty must be clear. The right toes turn in fully and the right leg bears the whole body's weight; only then can the left leg lift light and nimble.

2. The arms turn with the waist. It is through rotating the waist and turning the spine that movement is transmitted from the turning of the wrist and the turning of the upper arm to the tips of the hands. Therefore the movement of the arms must be as the boxing theory says, "the lord is in the waist" — one must not move only the arms without moving the waist.

3. It must proceed according to "when one part moves, no part is still; when one part is still, no part moves" and to the requirement of unbroken continuity — without corners, without pauses, rounded and coordinated. In the two movements of lifting the right foot and slightly lifting and setting down the left foot, the hands move as the feet move. Just as the settled posture of the hidden fist beneath the elbow is completed, the opportunity for the left-right opposing brace arises at this moment of seeming to stop and not stopping, and not as something joined and again broken; for the old force is spent and the new force not yet born, and this is the moment when one is most easily taken by an opponent seizing the opening.

4. The two feet must not double-weight; they must rise and fall in turn like a see-saw. When lifting the right foot or lifting the left foot, one leg must bear the body's weight.

5. When the two palms translate to the left, the right palm must not lie flat or swing down but must sit the wrist and stand upright; and the left hand must go forward while the right hand follows, at an equal distance.

6. In the settled posture the left knee must naturally bend slightly and the two shoulders must not shrug. The two arms form an arc and must not be held straight. The waist and hips must be relaxed, and the chest must not face the front squarely but turn slightly toward the right-front diagonal, while the two arms still face straight to the front (east), and the left palm must sit the wrist.

7. When the two hands translate eastward, the back of the left hand faces outward and the right palm faces left and outward; when the body turns to face the front (east) the left hand goes down first and the right hand goes forward afterwards — not both downward at the same time, because at this moment I use my left wrist to meet the opponent's right wrist flat on the outside and push it aside to the left, while the right hand goes to the left hand to meet his left hand; each has its own purpose.

Book page 87

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. Particular attention must be paid to the stepping: advance and retreat, and the transitions of solid and empty must be distinct. When the two arms begin to translate to the left, the right leg is solid and the left leg must be empty. When the body turns to the front, the left leg is solid and the right leg lifts easily; when the centre of gravity moves onto the right leg the left leg is empty and the landing step must be steady — the change of solid and empty is gradual, not sudden.

2. One must "let the hands follow the movement of the feet, and the feet follow the movement of the hands", with "upper and lower accompanying each other".

3. One must take the waist as the axis; the strength of the waist must be used appropriately, and only then does it aid the body's balance. The waist must not sway away from centre; therefore the body must not lean forward or backward.

4. When the right toes turn in, the right is solid and the left is empty; the centre of gravity should not shift left.

5. The movements of the hands must be clear. When the two hands swing level the distance between them is about 20 centimetres; too large or too small is incorrect.

6. The fingers should be slightly curved but must not be stiff. If the fingers are too curved, it is hard to carry the intent through to the fingertips; if they are too straight, that is stiffness. The intent must reach the fingertips, with the pads of the fingers exerting a very slight force; with long practice this makes the qi and blood flourish in the fingers.

Book page 88

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: the right foot is not turned in sufficiently, so the waist and hip cannot turn to the left fully. Main cause: the hip-root is not adducted enough and the knee is twisted too much, with too little foot-turning. Correction: lift the ball of the right foot slightly; the foot follows the knee and the knee follows the waist, so that the right sole turns in no less than 90°.

2. Error: when turning the foot in and turning the waist, the centre of gravity shifts left, producing double-weighting. Main cause: there is no right-fullness, and so no left-emptiness. The movement then cannot rotate freely, cannot gain power, and cannot keep a stable centre. Correction: the body's weight must settle fully on the right leg; during the turn the centre of gravity does not move — turn on the full right leg. The waist must be straight and the central axis must not sway, so that the upper body does not lean to one side. The waist-gap governs the two legs: on the solid side of the waist-gap, the leg below is also solid. Hence the left waist-gap must be empty.

3. Error: as the waist turns left and the left foot lifts and steps back to the left, the centre of gravity shifts left too quickly, destroying the principle of "uniform tempo in every movement." Main cause: the right foot is not fully turned in and the hip-root is not opened; added to that, at the moment the right foot turns in the centre of gravity is wrongly shifted left, so the right leg cannot exert its normal supporting power. The left leg is therefore forced to land quickly to gain support. Correction: turn the right foot in fully; the right knee stays under the centre of gravity without shifting; open the hip-root, and let the left leg step slowly.

4. Error: the two hands move left too high or too low. Main cause: insufficient attention to the application. The left hand meets the opponent's left hand flat, and the right hand connects with his left hand; if my hand is too high or too low it does not meet the requirement of "connecting." Correction: the proper height is with both hands level with the shoulders.

5. Error: after the body turns square (to the east), both hands press down at the same time. Main cause: insufficient attention to the application. The left hand should first push out to the left and then circle down in a small arc; the right hand then goes left-and-back, forming a fist that is carried lightly beneath the left elbow. Correction: the left hand goes down first while the right hand is still moving forward; the two hands must not press down simultaneously.

6. Error: moving the hands without moving the waist, so that upper and lower are disconnected. Main cause: there is no whole-body consideration governed by the waist — it is a tree without roots. Correction: when the hands go forward they must have a sinking, root-driven quality; the soles of the feet take the force, and as the waist and legs move forward the two hands move in the same direction.

7. Error: at the set position the upper body faces squarely to the front. Main cause: a shallow understanding of storing power. Correction: the body should be turned to the side. If the body faces squarely forward, the right fist that has turned in beneath the left elbow loses the stored impulse to strike at the ready, and the chest is also compressed, which obstructs the free flow of qi and blood.

Book page 89

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explanation (with emphasis on turning the foot in and on the movement of the two hands).

2. Demonstration of the whole movement.

3. Progressive-addition method:

  • ① Begin from the set position of Grasp the Sparrow's Tail / Embrace the Tiger and Return to Mountain, making a good link; immediately turn in the right foot while the two arms shift level to the left and to the right, arriving at the forward-right diagonal.
  • ② As above, then continue: the back of the left hand turns outward, the right hand forms a vertical palm; the left leg lifts, the upper body turns left, and the left leg steps forward with the heel landing first; the two arms follow the waist and transfer to the front of the body. Once ② is grasped at a basic level, join it to ①.
  • ③ Shift the centre of gravity forward; the two hands move forward with the waist; the centre of gravity gradually moves onto the left foot; the right leg lifts slightly; the left hand turns to a downward palm. Once grasped at a basic level, join ①②.
  • ④ Shift the centre of gravity back; the right foot shifts slightly to the right and comes down, seating the right leg; the left hand circles in a small arc inside the right arm and threads out; the right hand forms a fist and is placed beneath the left elbow; the left foot lifts and comes down slightly forward-left, heel landing first. Once grasped at a basic level, join ①②③.
  • ⑤ The complete movement. Note: in the progressive-addition practice, take particular care that the movement is unbroken and continuous, with no place where it halts.

4. Paired practice combining the application:

  • ① A — takes the set position of Embrace the Tiger and Return to Mountain (facing northwest); B — comes out from behind A (the east); A — turns the body left, seats the right leg, and shifts the two hands level to the left and right; turning the body left, A steps the left foot out to the front (east), meets B's right wrist level with his own left wrist, pushes out toward B's right, then drops and, clinging to B's wrist, circles inward in a small arc; the right hand meets B's left hand and adheres to it from above. ② A's left wrist rolls B's right wrist, while A's right hand turns

…the fist turns to beneath the left elbow, waiting there at the ready, or immediately strikes forward.

5. Mnemonic: turning left, turn in the right foot; both hands shift level as the body turns; left hand horizontal, right hand vertical palm; turning left, step out the left foot; the rear foot is reset; the front foot lifts and comes down again; the left arm circles in a small arc; the right fist hides beneath the elbow.

6. The student should first concentrate on training emptiness and fullness: the right foot turned in fully, the right leg seated solidly, the centre of gravity not shifting left. Lift the left foot toward the rear-left (east); the right leg must be steady, the hip must be open; as the body turns square, the right knee must follow the direction of the toes and must not twist inward. The body turns about 45° + 180°; so if the right foot is not turned in fully and the lower body is not stable, turning the body square is difficult. Hence emptiness and fullness must be practised repeatedly.

7. Turning the waist, shifting the centre of gravity, and the movement of the hands — these three are "upper and lower following one another," and may be practised separately (practising only the waist turn, only the weight shift, only the hand movement). This lets the beginner learn the movement rather quickly; but take care: separating is for the sake of joining, and in the end the upper and lower must follow one another. Fortunately, in the later stage of this movement the body turns slightly right, the left foot lifts slightly and comes down again, and at the same time the left palm threads out and the right palm becomes a fist — so that upper and lower do follow one another, rather than each going its own way.

Book page 90

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. In this movement one must first be clear about the change of direction. From the set position of Embrace the Tiger and Return to Mountain, where the body faces northwest, the two arms shift level first toward the southeast and then toward the southwest, and finally move to the east — and to this are added the changes of step of the two feet and the differing actions of the two hands… The movement is thus fairly complex. One must therefore concentrate on the progressive-addition method of learning: be clear about the direction, be clear about the movement, and climb as if going up stairs, one step at a time — firmly fix each part as you learn it, and only then add the next.

2. In this movement the body's weight is alternately supported on one leg. It looks like an alternation; but because the movement is slow, with one leg supporting and the other lifted clear for a long time, the actual time under static load is considerable. The demands this makes on the strength of the muscles of the waist, hips and legs are high. And precisely because of this, the muscles concerned are very well trained.

3. After the right foot is turned in and the right leg seated solidly, the left leg is empty and the left hip is relaxed. The leftward turn of the waist carries the two arms in a level shift to the left; at this moment the two shoulder-joints are required to line up level with the two shoulders, striving to achieve "shoulder and hip joined together." Therefore …the demands on the opening and relaxing of the hip-joint are very high; otherwise, with so large an angle of rotation, how could the movement be completed smoothly?

4. The burden carried by the full right leg is very great. It is like the movement of the trunk and branches of a great tree: because the root and limbs are as firm as a great root and a deep root, it stands steady and unmoving — and so this is a very demanding form of training.

Seventeenth Posture: Step Back and Repulse the Monkey, Left and Right (Zuo You Dao Nian Hou)

Book page 91

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the preceding posture: if the opponent uses his right hand to grip my left wrist or forearm tightly, and with his left hand supports the fist beneath my elbow, then I am first constrained by him and cannot execute my movement. At this moment I turn my left fist over upward, and with a sinking energy relax the waist and hip, withdrawing it back-left, while the left foot also steps back one pace, bending the knee and seating it solidly, and the right foot becomes empty. The opponent's grip is then lost at once. At the same time, the right hand separates to the rear, and at the instant he loses his grip I press forward swiftly. Although this posture takes one step backward, it can still repulse the opponent's energy — hence it is called "Repulse the Monkey." In this movement, take care to relax the shoulders and sink the elbows.

II. Movement Sequence
(A) Left Repulse the Monkey

1. The right hip-root draws in slightly; sit firmly on the right leg; the left leg lifts slightly with the toes hanging naturally; the body turns slightly right. At the same time the left palm drops slightly and extends slightly forward; the right fist becomes a palm, drawing from beneath the left elbow past the front of the abdomen, curving down-and-across to the side of the right hip; as it draws, the right arm rotates outward so that the palm gradually turns upward. The gaze follows the forward extension of the left palm (see the figures on this page).

2. The centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, and the body continues to turn slightly right; the left foot slowly lifts and draws in past the inside of the right ankle. At the same time the right palm continues to arc up to the rear and slightly right until it is level with the shoulder, the palm facing slanting upward. The left arm gradually rotates outward so that its palm faces slanting downward. The gaze follows the rearward lift of the right palm (see the figure on this page).

图 86
Right Repulse the Monkey set position: left palm extending forward, right palm lifted to the rear, the two arms drawing against each other front and back

3. The body gradually turns left; the left foot steps back one pace, touching down first with the toes; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the left leg the foot comes down flat (the foot set at a slant, toes pointing northeast). The right toes then turn to the front (east). At the same time, as the body turns, the right palm arcs slightly upward, drawing in past the side of the right ear and pushing out forward; the left palm turns palm-up and arcs back to draw in beside the left hip. The upper body turns about 90°, to the northeast, while the face still looks forward (east). The gaze follows the turn and looks level before it; the gaze must also take in the forward push of the right palm (see the figures on this page).

(B) Right Repulse the Monkey

The movement is the same, with the directions reversed (see the figures on this page).

(C) Left Repulse the Monkey

The movement is the same: the corresponding figures are as for the left-hand instance already described above.

Book page 92

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. A characteristic of this movement is the step backward. To keep the body balanced the lower body must be stable, and so when stepping back there must be a certain lateral distance; the two feet must therefore not be placed on a single line.

2. When one leg lifts and prepares to step back, the other leg must support; it must not rise or straighten up, and must still preserve the same height of the body's centre of gravity as in the original empty stance — that is to say, in the course of practising the form the centre of gravity must not rise and fall too much.

3. The chest must be contained and the back raised, the sacrum centred and upright; there must be no leaning forward or backward. When stepping back, in order to land slowly one easily tends to lift the upper…

图 89
Left Repulse the Monkey: the left foot steps back, the right palm arcs up to the rear-right until level with the shoulder
图 90
Repulse the Monkey: the right palm draws in past the side of the right ear and pushes forward, the left palm draws back beside the left hip
图 91
Repulse the Monkey: the two arms draw against each other front and back, the left foot planted firmly to the rear, the right toes turning square
图 92
Right Repulse the Monkey: left hand extending forward, right hand lifted to the rear, stepping back the right foot
图 93
Right Repulse the Monkey: right hand pushing forward, left hand drawing back, the gaze taking in the forward palm

…leaning the body forward to obtain balance. After the centre of gravity has settled back, when the two hands exchange front-and-rear before the body, it is easy to let the body pitch forward. One must therefore attend to the body method: the two shoulders and the two hips must advance and retreat together, neither leading nor lagging, so that from the crown of the head through the trunk down to the perineum point there is always a straight line. The Boxing Treatise says: "Baihui and Zhongji are threaded through by a single qi."

4. The two hands must exchange before the body, one going back and the other forward, moving without pause; neither hand may halt at the side of the body. Beginners, attending too much to the hand that extends rearward and to other actions, let the hand at the front very easily halt motionless. Both hands must therefore move evenly and unbrokenly; when one thing moves, nothing is unmoving.

5. When a palm draws back it must pass by the side of the hip; beginners often carry the hand too high and should alter this so that it passes by the side of the ribs. Otherwise the arm and elbow become an angle smaller than a right angle and no longer form an arc — it looks awkward rather than broad and comfortable, and the shoulder is also lifted.

6. For the front foot to step back, one must first lift the thigh, storing power in the knee, raising the heel with the toes hanging naturally; then slowly extend back, touching down lightly with the toes and the ball of the foot first, and then letting the heel come down firmly. Only thus is the requirement "stepping as a cat walks" embodied. Moreover, because the time supported on one leg is lengthened, the burden on the supporting leg is increased, which better trains the strength of the legs.

图 94
Right Repulse the Monkey: right palm pushing forward, left palm drawing back, the two arms drawing against each other front and back
图 95
Left Repulse the Monkey: the left foot planted firmly to the rear, the right arm lifted to the rear level with the shoulder
图 96
Repulse the Monkey: the step back is light and nimble, the body centred and upright without swaying
图 97
Right Repulse the Monkey: on the backward step the heel lands first, the sole then settling firmly
图 98
Left Repulse the Monkey set position: chest contained and back raised, shoulders relaxed and elbows sunk

7. Step Back and Repulse the Monkey, left and right, may be done three times each (in a single set of the form …the Repulse the Monkey occurs twice), or it may be done five or seven times each, but the number must be odd (five is generally appropriate). In addition, Cloud Hands should correspondingly be done three, five or seven times; otherwise, at the closing posture one cannot return to the starting place.

8. The gaze alternates its attention to the movement of the hands.

Book page 94

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. The shoulders must sink and the elbows hang. In Taijiquan, on the premise of relaxing the shoulders, "sinking the shoulders" is required; only with sunk shoulders can there be lightness and nimbleness. If the shoulders can relax, the whole arm's extending, contracting and coiling can be natural, lively and utterly un-sluggish, and after long practice one reaches the mutual tempering of firmness and suppleness.

2. The two shoulders must be level; the shoulder of a gathered arm must not be low while the shoulder of a forward-pressing arm is high, nor the reverse, for this destroys the uprightness of the body method.

3. When stepping back, with one leg supporting, the body must be stable and must not sway; it must be as firm as a great tree that cannot be shaken.

4. The waist rotation must be neither too large nor too small; turning to the two diagonals is the proper measure. For the body to face squarely forward and move only the arms without turning the waist is certainly wrong; but when the arms extend to the rear diagonal and the body has turned through some 90°, with the two arms almost straight front and back at some 180°, that is too much and does not meet the requirement of the application.

5. There must be "uniform tempo in every posture" and "unbroken continuity." The rearward-travelling foot must not land too fast, nor may the front leg lift too fast; it must be even, rising and falling slowly, using intent and not force, unbroken from beginning to end, returning again to the start, cycling without end.

6. Beginners at the front hand often turn it over too fast, producing the phenomenon of one hand halting while the other is still moving. Since the requirement is that when one thing moves nothing is unmoving, both hands should be in motion.

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: the body sways when stepping back. Main cause: the knee of the full foot is not stable, and the movement of the rearward-extending leg drags at the full leg, causing sway. Correction: the waist and hip must relax and sink, the buttocks drawn in slightly, the leg muscles steadying by force so that the knee-joint is stronger and the sole presses the ground more evenly and firmly; the lower body is then stable. Alternatively, if the shoulders are not relaxed, the movement of the arms drags at the upper body and disturbs its central uprightness, which also causes sway. 2. Error: when stepping back the two feet land on a single line. Main cause: a failure to understand the application. With the two feet on one line the base of support is small, and the slightest movement makes the already awkwardly placed legs unable to steady the centre of gravity — how then could one possibly neutralize and attack well? Correction: when stepping back the lateral distance between the two feet should be about the width of the shoulders.

3. Error: the two arms open out too widely, forming one arm forward (east) and one arm back (west), with the angle between the arms reaching 180°, which looks scattered. Main cause: an insufficient understanding of the circular movement of Taijiquan. If the arms open out too widely the movement becomes straight back-and-forth, and there is no longer "a marvellous hand whose every move is a taiji." Opening the arms too widely also drives the waist-axis to rotate too far; in combat this gives the opponent a gap — that is, it offers him an opening to attack.

4. Error: the front hand halts while the rear hand moves. Main cause: insufficient attention to "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoving." Correction: (taking Right Repulse the Monkey as the example) the left palm extends slightly forward and slowly rotates the arm outward so that the palm faces slanting down; then it slowly draws back… Meanwhile the right palm arcs up to the rear-right diagonal beside the right ear, and the left arm rotates almost "in place," with little visible change of shape. In fact, at this moment the shoulder, elbow and wrist joints and other parts of the body are all in motion; and as the right arm moves from below up and back, the two hands have precisely completed the preparatory action of the left hand drawing back and the right hand pressing forward — so that it is not one arm moving and one arm halting.

(The photograph at the foot of this page shows Fu Zhongwen demonstrating push-hands; it carries no figure number.)

…It is the same with the action of the foot: here too, when one thing moves nothing is unmoving. As the waist moves and the hands move, the foot below should at the same time slowly lift; as the right hand presses and the left hand draws in, at the same moment the left leg settles solidly and the right foot turns in exactly into place (facing squarely forward).

Book page 96

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explanation and demonstration (with emphasis on emptiness and fullness).

2. Breakdown method (taking Right Repulse the Monkey as the example):

  • ① First do the backward step. The right leg supports steadily and the left leg slowly lifts; the waist and hip must relax and sink, so that as the left leg travels from front to back the movement is even and does not drag the body into swaying. The teacher should lead the student to keep the waist "straight" and lifted. The teacher checks, and students check one another, on the lightness of the left leg's lift and backward step and on the lateral distance.
  • ② On the exchange position of the two hands front and rear — left hand forward, right hand beside the ear — as the body settles back the left hand draws in and the right hand presses forward; and while the hands move, the right toes slowly turn in to square. The teacher checks, and students check one another, on the coordination of hand and foot.
  • ③ The set position. The left leg is full (the knee not past the toes), the right leg is empty (the right knee slightly bent), the body turns slightly left, the left hand palm-up beside the hip, the right hand pressing forward in an arc (vertical palm), shoulders relaxed and elbows sunk, chest contained and back raised, sacrum centred and upright. Although the set position is a brief moment, that moment must certainly be present and must not be slurred over; one may pause in it for inspection.

3. Auxiliary practice: the right leg is full; slowly lift the left leg — extend it back; the ball of the front foot lands lightly — the heel comes down lightly until the whole foot is firmly planted. This may be repeated, and the legs may be alternated. The number of repetitions and the speed may be set according to each person's strength; after finishing, do relaxing exercises.

4. Movement mnemonic: turning left and raising right, lift the left foot; the body turns, the hands move, the leg moves slightly; the left leg must land to the rear light and nimble; left draws in, right presses, then settle back steady; hand and foot must be full and round and easy; the centre of gravity must not rise and fall;

5. Students should value the training of the legs and equally value the training of the hands, observing in one another the sinking of the shoulders and the hanging of the elbows during the movement of the hands.

VII. Technical Analysis

1. This movement is a backward step, so it trains muscles different from those used in stepping forward, and is all the more effective for training the body.

2. In stepping back it is comparatively difficult to "step as a cat walks." With one leg extending rearward, before the foot lands one must keep the other, supporting leg steady and the body unswaying, and land lightly and slowly — the demands this makes on every part of the body are very high. And the more one requires the rearward-extending leg to be slow and nimble, the higher the demand; the lower the stance and the longer the step, the harder it is to lift the front leg; and the farther the rearward leg extends, the longer the movement takes, so that the muscular burden on both the supporting leg and the extending leg is greater. Hence long practice in a fairly low stance is very effective for increasing the strength of the waist and legs and for health.

Eighteenth Posture: Diagonal Flying (Xie Fei Shi)

Book page 97

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the preceding posture: if the opponent strikes at my upper body from my right side, or presses with force between my right arm and wrist, I take the opportunity to sink and close downward, storing energy; at the same time I step out with the right foot, bend the knee and seat it solidly, and split the right hand out toward the upper-right corner, striking diagonally with an opening energy, as if flying out diagonally. The intent of the palm's delivery should also accord with the requirement of this movement.

Slanting variation: if the opponent presses my right upper arm, I contain the chest and relax the hip, first neutralizing his pressing energy; the left foot lifts and steps quickly down, the right foot lifts and is then put down, and the two hands first ward off and then press.

II. Movement Sequence

1. The centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg; the right leg lifts, and at the same time the waist turns slightly right. The left arm slowly rotates inward; the left palm-up hand, as it arcs up and to the right, turns over into a downward palm, the arm bent and placed before the left chest, the hand about level with the shoulder, the arm forming an arc, the elbow slightly sunk. The right palm, from the front, goes down and across the front of the abdomen, arcing down-left; as the right arm shifts, it rotates outward so that the palm faces upward, joining with the left palm above and below. The gaze takes in the left palm's arc (see the figures on this page).

图 99A
Diagonal Flying: the right palm splits out toward the upper-right corner, striking diagonally with an opening energy, the left palm at the left chest
图 99B
Diagonal Flying: bow the right leg and push back with the left, the right palm warding out toward the upper rear-right, the palm facing slanting upward

2. The body continues to turn right; the left leg seats solidly and the hip opens; at the same time the right foot steps out toward the rear-right (south). The heel lands first; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the right leg the whole foot settles firmly. Bow the right leg and push back with the left, forming a right bow stance. As the body turns, the right palm, using the ward-off side, wards out toward the upper rear-right, the palm facing slanting upward, at about the height of the forehead; the left palm arcs down-left …plucks down, at about the height of the hip, the palm facing down. The left foot pivots on the heel as the body turns, the sole turning inward. The gaze follows the turn of the body, looking level as it turns; the gaze must also take in the right palm's outward plucking (see the figures on this page).

Book page 98

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. The right leg slowly lifts and turns right with the waist, the body centred and upright, laying the foundation for the step to the rear-right.

2. In stepping the right foot to the rear-right, the body's balance is comparatively hard to control. Beginners tend to pitch the body forward, to lean crookedly, and to land heavily (the boxing proverb says: head bowed and back hunched — the boxing art is not high). The waist must both turn nimbly and stay "straight"; only with the central axis unbent can one support all eight directions. Hence one must sit solidly on the left leg, relax the waist and hip, and let the right leg, as the waist turns, gradually step out to the rear-right — only then will it look light and nimble.

3. When the right palm plucks out to the upper rear-right, the energy must arise in the foot, issue from the leg, be governed by the waist, and pass through the spine and back, from shoulder to elbow and elbow to hand, taking form in the fingers. Struck out with every joint threaded through, body, hand and step coordinated, arriving all as one — neither first nor last; the hand and the rest of the body must not be disconnected. One must attain "upper and lower following one another" and the requirement of the energy path; at the same time the right arm must not be fully straightened.

4. Because for beginners the supporting leg is not easily made stable, the body is not easily kept "straight," and the waist and hip are not easily relaxed, the movement is not easily controlled and the waist and leg actions tend to halt or go too fast. Hence the movement must change gradually and not abruptly, and the knee-joint of the supporting leg must be kept steady.

5. Because the stepping method is always best when advance and retreat are convenient, the stance is steady, and the hip-root is opened, when the waist turns and the right hand strikes out to the upper right, the left foot must plant and its front sole turn inward.

IV. Requirements

1. The movement must be done in one continuous breath, not broken up.

2. The waist must relax, sink and stand upright; no pitching forward, no tilting, no swaying.

3. The landing position of the right foot must be correct; it must not be too small, for if too small the waist becomes awkward.

4. The right leg must land lightly and nimbly.

5. The hand that plucks out to the upper right must turn with the waist.

图 100
Diagonal Flying: the right palm plucks out to the upper rear-right, the palm facing slanting upward, at about the height of the forehead
图 101A
Diagonal Flying: the right leg lifts and, as the waist turns, steps out to the rear-right, the body centred and upright
图 101B
Diagonal Flying: right bow-stance set position, the right hand plucking out, the left palm beside the left hip
Book page 99

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: after the right leg lifts, in the course of stepping out to the rear-right the leg does not travel by way of an arc. Main cause: an insufficient understanding of the requirement of spiral, arcing movement. Correction: in Taijiquan every movement's rise and fall, rotation, opening and closing, emptiness and fullness is constituted by arcs. Above, it is the turning of the wrists and the turning of the upper arms, taking form in the fingers; below, it is the turning of the ankles and the turning of the legs, reaching to the tips of the toes. The hip must urge the knee and the knee urge the foot. The right leg lifts and steps forward as the body turns — it must not first be brought stiffly in beside the inside of the left ankle and only then stepped out; rather it must arc out to the front-right as the body turns. Of course, withdrawing the leg straight sideways is also not good.

2. Error: after the right leg lifts it simply stops moving, and only after the body has turned does it step out to the rear-right. Main cause: an insufficient understanding of the requirement "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoving." Correction: at the same moment the right leg lifts, the waist and hip should gradually turn right; as they turn, the right leg, lifting, arcs out to the rear-right. The waist is turning, the hands are moving, and the right leg too is ceaselessly changing — attaining the gradual transition from opening to closing and closing to opening, from full to empty and empty to full.

(The photograph at the foot of this page shows Fu Zhongwen demonstrating push-hands; it carries no figure number.)

3. Error: when stepping out the right leg the upper body pitches forward and topples sideways. Main cause: in order to lighten the load when stepping out the right leg, because the left leg's support is weak, one borrows a forward pitch and sideways topple to keep balance. Correction: first of all the waist must be kept straight — that is, the central axis must not bend — so that all the weight above the waist is borne by the waist and legs. In addition, the leg strength must be increased so that the supporting leg is steady.

4. Error: the right hand plucks out to the upper right by moving the hand alone, without coordinating with the turning of the waist and hip and the extending and pressing of the left leg, so that upper and lower are disconnected. Main cause: a shallow understanding of "upper and lower following one another." Correction: as body, hands and legs go forward, the crotch energy must sink, the soles of the feet take the force, and the inner energy turns up from within the crotch, penetrating the spine and back and shooting straight out to the palm and fingers. Within going forward there must be a bracing behind; only thus will the right hand not be grasping at empty air.

5. Error: the left leg sits dead and unmoving. Main cause: the movement is not full and rounded, but wooden. Correction: when the waist turns, the left leg should carry a sinking intent and the waist and hip must be relaxed.

Book page 100

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explanation, demonstration, building the concept.

2. Teach by highlighting the difficult point. The difficulty of Diagonal Flying is the action when the right leg lifts and, as the body turns, steps out to the rear-right: either the body is not upright, or the landing is very heavy. This should therefore be taken as the key point and this barrier broken through:

  • ① Explain clearly the requirements of the correct movement and demonstrate it repeatedly.
  • ② Break through by stages.

A — The right leg lifts and draws back slightly; as the body turns, the left hand moves to the upper right and the right hand to the lower left; while the two hands join above and below, the right leg extends slightly to the rear-right. At this moment hold the correct requirements — the upper body upright, and so on — laying the foundation for the movement to follow; this part can generally still be managed. B — The body continues to turn right and the right leg continues to extend to the rear-right. As the suspended right leg goes on extending, the weight thus carried away from the support point continually increases, and so too do the demands on the muscles of the waist, back, hip and knee. Hence the beginner, wishing to keep the movement slow and nimble but lacking the strength, is forced to bring the right heel down quickly and heavily. Thus the requirement "stepping as a cat walks" is not attained. To overcome this difficulty the only way is …to strengthen the training of the muscles of the waist and legs; in time, as the muscles grow strong, the step becomes nimble. Hence, in practising the form one should repeatedly perform the lifting and stepping of the leg as the body turns.

3. The teacher inspects, and learners, in groups of two or three, inspect one another on: ① whether the body pitches forward, leans back or topples sideways; ② whether the turning of the waist and hip is full; ③ whether the right leg, when stepping out to the rear-right and landing, is heavy or light.

4. On the basis of having practised the earlier requirements well, then progressively resolve the details.

5. Paired practice combining the application: A — takes the set position of Repulse the Monkey. B — stands at A's right side and strikes down from above with the right hand, or presses between A's right arm and wrist. A — takes the opportunity to sink; the two hands join above and below; sit solidly on the left leg and step the right leg out to the rear-right; at the same time the right hand splits out and plucks toward the upper-right corner. The two then exchange roles.

6. Attention must be paid to stability of the lower body: one must practise the left leg's solid seating well, and repeatedly practise the left leg's steadiness during the waist-and-hip turn, the leg lift, and the step.

7. When the right foot lands, begin the two-way even division. One must practise well the energy arising from the foot and reaching the elbows and hands through the waist and back. Repeatedly experience this, so as to attain "upper and lower following one another."

8. The teacher should observe the changes in each part of the learner's body at every stage.

Book page 101

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. The body moves from a northeast-facing position to the south, a shift of about 135°. Since the left foot is fixed, the left knee tends somewhat to the northeast, while the right leg steps toward the west-southwest; hence as the two legs open out, the actual angle approaches 180°. Thus not only are the demands on the left leg's support extremely high, but the lifting and moving of the right leg also makes it extremely hard to train the upright centring of the upper body's sacrum. It requires that the left hip be adducted and seated solidly, the lower body steady, the waist relaxed and sunk; the central axis must on no account bend — only then can the inner energy support all eight directions, and only then will there be no left-right crookedness nor forward-and-backward pitching.

2. In outward form Diagonal Flying is the right palm plucking out to the upper rear-right; at a glance it seems to be only the action of a hand. But unless the energy arises in the foot, issues from the leg, is governed by the waist, passes through the spine and back, and goes from shoulder to elbow and elbow to hand, threaded through joint by joint, one cannot attain the requirement of the application nor the better …requirement of training the body. Therefore, after the right foot lands, one must begin the release of energy from the foot, reaching gradually upward to the wrist and fingers.

Nineteenth Posture: Raise Hands and Step Up (Ti Shou Shang Shi)

Book page 102

I. Application

I. Application

The same as the Fifth Posture, Raise Hands and Step Up, above.

II. Movement Sequence

The waist and hip sink slightly; the centre of gravity shifts forward and is placed entirely on the right leg; the left foot lifts slightly and comes down a little forward (essentially in place); the centre of gravity then gradually shifts back until it rests entirely on the left leg. The body turns slightly left; the right foot lifts slightly and comes down essentially in place, landing on the heel, the toes slightly raised and pointing forward, the knee slightly bowed, forming a right empty stance. At the same time the right arm rotates inward; as the elbow sinks and draws inward, the right palm gradually turns downward and slants down; the left palm arcs forward and upward; the two palms close toward the chest. The right palm is in front, the fingers at about the height of the midpoint between the eyebrows, palm facing left, a vertical palm; the left palm's fingers are at about the height of the chest, palm facing right (slightly downward), squarely facing the right elbow-joint. The waist turns slightly left. The gaze passes over the right palm and looks level forward. See the figures on this page (the last of which is the same posture as shown in the earlier Fifth Posture).

III. Key Points

1. The centre of gravity moves forward and back, but the body must not rise and fall greatly; it must be steady.

2. From the beginning to the end of the whole movement, the waist and hip and the upper and lower limbs must all begin at the same moment and finish at the same moment.

IV. Teaching Method and Practice Method

The learner must understand that although the Nineteenth Posture and the Fifth Posture are both Raise Hands and Step Up, the linkage is different. In teaching and learning, the linking process must be made clear.

All other points are the same as for the Fifth Posture.
