Twenty-Second Posture: Needle at the Bottom of the Sea (Hai Di Zhen)

Book page 105

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the preceding posture: if the opponent uses his right hand to pull my right wrist, I bend my right elbow, sit on my right leg and turn my waist, drawing my right hand back. At the same time the left hand goes left and the left foot is drawn back with it, touching the ground with the toes. If the opponent still has not let go, and instead wishes to press his advantage further and attack me, I let my right wrist go slack in the direction of the movement, fold at the waist and sink down, the gaze looking forward, the fingertips hanging down, as if searching for a needle at the bottom of the sea. At this moment, though the opponent means to pluck or to attack me, his incoming force is a single straight force; he does not expect that, checked by my one fold, his root-force snaps by itself — and I take the opening to strike him.

II. Movement Sequence

If the opponent uses his right hand to pull my right wrist, I immediately sit on the right leg, bend the right elbow and turn the waist to the right, drawing the right hand back; the left foot is at once drawn back, touching the ground with the toes. The purpose is to break free of the gripped right hand: taking the seated right leg as the base, using the turn to change the direction in which he pulls me, using the outward rotation of the right arm and the leftward turning of the palm to alter the opponent's grip, and using the drawing back of the left leg to increase the distance of withdrawal and to make attack and defence easier.

1. The centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg; the right foot lifts and comes down a little forward (about a foot or a little more). At the same time the right arm rotates outward so that the palm faces left, and turns from a vertical palm with a seated wrist into a flattened one; the right hand sinks slightly and the left hand shifts slightly forward and sinks (see the figures on this page).

图 113B
Needle at the Bottom of the Sea: after joining hands, the right hand bends at the elbow and draws back, the left hand extending forward to guard the inside of the right elbow
图 114
Needle at the Bottom of the Sea: the centre of gravity shifts onto the left leg, the right arm rotates outward, the palm turning left
图 115
Needle at the Bottom of the Sea: the right hand turns from a vertical palm with seated wrist to a flattened one, the left hand shifting slightly forward and sinking
图 116
Needle at the Bottom of the Sea: the two hands rise slightly with the shifting centre of gravity, the gaze taking in the drawing back of the right wrist

2. As the centre of gravity gradually shifts back until it rests entirely on the right leg, the left foot lifts, the waist turns slightly right, the right elbow bends and the right wrist draws in and back; the two hands rise slightly with the shifting of the centre of gravity. The gaze takes in the drawing back of the right wrist (see the figures on this page).

3. If at this moment the opponent still has not let go, and instead wishes to press forward and attack me in the same direction, I fold at the waist and sink down, changing the direction of his force. Therefore the left foot draws in slightly and comes down, touching the ground with the toes, forming a left empty stance; the waist turns slightly left, the right leg sits solidly, the left hip-root adducts, and the waist folds and sinks. At the same time the right palm, with the turning and folding of the waist, drives forward-and-down; the left palm arcs down to rest beside the left hip. The eyes look forward; the gaze must take in the right palm's downward drive (see the figures on this page).

Book page 106

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. As the centre of gravity moves forward and back, the two hands sink slightly and rise slightly; but the upper body still maintains "the sacrum centred and upright."

2. When the left foot lifts and comes down after drawing in slightly, and the upper body folds at the waist and sinks, the right leg must gradually squat, the left toes merely touching the ground in emptiness, and the centre of gravity must be borne entirely by the right leg.

3. When the right wrist draws inward and back, one must guard against shrugging the shoulder and lifting the elbow.

4. When the right palm, having drawn back, drives up, forward and down, its arc must accompany the squatting of the right leg and the folding of the waist, and the shoulder must urge the elbow and the elbow the hand, driving down with every joint threaded through.

5. In folding the waist, the neck and the waist-and-back must be kept in a single straight line; one must not bow the head or hunch the back. One must attend to the uplifting energy and the sinking of qi, threading one qi through above and below.

6. While driving down, the eyes look before the right palm, but the head must not be raised.

7. One must practise well "when one thing moves, nothing is unmoving." If the right palm has a drawing-back action, the left palm must likewise move forward and back with the centre of gravity and act together with the turning of the waist; one must not move only the right hand and not the left. The two arms must not be fully straight; they must be slightly bent.

8. When the right arm draws back the waist turns slightly right; when the waist folds and drives down it must turn slightly left. One must not move the hand alone without moving the waist; one must meet the requirement "the waist is the governing authority."

IV. Requirements
图 117A
Needle at the Bottom of the Sea: the right palm draws back, the right elbow bent, the right wrist turning inward, the two hands rising slightly
图 117B
Needle at the Bottom of the Sea: the waist folds and sinks, the right palm drives forward-and-down, the left palm arcs down beside the left hip
图 117C
Needle at the Bottom of the Sea: left empty stance, toes touching the ground, sitting solidly on the right leg, the gaze taking in the right palm's downward drive

1. When folding at the waist and sinking, the neck and the waist-and-back must keep a single straight line; the buttocks must not protrude — protruding buttocks easily twist the arms and impair "the sacrum centred and upright."

2. After the sole of the right foot lifts, it must be set down with the palm of the foot at a slant; thus the lower body is easily made stable.

3. When folding at the waist and sinking, the right must be full and the left empty; otherwise one's own stance is unsteady and one is easily dragged about by the opponent.

4. The right hand's downward drive must seat the wrist; it must not be slack and powerless.

5. When folding at the waist the head must follow naturally, neither raised nor lowered; otherwise the qi and blood are made to flow poorly.

Book page 107

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Common Errors, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Error: the right hand does not bend at the arm when drawing back. Main causes: ① attending to the foot and neglecting the hand; ② insufficient understanding of the application. In the action of bending the arm there are sinking and turning actions, and the distance the held point must travel is increased, which readily snaps the opponent's root-force. Correction: when the right hand draws back, one must at the same time shift the centre of gravity back, turn the waist right, and bend the arm.

2. Error: when the left foot comes down, it is not "sent down" by the squatting of the right leg; instead the right foot sits motionless and the left foot comes down by itself. Main cause: insufficient understanding of the application. If the right leg does not squat, then to sink and break free of the opponent's wrist-grip one can only rely on the strength of the hand, or at most of the waist and abdomen, and cannot bring the strength of the whole body into play.

(The photograph at the foot of this page shows Fu Zhongwen and Fu Shengyuan demonstrating push-hands; it carries no figure number.)

Correction: the right leg sinks to "send" the left foot down, and at the same time the right leg bears the whole body's weight as it squats.

3. Error: lowering the head and rounding the back. The main causes are: ① the right leg lacking the strength to squat. ② a shallow understanding of "the tailbone centred and upright". ③ a shallow understanding of the application. With the head lowered and the back rounded one cannot see the opponent's movement and cannot know him; how then can one attack and defend? Only by practising with the tailbone centred and upright can one be calm and comfortable. A rounded back and hollowed chest is a sickly posture and is unfavourable to breathing. Correction: the crown of the head, the trunk and the perineum must form one straight line.

4. Error: when turning the waist right to draw the right hand back, the turn is too wide — approaching 90° to the right. The main cause is a subjective pursuit of expansiveness, which results in scattering. Correction: the turn should be slight.

Book page 108

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. Explain and demonstrate (with a student as assistant, demonstrating the backward raise and the sinking).

2. Mnemonic: shift forward and sink slightly, then raise; turn the waist and bring the arm back, sinking down; the right leg solid and the left leg empty; fold at the waist, draw in the buttocks, and look ahead.

3. Group practice: ① while the centre of gravity shifts forward and back, observe the alternation of solid and empty in the two feet; one may support on one leg and lift the other, holding it off the ground for the moment and then slowly setting it down, to deepen the experience of solid and empty. ② in the left empty stance, squat slightly on the right leg while the left leg lifts empty and does not touch down, to strengthen the right — the solid leg — and deepen the experience of solid and empty.

4. Those of weak constitution should not squat deeply on the right leg; the stance may be higher, to reduce the amount of exertion.

5. The focus of teaching may be placed on folding at the waist and sinking, on improving the solidity and emptiness of the legs, on drawing in the buttocks, and on correcting such faults as lowering the head, rounding the back and crooking the spine.

6. In the course of practising the form the student must be brought to understand the application. The Needle at the Bottom of the Sea is not only the application of the right arm thrusting down; before it there is also the movement of drawing the right arm back, and in this way one gains an understanding of the whole process.

7. Whole-form practice, improving the movement of the two hands. The centre of gravity shifts forward, the body rises slightly, and the two hands rise slightly with it, forming the left empty stance. The right leg squats, the right hand thrusts down, and the left hand presses down. Practise repeatedly, experiencing the requirement of "when one part moves, no part is still".

8. Paired practice using the application: A — performs Brush the Knee and Twist the Step, and offers the right wrist to be gripped by the partner, B. A — shifts the centre of gravity back, turns the body slightly right, and draws the right arm back, feeling the strength of the backward draw, then thrusts the right arm down and lowers the centre of gravity, and so on, to experience the application of Needle at the Bottom of the Sea and to feel how one snaps B's root strength. Practise repeatedly and exchange roles.

Book page 109

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. The first difficulty of Needle at the Bottom of the Sea lies in the squat of the left empty stance. For it makes high demands not only on the quadriceps and other muscles of the front of the thigh, but also — because the upper body folds forward, the left leg hangs empty and the body's centre of gravity shifts forward — on the muscles of the waist and back and the gluteals. Hence a good many muscles are brought into play, which raises the training effect. At the same time, because the upper body bends forward, it squeezes and massages the internal organs of the chest and abdomen, which is a great help in strengthening the constitution.

2. The characteristic of Needle at the Bottom of the Sea is that it folds the body forward, and in the whole of the Yang-style form this is rather conspicuous. Bending forward, lowering the head, bending the waist and crooking the back — this loses the upward energy of the empty collar and loses the containing of the chest. But in a correct fold-and-sink, although the bend at the waist is large, one still maintains "the crown point, the central pole, one breath running through"; for although this is a deviation within centredness, the inner energy is still centred and undeviating. Therefore the head must follow naturally — one must not lower the head, must not protrude the buttocks, and must draw the buttocks in.

Twenty-third Posture: Fan Through the Back (Shan Tong Bei)

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent again strikes with his right hand, I hastily raise my right hand from in front upward until it is beside my right temple, and at once turn the palm outward, using it to support the strength of the opponent's right hand; the left hand at the same time comes up in front of the chest, bursts open with the palm, and drives straight at the opponent's ribs, sinking the shoulders, dropping the elbows, sitting the wrist and relaxing the waist. At the same time the left foot steps forward, the knee bends and sits solid, the toes pointing forward. The gaze follows the left hand forward, and the right leg's hip and waist extend and send the strength out. Its energy issues from the back; the two arms open out, so that the fan opens through the back.

II. Course of the Movement

1. Sitting solidly on the right leg, the waist straightens as it turns right, and the left foot lifts and moves back; at the same time the right palm is raised from in front of the body, rotating inward as it rises so that the palm faces right and the fingers slant downward; the left palm is raised from beside the left hip up to in front of the chest, its palm also facing right, the fingers slanting upward. When the right arm has been raised to the height of the chest, the gaze must attend to the right palm's rising (see the first two figures at the right-hand side of this page).

图 118A
Fan Through the Back: sitting solidly on the right leg, the waist straightening as it turns right, the right palm raised from in front of the body
图 118B
Fan Through the Back: the right palm raised to the height of the chest, palm facing right, the gaze attending to the right palm's rising

2. The left leg lifts and steps forward a pace, touching down heel first, the toes pointing forward; as the centre of gravity gradually shifts onto the left leg the whole sole presses flat, the left leg bows and the right leg pushes, forming a left bow stance; at the same time the right arm continues to rotate slightly inward and bend at the elbow, and the right palm arcs outward to support, the left palm moving right to come close to the right forearm; the right hand is drawn back to the right side of the forehead, no higher than the crown, and the left hand strikes forward, the fingers no higher than the eyebrows. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze attends to the left palm's forward push (see the third figure at the right-hand side of this page).

图 119A
Fan Through the Back: the left leg stepping forward into a left bow stance, the left palm striking forward, the right hand drawn back to the right side of the forehead
Book page 110

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. The linking of the movements is very important. Once the right arm of Needle at the Bottom of the Sea has thrust down into place, the upper body must rise, the left leg draw back and the two arms be raised; there must be no pause anywhere. Inside and outside, above and below, left and right, front and back must be coordinated; upper and lower accompanying each other, done in one breath — only then does one gain the opportunity and the advantage.

2. The difficulty of Fan Through the Back lies in doing the slow forward step of the left leg well while supported on the right leg alone, and in requiring an even speed and a clear distinction of solid and empty. The right hip root must draw in, the right abdomen be full, and one must sit steadily on the right leg; then the left leg slowly advances a pace. Hence beginners find this movement hard to do well: they usually fail to control the centre of gravity, so that the left leg lands quickly, or the right leg straightens; this fails to meet the requirement of unbroken continuity and of stepping like a cat, and also produces the error of the centre of gravity rising and falling violently. Therefore attending to the stability of the right leg is of great importance.

3. In changing from the right empty stance into the left bow stance, the left leg bowing forward, the right leg pushing back, the left palm pushing forward and the right palm supporting upward — these four movements must be as one. In this way, while the upper frame is set, the left palm drives straight at the opponent and one achieves the effect of attacking where he is empty.

4. The right palm's upward support must sink the shoulder and drop the elbow; do not shrug the shoulder or lift the elbow, for lifting the elbow exposes the ribs. The left palm's push must sit the wrist, and the palm must not face squarely forward.

5. In the course of the movement the arms are often easily held straight, which does not accord with the requirement "strength is stored in the bends and has surplus" — the movement should leave room for extension, and one should be storing power everywhere and able to release power everywhere. Therefore, throughout the whole set of tai chi chuan movements, neither the two arms nor the two legs may be straightened or held rigid.

6. In the movement one must not throw the chest out; throwing the chest out does not accord with the requirement of "containing the chest and raising the back". For the right hand's support and the left arm's level push both require the strength to issue from the spine. The function of containing the chest is to favour the dissolving of energy, and the function of raising the back is to favour the rolling and releasing of energy; in combat they are related as storing and issuing, each transforming into the other.

7. One must "keep the tailbone centred and upright, and support the eight directions": never allow any part of the body to slacken and lose its centre, and however the limbs may turn and change, from the crown of the head to the perineum there is always one line. When the left leg steps, the body must not lean forward or backward, nor tilt to left or right; one must both have upper and lower accompanying each other and keep upper and lower essentially one line.

Book page 111

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. As the body straightens and the left foot is drawn back, one must sit solidly on the right leg, not lower the head or stoop, and not sway the body from side to side.

2. At the same time as the upper body straightens, the left foot, left hand and right hand — together with a slight turn of the waist to the right — must all move together.

3. The right palm must turn as it rises; by the time it has risen to shoulder height the elbow joint should already be hanging down. The left palm, raised to beside the right forearm, should be no higher than the shoulder; otherwise the left palm will not be driving straight forward.

4. The left foot steps forward, touching down heel first, and is required to be light and slow.

5. In stepping the upper body must not fall forward or lean back; the tailbone must be centred and upright.

6. The waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower limbs. In issuing the left palm, the waist turns slightly right, the leg bows, the leg pushes, the waist wrings, and finally the palm is issued. If the strength of the waist is used appropriately it reinforces the issuing of power and concentrates the whole body's force at one point.

7. The left leg steps forward and only after the heel has landed does the left hand push forward.

V. Errors Easily Committed, Their Causes, and Their Correction
图 119B
Fan Through the Back: the upper body straightening, the left foot drawn back, the right palm turning as it rises, the left palm pushing forward

1. Error: the left leg steps forward and lands fast and heavily. The main cause is that the upper body has not been raised and the body — the body's centre of gravity has moved far from the support point of the right foot; the moment the left foot is lifted empty, the body rushes forward, so the left foot has no choice but to land heavily and in haste. Correction: the upper body must be raised and kept upright, "containing the chest and raising the back", and the body's weight placed entirely on the right leg, so that the lower body is first made stable. Then the left leg is slowly stepped out, and in this way one can be light and nimble.

2. Error: when the movement begins, only the hands and feet move and the waist does not turn. The main cause is that the practitioner has not deeply grasped that "the waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower limbs", nor deeply experienced the change of the whole body's movement and the transmission of energy to every part of the limbs. Correction: from the very start of the movement the waist must lead the hands and feet. Hence "in the change of solid and empty one must be attentive".

3. Error: the left leg has bowed into place but the two hands are still moving. The main cause is an insufficient understanding of the application. "Within going forward there must be a bracing behind." When body, hands and leg go forward, the crotch energy sinks, the sole takes the weight, and the force passes through the spine and reaches the palm and fingers to shoot straight. Hence where there is forward there must be backward; this is what must be done well to reinforce the reactive force. Correction: the hands must arrive, the feet must arrive and the eyes must arrive.

4. Error: the right elbow lifts as the right hand rises. Some lift the elbow above the shoulder; some let the elbow stick out far from the body. The main cause is a shallow understanding of the requirement to "sink the shoulders and drop the elbows". A lifted elbow point is a lifting energy; it both hinders the sinking of the shoulder and affects the sinking of the breath, and exposes the ribs too much. Correction: the elbow must always be slightly bent and carry a downward-sinking energy, and the right elbow must be lower than the right palm.

Book page 112

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. In group practice, bring out the common errors and faults.

2. Mnemonic: sit solid on the right leg, its root unmoving; the two hands gradually rise as the body straightens; lightly step the left leg out, the eyes looking forward; the left drives while the right supports — a fan through the back.

3. Paired practice using the application: A — takes up the posture of Needle at the Bottom of the Sea. B — strikes straight at A with the right hand from the front. A — at once straightens the upper body and, as the left foot steps forward, raises the right hand to support B's hand beside the right temple, and at once drives the left hand from the chest to strike B's left ribs. The two exchange roles.

4. The emphasis of this movement must be placed on the supporting leg — the right leg. Sitting solidly on the right leg, the body straightens as it turns right, and the left foot lifts and moves back. At this moment the right leg must not straighten: that is, one must keep the right leg bent while doing the movement, so that the right leg is close to an isometric exercise. Gradually master the method of threading energy into the lower limb — the sacrum must sink powerfully, the girdle vessel be fully filled, the strength of the buttocks be threaded through to the heel, and the energy of the right foot be as if wound into the ground. In this way, only when the right is solid can the left be empty, and only then can the left leg step light and nimble; the body will naturally not sway.

Twenty-fourth Posture: Turn the Body and Swing the Fist (Zhuan Shen Pie Shen Chui)

Book page 113

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent strikes with his hand at my back or at my ribs from behind, I immediately shift the left foot slightly and sit solidly, the right foot becomes empty, and I turn the waist so that the body turns to face the front (from east toward south); at the same time the right hand forms a fist and is held for the moment at the left ribs, with the left palm slanting upward, joining to protect the left corner of the forehead. The body continues to turn right (toward west), and at the same time the right fist circles upward and swings out, meeting the opponent's hand, and with a sinking energy sits firmly at the side of the right ribs, while the left hand, from the left side, darts at the opponent's face. In this way the opponent loses the measures of attack and defence he ought to have.

II. Course of the Movement

1. The body slowly turns right (toward south), and at the same time the left toes turn in, the left leg sits solid, and the right foot becomes empty. With the turning of the body the right palm arcs down. It forms a fist and is held for the moment in front of the left ribs, the elbow bent and the arm across, the fist's centre facing down, while the left palm is drawn back, arcs up and is placed above and in front of the left corner of the forehead. The gaze attends slightly to the right hand's arc, then looks level ahead (see the figure at the left-hand side of this page).

图 120
Turn the Body and Swing the Fist: the body turning right, the left toes turning in, the right hand forming a fist and held for the moment in front of the left ribs, the left palm arcing up to be placed above and in front of the left corner of the forehead

2. The body continues to turn right (toward west), the centre of gravity shifts entirely onto the left leg, and the right foot lifts; the left palm, with the turning of the body, at the same time arcs from the right downward, passes outside the right forearm and comes down level with the right elbow, while the right fist circles upward (slightly higher than the left elbow). The eyes follow the turning of the body, looking level ahead and attending to the movement of the two hands (see the first figure at the right-hand side of this page).

图 121
Turn the Body and Swing the Fist: the body continuing to turn right, the right fist circling upward, the left palm coming down outside the right forearm level with the right elbow

3. The right foot comes down forward (slightly to the right), toes pointing forward, touching down heel first, and at the same time the right fist swings out forward. As the centre of gravity shifts onto the right leg and gradually comes entirely flat, the right leg bows and the left leg pushes, the left heel pivoting on the ground, forming a right bow stance. At the same time the body continues to turn right and the right fist, with the turning of the body, continues to arc down and swing out, then is drawn back to the side of the waist, the fist's centre facing up; the left palm continues to circle past the left side of the chest and pushes forward above the inside of the right forearm. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must first attend to the right fist's swing out and then to the left palm's forward push (see the second and third figures at the right-hand side of this page).

图 122A
Turn the Body and Swing the Fist: the right foot coming down forward, the right fist swinging out forward
图 122B
Turn the Body and Swing the Fist: the right leg bowing and the left leg pushing to form a right bow stance, the left palm pushing forward above the inside of the right forearm
Book page 114

III. Key Points

III. Key Points

1. "The thousand changes and ten thousand transformations are moved by me; the two feet of the lower body fix the foundation." If the foundation is not stable, one cannot keep one's balance. Therefore the right leg, in stepping out, must be placed slightly to the right; the two feet must on no account stand on one line, which would make the body sway. Hence one must make the lower body firm in order to gain freedom in the upper body.

2. The right toes must point straight ahead; they must not splay outward or turn in, for the direction the toes point bears on how far the hip roots are opened and on the amount of exertion. If the right toes turn in, then the opening of the hip roots is affected, the two hip roots form a pinched inverted V, and the body too will be off to the left instead of facing squarely forward.

3. As the waist and hips turn, the left foot must be turned in with the turning; that is, turn the foot as you turn the body. The boxing theory says "the lord is in the waist" and also "the waist is the axle of the cart, the breath like the wheel". The waist, then, is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body; if the central axis does not bend, the body will not sway.

4. When turning the waist the buttocks must not protrude but be drawn in — this is "drawing in the buttocks". If the waist is not drawn in and not upright, the buttocks easily protrude, and this adversely affects both "the spirit threading through the crown" and "strength issuing from the spine".

5. The movements of the two hands must be "clear". The right hand uses a fist, the left hand uses a palm, and the right hand's stay at the front of the left ribs is temporary (held for a moment). It swings out in the instant of seeming to stop and not stopping; after swinging out there is still a sinking energy — this is the plucking energy used in secret. The left hand closes and guards in front of the left forehead, then arcs downward and strikes out from in front of the left chest. When the two hands circle, the left hand is outside and the right fist inside. All these movements must be clearly understood from the application and must not be left vague.

6. The right leg is lifted and steps straight forward; do not draw it back close to the left ankle and then step across.

Book page 115

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. When the left foot turns in and the body turns, the body must be straight, the posture steady, the left leg solid and the right leg empty; otherwise one is unstable and cannot make the attacking and defending movements.

2. The movements must be linked without a break. Each movement is at the point of seeming to stop and not stopping; the breath moves gradually and the inner energy is then poured in fully. The opportunity for the next posture arises of itself. Therefore, although the direction the body faces is changing, the movements of hands and feet must be unbroken.

3. The left foot must turn in fully (past 90°); otherwise, when the right leg steps forward (toward west), the crotch opens too wide, which makes the left leg's support unstable and the direction in which the right leg lands hard to control — not only awkward, but losing the bracing strength behind.

4. During the turn one must not tense and exert force; it should be "use intent, not force". Tai chi chuan must be practised from looseness into softness; attend to relaxing the waist — do not press down hard on it, lest it hinder the freedom of the waist's rotation.

5. The fist that swings out must not swing too wide or too narrow. Too wide easily raises the shoulder and makes the movement slack; too narrow does not meet the requirement of the application.

V. Errors Easily Committed, Their Causes, and Their Correction

1. Error: the movement pauses after turning right. The main causes are: ① the left foot is turned in without the waist leading it, so the turning is awkward and the attention is on the leg, which causes the upper body's movement to pause. ② the right fist's temporary stay at the left ribs is not deeply understood — that in the midst of seeming to stop and not stopping, the right fist immediately circles up and swings out. Often, after the two hands have arrived in position, all movement stops and only the right leg's drawing back remains. ③ a shallow understanding of the pattern of continuous liveliness and symmetrical coordination. Correction: as the body turns and the left foot turns in, with the left hand guarding above and the right hand staying temporarily at the left ribs, the body turns right without pause and the two hands circle — at the same time the right foot lifts. Do it unbrokenly.

图 123A
Turn the Body and Swing the Fist: the left foot turning in and the body turning, the right fist staying temporarily at the left ribs, the left hand guarding above in front of the forehead
图 123B
Turn the Body and Swing the Fist: the body turning right without pause, the right foot lifting as the two hands circle

2. Error: the two hands lift the elbows. The main cause is that the left shoulder uses force and the right elbow leaves the ribs. Correction: the elbows must always be slightly bent and carry a sinking energy. When the left hand is raised to the front of the left corner of the forehead the elbow ends up higher than the shoulder, but the inner energy of the elbow is still falling and sinking. If the elbow point is raised, that is a lifting energy, and it does not accord with tai chi chuan's "sink the shoulders and drop the elbows". If the right elbow lifts, the ribs are exposed and are easily attacked. Lifting the elbows inevitably hinders the sinking of the shoulders and also affects the sinking of the breath.

3. Error: after the turn, the right leg is drawn back and then steps out too far. The main cause is a shallow experience of the application. Correction: it should be lifted slightly and at once step forward, so that when the right fist swings out and meets the opponent's arm, and sinking energy is used, there is firm support.

4. Error: when the left hand strikes forward it is not hand-arrives-with-foot-arrives; usually the right leg has already formed the bow stance while the left palm is still extending forward. The main cause is a shallow understanding of "when one part moves, no part is still; when one part is still, no part moves" and "within going forward there must be a bracing behind". Correction: when the hand and fist are striking forward and applying force, there must be firm support from the left leg. When the left palm arrives, that is precisely when the bow stance is completed — hand arrives, foot arrives — and this meets the requirement of combat. When body, hands and leg go forward, the inner energy turns up from the crotch, passes through the spine and back and shoots straight out through the palm and fingers, and the waist and the spine's gate of life must brace behind; the palm presses forward with far-reaching intent and long energy, while the back of the hand still has the intent of drawing in and bracing behind. If the foot has arrived while the hand is still moving, this does not accord with the principle of upper and lower accompanying each other; hence the hand must arrive when the foot arrives.

5. Error: protruding the buttocks while turning the body and the foot in. The main cause is failure to attend to drawing the buttocks in, the waist not being relaxed, sunk and upright. Correction: one must "draw in the buttocks" — that is, not stick the buttocks out but draw them in naturally. This stabilises the lower end of the spine, helps increase the spine's flexibility and the elasticity of the back muscles, and prevents the back from being bent and crooked.

Book page 116

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods

1. Focused broken-down practice: ① after turning the body (toward south), check the degree of the foot's turning in, whether the buttocks are protruded, and the position of the two hands. ② after continuing to turn the body (toward west), the place where the right foot lands and the circling movement of the two hands. ③ the coordination of the left palm's forward strike with the bow stance.

2. The demonstration should also include a front-facing mirror demonstration, for with the back to — the learner cannot see the teacher's arm movements, especially the right arm; when the two arms circle, one should also demonstrate one arm at a time separately, and finally the two hands circling together. This makes it easier for the learner to understand.

3. Mnemonic: turn the foot in after first loosening the hips; the right fist and left palm come together; face south, then turn west; the right swings out, the left palm issues.

4. First practise the direction and the positions of the hands' and feet's movements, and only then learn "looseness" and "evenness", so that the movement has neither fast nor slow, nor pauses.

5. Paired practice using the application: A — takes up the settled posture of Fan Through the Back. B — strikes straight from behind A. A — turns the body and turns the foot in, lifts the right foot and steps forward (toward west), the right fist swings out and meets B's hand, sits firmly at the side of the right ribs with sinking energy, and drives the left palm quickly at B's face. The two exchange roles, experiencing the swing, the sink and the strike.

6. Practise repeatedly the turning of the body and the turning in of the foot, to raise the quality of the straight body and the "drawing in of the buttocks".

7. Practise repeatedly the support on the left leg, with the right leg lifting lightly and stepping out slowly, to raise the left leg's capacity to bear the body's weight and thereby strengthen the constitution.

8. Practise the arm movements repeatedly. When the right fist swings out, attend to using the elbow as the axis, not the shoulder. Using the shoulder as the axis draws too large an arc and produces "scattering". When the two arms circle, be clear that the left hand is outside and the right fist inside.

Book page 118

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. The swinging-body fist is an attack-and-defence method against a strike from behind: turning the body and swinging the fist dissolves and defends, and the issuing of the palm is used to attack.

2. The left foot turns as the solid leg, which makes high demands on relaxing the waist and hips. If one cannot let the waist lead the movements of hands and feet, one will stick the buttocks out and lower the head and bend the waist. Hence the demands on the turning of the solid left leg are very high.

3. Under the guidance of intent, the movement is required to be light and unhurried, neither slow nor rushed, and throughout the course of the movement to keep the posture correct everywhere, so that the movement is correct: above, the two arms are linked, and below, the two legs accompany each other. Only then does the turning avoid stiffness and slackness.

4. After turning the body to the rear, the right fist is placed at the left ribs and the left hand closes and guards the left corner of the forehead; there must be a closing energy and a sense of guarding. In the previous posture, Fan Through the Back, the right ribs are exposed — if the opponent attacks from behind he will strike either the ribs or the head. So in turning the body hurriedly without knowing his intent, one hand guarding the forehead and one hand's fist staying at the ribs (in fact the right elbow guarding the ribs) meets the requirements of combat and also the requirements of opening and closing and of storing the posture. Therefore the two hands must on no account be dropped at random. Once moved, one must concentrate wholly and continually use intent to guide the correctness, continuity and roundness of every movement. Throughout the movement, the opening and closing, the solid and empty, and the turning and changing of the inner and the outer must seek upper and lower accompanying each other, inner and outer as one, intent arriving and energy arriving, and every movement in accord with method.

5. When the right fist swings out, what position should the right foot be in for it to be reasonable? There are generally two: one is that the right foot has been lifted but not yet stepped out and the right fist has already swung out — this is a mere form and is empty, because on one leg's support neither the swing nor the sink has any power. The second is that the right knee has already bowed out while the right fist has not finished swinging — by then one is already too close to the opponent, which is unfavourable to sinking, one cannot use the whole body's strength, and the left palm's strike is powerless. Therefore the correct way is: when the right fist swings out the right foot has already stepped out, and when the left palm issues the right knee has just bowed into place — hand arrives, foot arrives — in accord with the requirement of the application.

6. "Looseness". If the movement is practised badly, especially at the moment of turning the body, turning the foot in, lifting the leg and stepping, one tenses very easily. In practising tai chi chuan the whole body must loosen, without a hair's-breadth of clumsy force to stagnate in the sinews, bones and blood in between, binding oneself; only then can one change lightly and nimbly and turn freely and smoothly, with breath and blood flowing, poured through day after day and circulating the whole body — which is of the greatest benefit to improving health.

Twenty-sixth Posture: Step Up and Grasp the Bird's Tail (Shang Bu Lan Que Wei)

I. Application

The same as the third posture, Grasp the Bird's Tail.

II. Course of the Movement

The body gradually turns left, the left toes splay outward and press flat, and the centre of gravity gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg, while the right leg is lifted and brought forward; at the same time the left elbow sinks as it draws back to the left, naturally carrying the left palm in an arc to in front of the left side of the chest; the right fist changes to a palm, goes from the front downward, and scoops in an arc to the left to in front of the abdomen, rotating outward as it scoops so that the palm turns to face slantingly up-left and joins with the left hand, both arms forming arcs. The eyes attend slightly to the left forearm, then turn to look level ahead in front of the right arm (see the figures on this and the following two pages — the same as the plates of the third posture).

The remaining movements are the same as the third posture, Grasp the Bird's Tail (except the left ward-off). (This page is a full-page plate sheet with no running text. The nine photographs below are the continuous illustration of the movements of Step Up and Grasp the Bird's Tail.)

Twenty-eighth Posture: Wave Hands Like Clouds (Yun Shou)

Book page 123

I. Application

I. Application

Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent attacks my chest or ribs with his right hand from the right of my front, I immediately lower my right hand with the palm facing inward, and join the upper side of my wrist (the radial side) to the lower side of the opponent's wrist (the ulnar side), warding from the left upward and rotating to the right; then I turn it downward and move it across to the left, drawing one great circle, like white clouds drifting in the sky, without a break. The left hand at the same time lowers, palm facing down, with the same intent as the right hand. The body also turns with the right wrist, and the gaze follows the wrist, attending as it turns.

the hand and chest turning, the gaze following the wrist as it turns, attending as it turns.

The right foot moves half a step to the left from the right rear side and settles firmly, and the left foot at once steps out one step to the left, the weight shifting left into a horse-riding stance (for an instant). At this moment the two hands have arrived exactly opposite the chest and navel, and then the right foot again becomes empty and moves half a step further in to the left, and the second movement continues. But when changing from empty to full and back in the interwoven turning, there must never be any intent of concavity, convexity, interruption or discontinuity. The subtle use of this posture lies entirely in turning the waist and hips: because the turning can draw along the opponent's root strength, one turns the hand out in response. The learner should savour and grasp this carefully.

The slanting application: when the opponent thrusts straight in with his right palm or right fist, I ward with my right hand, and at the same time immediately hollow the chest and sink onto the back leg, turning the waist and sinking downward to neutralize the force of his incoming energy; then I may use Shoulder or Elbow, or attack out with Press.

Book page 124

II. The Course of the Movement

II. The Course of the Movement

1. Turn the waist slightly to the right without changing the weight; turn the left toes inward and set them down firmly, toes pointing forward. At the same time the left palm, following the turning of the body, bends the arm slightly and sinks the elbow, palm facing down, and moves naturally and very slightly to the right. The right hook hand changes into a palm and arcs down from the right, moving across horizontally at the bottom of the arc to the front of the right abdomen. The gaze attends to the right palm as it moves down (see the first figure at the right-hand side of this page, the second figure at the right-hand side of this page).

2. The weight gradually shifts entirely to the left leg; the right foot lifts and draws in towards the left (the heel leaving the ground first), the body turns slightly left, and the left palm follows the waist's turning. At the same time it transports out to the left (with a slight arc), and as the arm turns inward the wrist is held upright so that the palm slopes downward and gradually turns to face down. The right palm, following the turning of the body, travels in an arc from the lower right across the front of the abdomen to the left, and as it travels the arm turns outward so that the palm faces inward, and it gradually travels up to the left to near the left wrist. The gaze shifts as the body turns, looking level ahead, and it must attend to the right palm travelling left (see the third figure at the right-hand side of this page).

图 149
Wave Hands Like Clouds: the right hand changing from the hook hand into a palm and arcing down from the right to the front of the right abdomen
图 150
Wave Hands Like Clouds: the left palm bending the arm and sinking the elbow as the body turns, palm facing down and shifting slightly right
图 151
Wave Hands Like Clouds: the right palm travelling in an arc across the front of the abdomen to the left, arriving near the left wrist

3. The left leg continues to squat down and "sends" the right leg down (the right foot half a step towards the left), the toes touching the ground first, and as the weight gradually shifts right the whole foot is set down firmly; the two feet are about a shoulder's width apart, parallel and facing forward, and the left foot at once becomes empty. At the same time the body turns slightly right. The right palm, following the waist's turning, travels in an arc from the left upward and to the right (the fingers level with the shoulder), the palm still facing inward. This is joining the upper side of my right wrist to the lower side of the opponent's wrist, rotating from the left downward and then upward again, using the strength of the turning waist and hips to turn out to the right, so as to draw along the opponent's root strength. The left palm at the same time arcs down from the left and towards the right, and as it travels the arm turns slightly outward so that the palm gradually turns to face inward (slanting slightly upward). The two hands have travelled up and down to exactly opposite the chest and navel, the right hand above and the left hand below. The gaze accompanies the turning of the body, attending to the right palm travelling right (see the first figure at the left-hand side of this page).

4. The weight gradually shifts entirely to the right leg; the left foot lifts (the heel leaving the ground first) and the body continues to turn slightly right, and at the same time the right palm, following the turning of the body, arcs to the right and downward, and as it travels the arm turns inward so that the palm gradually turns to face down. The left palm, crossing the front of the abdomen, continues to travel to the upper right, drawing near to the right wrist to the right. The gaze attends to the right palm travelling right (see the second figure at the left-hand side of this page).

5. Repeat from the start of movement two. The left foot strides half a step across to the left, the toes touching the ground first, and as the weight gradually shifts left the whole foot is set down firmly, toes pointing forward; at the same time the body gradually turns left, and the left palm, following the turning of the body, continues from the right upward past the face (the fingers level with the eyebrows), travelling to the left. This is joining the upper side of my left wrist to the lower side of the opponent's wrist, rotating from the left downward and then upward again, using the strength of the turning waist and hips to turn out to the left, so as to draw along the opponent's root strength (the application is the same as for the right hand). The right palm continues to travel in an arc from the right downward and to the left, and as it travels the arm turns slightly outward so that the palm gradually turns to face inward (slanting slightly upward) and travels to the front of the abdomen. The two hands have travelled up and down to exactly opposite the chest and navel, the left hand above and the right hand below. The gaze shifts as the body turns, looking level, and must attend to the left palm travelling left (see the third figure at the left-hand side of this page, the fourth figure at the left-hand side of this page).

6. The weight gradually shifts entirely to the left leg; the right foot lifts to the right and towards towards the left (the heel leaving the ground first), while the body continues to turn left and the left palm continues to travel in an arc from above, downward to the left. As it travels the arm turns inward so that the palm gradually turns to face down. The right palm, following the turning of the body, continues across the front of the abdomen to the left, and travels in an arc from below upward to near the left wrist. 7. Repeat the movement: the three plates at the foot of the next page repeat, in order, the third, first and second plates at the sides of this page.

In order to increase the amount of exercise, "Wave Hands Like Clouds" may also be done as three, five, or seven movements.

But the number must be odd, and "Step Back and Repulse the Monkey" must likewise be done three, five, or seven times accordingly. Otherwise, when one comes to the closing and gathering up, one will not be able to return to the original place.

Book page 126

III. Essential Points

III. Essential Points

1. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" requires unbroken continuity, with intent and without force. One "Wave Hands Like Clouds" must follow another, endlessly continuous, going round and round without end. What the boxing treatises say — "like the long Yangtze and the great sea, rolling on and on without cease, threaded through as one breath" — means exactly that there must be no place of pause in the middle of the movement.

2. The two feet must not be double-weighted — that is, the two feet must not bear the body's weight on the ground at the same time. As soon as the heel of the descending foot has set down firmly, the other foot's heel must immediately leave the ground, rising and falling in turn like a see-saw, so that the two feet alternate without ever pausing.

3. The circling of the hands must take the turning of the waist and hips as its foundation: the waist is like an axle, the four limbs like wheels. The waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower body, and it plays the principal role in the changes of the whole body's movement, in adjusting and steadying the centre of gravity, and in driving the jin power out to every part of the limbs. Therefore the turning must take the waist and spine as its axis and turn slowly; one must not swing about at random, the upper body must not lean or slant, must not stoop forward or lean back, and one must maintain "the tailbone centred and upright."

图 156

图 158

图 159

图 160

图 161
Wave Hands Like Clouds: the two hands travelling until level with the chest and navel, the left hand above and the right below (the same as figure 155).

4. The two arms must travel with the waist: turning left, the left hand's upward scooping leads; turning right, the right hand's upward scooping leads. When the left hand leads, the right hand follows; when the right hand leads, the left hand follows — one up, one down, one left, one right, closely coordinated better still.

Twenty-ninth Posture: Single Whip (Continuing from the twenty-seventh posture, Single Whip; both the application and the course of the movement are identical.) (See the figures on the following pages.)

circling without scattering or stagnating; when the turn reaches the top the elbow must not lift, and the forearm must ward loosely and keep circling. The two arms must maintain their arcs.

5. There must be "evenness from form to form". When the left leg steps out the movement must be slow and set down lightly; when the right leg lifts it must rise slowly and draw in towards the left, to a shoulder's width, and must not be sometimes fast and sometimes slow.

6. Every movement of Yang-style Taijiquan is constituted by a circle — hence the saying, "a marvellous hand is one movement, and one movement is a taiji." Within this circle are contained the two forces of yin and yang: there must be softness and there must be firmness, emptiness and fullness, firmness and softness assisting each other, emptiness and fullness interpenetrating. The carrying out of its movements always has the appearance of drawing circles and travelling along arcs; it never goes straight out and straight back — this too is a characteristic of Taijiquan. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" is a typical movement of this kind, and it plays an important part in raising the standard of the techniques of "continuous adhering and following" and "drawing in to make the opponent fall into emptiness."

Book page 128

IV. Requirements

IV. Requirements

1. The circling of the hands must be led by the waist, and the waist and hands must not come apart. When the opponent uses his right hand to strike my chest or ribs from the right of my front, my right wrist receives his wrist, turning up and over from below, to the left and then to the right; this must be coordinated with the turning of the waist and hips for the power to be obtained.

2. The two feet stand parallel, about a shoulder's width apart, neither too wide nor too narrow, and the two feet must not turn into the inward splay or the outward splay. The feet are the foundation of the stance forms and the stepping methods; if the foundation is unsteady, then at the least deviation the stance forms and stepping methods are certain to go awry.

(This page carries one unnumbered push-hands photograph at the foot; it has no figure number and no caption.)

3. There must be no double-weighting, for double-weighting makes one sluggish. The left foot supports while the right foot lifts and draws in towards the left; when the right foot squats down and the right heel drops, the left heel must lift at the same moment, otherwise it is double-weighting.

4. When the two arms circle they must not be straightened but must form an arc, and the distance from the body must be appropriate. If the arms are too far from the body they will be strained straight; if too close they will "deflate".

5. The two hands must have ward-off jin; they must not go slack, but neither may they use stiff force.

6. The movements must be continuous — this is the requirement of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" that stands out most. The circling of the hands must be like white clouds moving across the sky, without a break.

7. The shoulders must be relaxed, but not relaxed to excess such that they become "empty" or "loose".

8. The hand circling below must embody the action requirement of "scooping".

Book page 129

V. Common Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

V. Common Faults, Their Causes, and How to Correct Them

1. Fault: "double-weighting", that is, the two feet bearing the weight at the same time. The principal cause is an insufficient grasp of the clear division of empty and full. "When one side is heavy it follows; when double-weighted it is sluggish. One constantly sees those with several years of pure practice who cannot transform, and in every case they end up being controlled by others: the fault of double-weighting has not been understood." Therefore one foot must be on the ground bearing the whole body's weight, so that the empty foot can be light, nimble and lively. Correction: as the right heel sets down, the left heel must leave the ground at the same moment.

2. Fault: the foot moves sideways while the two hands move up and down, and the beginner's body tends to keep facing straight forward (south) without the waist and hips turning. The principal cause is that the movements of the limbs do not take the waist as their guiding principle and as their hub. If the waist is used properly it helps both to maintain the balance of the whole body and to keep the circulation of internal jin full and concentrated. Otherwise, the movement that moves the hands without moving the waist is a tree without roots, and internal jin cannot travel from the waist and spine out to the limbs — whereas the whole subtle use of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" lies in turning the waist and hips. Otherwise, when my wrist joins the opponent's wrist and turns up and over, it will appear powerless. But the waist must not turn too far either: some turn the waist and hips so much that they reach 90°, almost turning to due east or due west, and thus the body and limbs are thus overdone, which on the contrary gives the opponent a chance to attack. Correction: as the two hands and waist and hips turn the body, it is best to take an oblique angle a little to the east, or towards the south-west.

3. Fault: the two feet turning into the inward or outward splay. The principal cause of the inward splay of the two feet is that when the left foot steps out sideways the heel is pressed out too far; the outward splay comes from the left foot stepping out to the left without the heel pressing slightly outward, while the right foot, drawing in to the left, is not properly set straight. The direction the toes point governs how far the hip joints open and how great the amount of exercise is; therefore the outward turning and inward drawing of the toes, and the leftward and rightward turning of the heels, must all be clear and orderly in their empty and full, principal and subordinate. Correction: in "Wave Hands Like Clouds" the toes of both feet should point straight forward. Take special care that when the left foot steps out to the left, after the ball of the foot has landed you must let the left heel gradually press out towards the left, pressing and setting down as you go until the whole sole is firmly planted; in this way the toes will point straight forward and the requirement of the two feet being parallel will be met.

4. Fault: the movement is uneven, sometimes fast and sometimes slow, which is especially obvious when the left foot is about to land after stepping out to the left and when the right foot has just lifted. The principal cause is that when the strength of the legs and of the waist and hips is insufficient the speed suddenly increases, and thus the whole movement becomes uneven in pace. The movement must, within its continuous and threaded arc, be complete and rounded, neither hurried nor sluggish, neither concave nor convex, with no defects and no sharp corners. The changes must be light, nimble and lively, so that emptiness and fullness can interchange and turn. Correction: practise more to strengthen the leg power step by step, and take care that when the left leg steps out the right leg is set solid, and when the right leg lifts the left leg is set solid; only when empty and full are clearly divided can the movement be light and nimble.

Book page 130

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

VI. Teaching Method and Practice Method

1. Explain the essential points. 2. Demonstrate the movement; demonstrate the application. 3. First practise it broken down; then immediately follow with whole-movement practice, alternating fast practice and slow practice. 4. The two hands hang loosely. The two feet stand a shoulder's width apart, in a half squat. The left foot lifts and steps out to the left, and the weight gradually shifts onto the left foot. The right leg lifts and draws in to the left, setting down at a shoulder's width; the weight gradually shifts onto the right foot, the left foot lifts and steps out to the left … practise in this continuous way to master the leg movements well — empty and full, the two feet parallel and pointing forward, the centre of gravity not rising and falling, and so on.

5. The two feet stand a shoulder's width apart, in a slight squat, the right hand above and the left hand below. The left hand moves in an arc from below to the right, upward and to the left, while the right hand turns its palm outward and moves from the right downward, turning the palm inward and travelling across the front of the abdomen to the left (palm facing inward). Immediately afterwards the left palm turns outward, and from the left it turns downward and inward and travels across the front of the abdomen to the right, while the right hand goes upward and to the right. At this moment the two hands are again one above and one below in front of the body, returning to the starting position — that is, one movement of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" is completed. Practise continuously in this way to master the hand movements well — the path of the hands, the direction the palms face, the height of the hands, when to turn the palm, and so on.

6. Whole-movement practice must follow on closely, otherwise a split will form; one should follow the teacher's movements at a slower pace, one movement at a time, and so learn.

7. The improvement of empty and full may be undertaken once whole-movement practice is basically mastered. The left leg is set solid and the right leg lifts; when the right leg, having drawn in to the left, is about to land, the left leg must "send" the right leg down. When the left leg steps out to the left, the right leg must be firmly set solid, and the weight must not be moved before the left heel has landed.

Book page 131

VII. Technical Analysis

VII. Technical Analysis

1. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" should be performed as 3–5 continuous movements. Its distinguishing feature is "unbroken connection", threaded through movement after movement, so that at the moment of seeming to stop and not stopping, the opportunity for the next movement arises of itself. Therefore there must be no place of pause; the inside and outside, above and below, left and right, front and back must be coordinated as one, so that above and below follow each other and "one breath runs through". For this reason the movement of "Wave Hands Like Clouds" must be continuous, rounded and lively.

2. "Wave Hands Like Clouds" makes high demands on the two hands: it requires that "the whole movement depend on the two hands turning without leaving the centre line." The left hand governs the left half of the body and the right hand the right half, with the nose and navel as the centre line between them, so that even in the circular turning the movement does not leave the centre line. The arms must be relaxed, soft, rounded and lively, with firmness and softness assisting each other; they must rotate along arcs — across and straight, with and against, rising and falling, extending and withdrawing must all travel along curved lines — and they must turn with the waist and hips, and the two hands must not be allowed to go slack.

3. This movement should be done 3–5 times, and throughout those 3–5 movements the frame must not be sometimes high and sometimes low — that is, the centre of gravity must not rise and fall. The stepping out of the feet and the lifting of the right leg must both be light and nimble, and this requires that throughout the whole movement the centre of gravity stay always on one level, without rising or falling. If the centre of gravity rises and falls, it will lead to uneven pace in the movement.

attend to the gradual change when empty and full interchange.

4. The gaze in "Wave Hands Like Clouds": the beginner tends to watch the palm as it turns, which is of course wrong. But some simply look straight ahead, which is also wrong: the method of the eyes is to follow the movement of the principal hand while looking level ahead. The gaze must first look ahead in the direction one is intending to go, and then the body method, hand method and step method follow.

I. Application

The body continues to turn slightly right, and the weight gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg; the left leg lifts. At the same time the right palm, following the turning of the body, extends slightly to the right oblique, and as it extends the arm turns inward so that the palm gradually turns to face down, and the five fingers droop and gather together to form the hook hand; the left palm continues to travel to the upper right, drawing near the right wrist. The gaze attends to the right palm travelling right, and attends to the left palm travelling left (see the figure at the right-hand side of this page).

The movements that follow are the same as movement four of the fourth posture, "Single Whip"; see the three figures in the bottom row of this page (the same as the plates of the fourth posture).

The essential points and so on are all the same as those of the fourth posture.
