Posture Seventy-Two — High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm

Posture Seventy-Two — High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm

I. Application The application of the first part is the same as High Pat on the Horse. In the second part, while my extended right hand is being held by the opponent's left hand, I immediately draw the right hand back with the centre of the palm facing down, and the left hand, raised slightly, threads through with the palm and thrusts at the opponent's throat, while the right hand remains hidden below the left elbow, ready to meet any change.

II. Sequence of movement (a) The movement of High Pat on the Horse is the same as Posture Thirty, High Pat on the Horse. See the second to the fourth figures on this page (the same as the hundred-and-seventieth to the hundred-and-seventy-second figures).

(b) Threading Palm, Left 1. The right leg gradually crouches, and the left leg is lifted and drawn back. At the same time the right arm gradually bends at the elbow and lies across, the arm curved, and is drawn in with a downward-left arc; as it is drawn in the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns to face upward; the left palm gradually turns palm-upward and threads up above the right palm. The eyes look level ahead (see the fifth figure on this page).

2. The left foot steps forward one pace, the heel touching first; as the weight gradually shifts onto the left leg the whole of the sole presses down firmly, the left leg bends and the right leg presses out to form the left bow stance. At the same time the left hand continues to thread forward and upward; as the left forearm passes above the right palm, the right arm immediately rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns to face down, and the right palm comes to rest below the upper left arm, while the left palm threads out above the right palm, its centre still facing up, at the height of the chin. The gaze attends to the right palm as it is drawn in, and then to the left palm as it threads forward (see the sixth figure on this page).

III. Key points 1. When the left leg steps forward the right leg must crouch, so that the left leg takes a somewhat larger step. This both achieves the martial effect and increases the amount of exercise.

2. As the left palm threads through and the bow stance is about to form, the body turns slightly right in coordination.

3. When stepping, the upper body must be centred and upright, not leaning forward. The body method of taijiquan must be nimble, relaxed and calm, but it is not permitted to drop the head forward or to bend the trunk forward.

4. The step must be set down nimbly; strive to "step as a cat walks". Therefore, as the left leg steps forward, the right leg must "sink" and "send" the left leg forward; otherwise the step will easily become tense.

图 437
The opening of High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm: the two hands spread apart front and back, the right hand extends forward and the left hand is drawn in beside the left waist, and the weight sits back.
图 438
The High Pat on the Horse movement: the right hand extends forward to the front of the chest, the left hand is drawn in beside the left waist, and the body is centred and upright.
图 439
The settled High Pat on the Horse: the right palm reaches forward at shoulder level, the left palm is drawn in beside the left waist, and the left leg is forward in the empty stance.

…forward; otherwise the step will easily become tense.

5. When the left palm threads out, the right arm must be curved and a space must be kept at the right armpit; it must not be clamped shut. Otherwise, on the one hand the posture will look awkward and fail to meet the requirement of roundness everywhere; on the other hand, the right hand under the armpit is there to meet changes, and if it is clamped shut it will lose its roundness and liveliness and its usefulness in meeting change will be reduced.

IV. Requirements 1. Although the lower limbs are changing step, "the hundred meetings and the central pole, one breath running through" must still be achieved; do not lean forward or backward.

2. The movements must be continuous without pause. When High Pat on the Horse has reached its position, immediately perform the threading palm; the two movements must not be separated but must be "unbroken as a thread".

V. Common errors, their causes, and how to correct them 1. Error: the threading arm is fully straightened. Straightening tenses the muscles, which makes the force excessive and the movement sluggish. The main cause is generally that the hand is thrust out with too much force, or that one subjectively wants the hand to reach farther, supposing that a thrust must strike home. The Boxing Treatises say that the principle is originally "give up yourself and follow others", but many mistakenly "give up the near and seek the far". The so-called difference of a hair's breadth leads to an error of a thousand miles. Therefore over-extending is harmful. Correction: leave a margin when the hand goes out, and keep the arm slightly curved when threading the palm.

2. Error: when the left foot steps, the right leg does not crouch, or crouches very little, and only the body's centre of gravity moves forward so that the left leg steps forward. The main cause is that the application is not deeply understood. Because the right hand I have extended is being held and gripped, a crouch gives the withdrawing right arm a sinking strength which can draw the opponent along, and I then thread the left palm straight through to the opponent's throat. Moreover, in form practice High Pat on the Horse is one of the few movements that bring the body to standing. For this reason, when threading the palm one should return to practising the form in the half-crouched state, so as to train and strengthen the legs. Correction: from the very start of the threading palm the right leg must crouch.

3. Error: upper and lower are disconnected, so that when threading the palm either the hand arrives first or the foot arrives first. The main cause is that the application is not deeply understood. For the issuing of strength there must be a root: the strength starts from the heel, is governed by the waist, is issued from the legs, and takes form in the fingers. If hand and foot are disconnected, from where will the strength start, and how will it reach? Correction: the thrust of the hand necessarily requires the supporting coordination of waist and legs; in practice strive to have the hand arrive when the foot arrives, and take particular care that the bowing leg does not move too fast.

图 440
The threading palm in transition: the right arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns to face upward, and the left palm turns palm-upward and threads up above the right palm.
图 441
The left foot steps forward, the left palm continues to thread forward, and the right palm comes to rest below the upper left arm.
图 442A
The settled threading palm: the left bow stance, the left palm threaded forward at the height of the chin, and the right palm resting below the upper left arm, the eyes looking straight ahead.

…coordination of waist and legs; in practice strive to have the hand arrive when the foot arrives, and take particular care that the bowing leg does not move too fast.

4. Error: threading and striking are not clearly distinguished, so that the left hand first goes up and then down. The main cause is a failure to understand the application. The threading palm thrusts at the opponent's throat; striking downward can only hit the chest. Correction: the palm must thread up along a downward-slanting line; it must not arc downward to strike.

VI. Teaching and practice methods 1. Mnemonic: at High Pat on the Horse the hand is held; bend the right leg and draw the right palm back; step the left leg nimbly forward; the left threading palm goes straight to the throat.

2. Constantly sharpen the distinction of empty and full. In the first half, when the Single Whip joins High Pat on the Horse, as the left foot is drawn back the right leg must be settled firm and the left leg lifted lightly; take care that the centre of gravity moves back, that the upper body does not lean forward, and that the left foot is not drawn back scraping the ground. When threading the palm, take care to settle the right leg firm so that the left leg steps forward nimbly. In teaching, observe and correct repeatedly so that the weight moves onto the supporting point and empty and full are clearly distinguished.

3. The learner should frequently and repeatedly practise the half-crouch position of the right leg, and the stepping forward and drawing back of the left leg, and may also alternate the legs, in order to feel empty and full and strengthen the legs.

4. Paired practice using the application: A — assumes the settled High Pat on the Horse; B — holds A's right hand with the left hand; A — crouches the right leg, draws the right hand back, steps the left leg forward and threads out the left palm; B — retreats slightly. In practice the teacher should explain the meaning and requirements of each detail of the movement, so that the learning becomes vivid.

5. So that beginners may simplify the movements while learning, they may learn with the hand still and the foot moving, or with the foot still and the hand moving, so that it is easier to watch and to imitate; but having once made clear the separate parts of hand and foot, they must immediately practise the hand and foot moving together. In this way they learn quickly and yet do not fall into disconnection and ruin of the movements.

VII. Technical analysis In High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm, attention must be paid to nimbleness; if the body is sluggish one cannot advance or retreat at ease. Therefore the body must be nimble: no sooner has the opponent's force touched my skin than my intention has already entered his very bones.

图 442B
The settled threading palm from another angle: the left bow stance, the left palm threaded forward and the right palm resting below the upper left arm, the body centred and upright, the eyes looking straight ahead.

Posture Seventy-Three — the Cross-Shaped Leg

Posture Seventy-Three — the Cross-Shaped Leg

I. Application Continuing from the previous posture. If an opponent strikes across at me with his right hand from behind on my right, I quickly turn my body toward the right rear as I roll and turn, and at the same time the left arm turns up and bends back; as it embraces the right arm one above the other, I quickly separate the two hands forward and back to bar the opponent's hand. At the same time I quickly lift the right leg and thrust the heel at the opponent's right ribs; the opponent will then certainly fall back with the kick.

Note: In Master Yang Chengfu's book The Complete Book of Taijiquan: Substance and Application, Part One (1933 edition), only one plate of the settled Cross-Shaped Leg posture is given here; no sequence plates are listed, and the original way of practising it was the single swing-lotus leg. The method in this book is the form as finally revised and settled by Yang Chengfu, which has long been in wide circulation, and it is therefore taken as the final settled form of the present time. So that readers may understand something of the original way of practising it, it is described as follows:

After the left threading palm, the left toes turn inward and press down firmly, the body gradually turns right, and the weight gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg. At the same time the left palm, with the elbow bent, moves in an arc to the right past the face with the turn of the body, while the right palm remains below the upper left arm. The body continues to turn right, and the right foot is lifted and swings outward in an arc from left to upper right, the knee naturally slightly bent, the foot no higher than the shoulder, the instep turned somewhat to face right. At the same time the left palm strikes from above rightward and then leftward to meet the right foot.

Another method (a counter):

1. To counter the Cross-Shaped Leg, one may first brush the knee and then attack by other means.

2. To counter the Cross-Shaped Leg, one may also ward upward with the left hand, step the right foot forward, and use the right planting punch to counter it.

II. Sequence of movement 1. The body gradually turns right, the left toes turn inward and press down firmly, the weight gradually shifts entirely onto the left leg, and the right foot is lifted (the heel leaving the ground first). At the same time the left arm bends at the elbow and moves right, the centre of the palm facing inward, and the right palm, passing along the outside of the left arm, joins with the turn of the body to the right; as it joins, the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm turns to face inward, so that the two palms cross in front of the chest. The eyes follow the turn of the body and look level to the right, and the gaze must attend to the two palms embracing (see the first and second figures on this page).

2. The two palms separate to left and right. At the same time the right foot slowly…

图 443
The opening of the Cross-Shaped Leg: the body turns right, the two palms cross in front of the chest, and the right foot is lifted with the heel leaving the ground first.
图 444
The Cross-Shaped Leg in transition: the two palms separate to left and right, and the right foot is lifted and swings outward in an arc from left to upper right.
图 445A
The Cross-Shaped Leg thrust out: the right leg thrusts out to the right front with the heel, the two palms spread to left and right, the body is centred and upright, and the eyes look to the right.

…slowly outward to the right, the toes pointing up; as the right leg thrusts out the left leg gradually straightens, though at the settled posture the knee is still slightly bent. The gaze attends to the right palm as it separates out, and looking level to the right past the right palm (see the first figure on this page, and compare the rear view in figure 210).

III. Key points 1. The waist and hips turn right and the left heel closes in, but the upper body must not lean forward or backward. The coccyx must be held centred, the central axis must not bend, and the turning must not sway, so that the inner strength can reach the nimble, lively use that supports all eight directions.

2. The left hand, following the right turn of waist and hips, moves from left to right in coordination, while the right hand arcs upward from below; the two hands cross and embrace in front of the chest, and must be full, neither loose and scattered nor shrunk.

3. To thrust out the right leg one must first lift the leg and concentrate the strength at the knee joint, stretching the ligaments of the hips (the lifted knee should generally be no lower than hip level); thus the leg can thrust to the ribs and meet the requirement of the application.

4. After the thrust, when the body is supported on the single leg, the body must be upright, with the upper and lower essentially in one line. Chen Xin says, "When the body method is correct the body's pillar is upright, leaning nowhere, containing emptiness and spirit within." Therefore at that moment, from the crown of the head to the perineum, there must always be a vertical line; leaning forward or backward, tilting left or right, all fail the requirement of the body method. This requires the whole body to relax so that the movement and the shifting of waist and legs become harmonious and coordinated.

IV. Requirements 1. The direction must be true. From High Pat on the Horse with Threading Palm facing east, turn the waist and hips and thrust out with the right leg. The direction of the thrust is due west, and the face is also toward the west.

2. The stance must be steady; when thrusting the leg one must not pull the body about and set it askew.

3. The foot must arrive and the hand must arrive.

4. Empty and full must be clear. From the moment the left toes turn inward, the weight shifts onto the left leg, so that the right leg may lift its knee nimbly.

V. Common errors, their causes, and how to correct them 1. Error: when the left foot turns inward, the weight shifts to the right. The main cause is that the application is not deeply understood. The opponent strikes across at me from behind my right; if I shift my weight right as I turn, my body leans right, and I thus deliver myself to be struck. At the same time this hinders a rapid turning of the body, and so increases…

图 445B
The settled single-leg support in profile: after the right leg thrusts out the body is supported on one leg, upper and lower in one line, the two palms spread to left and right, and the waist and hips turned right.

…increases the difficulty of observing the opponent's movements, which is unfavourable for meeting the attack quickly. Moreover, with the weight shifted right the two feet are double-weighted, which is unfavourable for both attack and defence, and because the load on the legs is reduced the benefit of the training is also reduced. Correction: the left foot turns inward, the weight remains on the left foot, the waist and hips turn, and the upper body turns toward the south-west; this then creates favourable conditions for the kick that follows.

2. Error: the two hands cross in front of the chest too tightly and too flat. The main causes are, first, that one attends only to the arcing movement of the left hand and neglects the movement of the right hand, and second, that the application is not sufficiently understood. Tightness and flatness both narrow the protective range of the two hands, making one easy to attack. Correction: attend to fullness, and the right hand must go outward and upward.

3. Error: the direction of the kick is not true. The main cause is generally that the left foot does not turn in enough, so that the direction of the kick leans toward the south-west; secondarily, a failure to understand the application. The opponent attacks from behind my right, so the main direction of my kick should be to the rear, that is, due west. Correction: the key is that the left foot must turn inward by more than 90 degrees; then the right foot's thrust will not only find the true direction easily but will not be awkward.

4. Error: the movement is uneven, sometimes fast and sometimes slow. The main cause is insufficient strength in the legs: the foot turns in quickly, the knee lifts slowly, the kick goes out quickly. Taijiquan is one of the internal martial arts, and it requires "from within to without" and "drawing the within out by the without" in order to raise the benefit of the training; under the guidance of intent it requires that the movements be light and unhurried, neither slow nor hurried. Therefore one must "let the form follow the movement of intent", striving to make inner and outer join, intent and breath link, and to leave no place of interruption or of fast and slow. Correction: the foot must turn in with the turning of the waist, the left foot settling firm, then lift the leg lightly and slowly, and as the left leg gradually rises slowly thrust out the right foot.

VI. Teaching and practice methods 1. The teacher observes the degree of the left foot's inward turn from the south, and the direction of the kick from the west.

2. The emphasis in teaching should be placed on the kicking leg: practise much and repeatedly supporting on the left foot alone and lifting the right leg to kick, in order to strengthen the legs and attain the requirements of steadiness and nimbleness.

VII. Technical analysis 1. In the Cross-Shaped Leg, what defends is the hand and what attacks is the leg; the hand merely bars, and the application lies chiefly in the leg.

2. If the kicking leg is not practised well it is easy to hold the breath. The breathing of Yang-style taijiquan is required to be entirely natural: one should adopt the natural method of breathing — long, even, fine, slow, neither hurried nor sluggish.

Book page 225

Posture Seventy-Four — Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist

Posture Seventy-Four — Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist

I. Application Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent withdraws his hand, I immediately set the right foot down while the left foot advances and the knee bends and settles firm. At this moment, if the opponent again kicks up from below with his right foot, I quickly use my left hand to deflect the opponent's right foot outward past my left knee, and the right hand immediately closes into a fist and strikes (points) at the opponent's groin, the body leaning very slightly forward.

II. Sequence of movement 1. The left leg gradually crouches, the right foot is set down and held suspended, and the body gradually turns right. At the same time the right palm arcs from the right downward, passes in front of the upper abdomen and circles to the left; as it circles the arm rotates inward so that the centre of the palm turns downward; the left palm, too, sinks as the left leg crouches and the body turns right, and arcs forward and upward to the right (see the first figure on this page).

2. The body continues to turn right, and the right foot steps forward and to the right (west by north), the heel touching first; then the right toes swing outward 45 degrees, and as the weight gradually shifts onto the right leg the whole foot presses down firmly. With the turn of the body the right palm moves from the left upward and past the chest to the right; as it moves the arm rotates outward so that the centre of the palm gradually turns downward. The left palm arcs across to the front of the left chest (see the second figure on this page).

3. The weight gradually shifts entirely onto the right leg, and the left foot steps forward from the inner side of the right ankle, the heel touching first, while the body continues to turn slightly right. At the same time the right palm, following the turn, continues right, back and forward in an arc and is drawn in beside the right waist and closed into a fist, while the left palm brushes downward in an arc from front to right and then left. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must attend to the left palm (see the third and fourth figures on this page).

4. The body continues to turn gradually left, and the weight gradually shifts onto the left leg until the whole foot presses down firmly, the left leg bending and the right leg pressing out to form the left bow stance. At the same time the left palm brushes in an arc to the front of the left knee and comes to the side of the left knee, while the right fist is driven forward and down at the height of the abdomen, the body folding slightly at the waist. The eyes look level ahead, and the gaze must attend…

图 446
The opening of Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist: the body turns right, the right palm arcs from the right downward, passes in front of the upper abdomen and circles left, and the left palm accordingly arcs forward.
图 447
The right foot steps forward and to the right; the right palm passes the chest and moves right with its centre turning downward, and the left palm arcs across to the front of the left chest.
图 448
The left foot steps forward from the inner side of the right ankle; the right palm arcs and is drawn in beside the right waist and closed into a fist, and the left palm brushes downward in an arc.

…and the left palm's brushing to the left and the right fist's striking out (see the fifth figure on this page).

III. Key points 1. As the right foot descends there must be a downward "sending" by the left leg (bending the left leg), and attention must be paid to keeping the upper body upright.

2. As the left foot advances, when the waist and hips turn left the left hand's brushing of the knee and the right fist's forward strike must be performed at the same time, with upper and lower, left and right mutually drawing and linking one another, so that the movement is not scattered. If the turn of the body is too great, it will overshoot.

3. The right fist's forward strike must be coordinated with the left leg's bending, the right leg's pressing out and the body's slight forward lean, so that body arrives, hand arrives and step arrives.

IV. Requirements 1. Empty and full must be clear: as the right foot descends the left leg must sink and settle firm.

2. The line of the fist's travel must be correct: it should be slightly curved, driven from the waist forward and slightly downward.

3. While brushing, the weight is on the right leg.

V. Common errors, their causes, and how to correct them 1. Error: the fist is closed too early. The main cause is that the application is not sufficiently understood. Correction: the strike follows immediately upon the brushing movement, so the fist should be closed at the moment when the left hand has finished brushing and the right hand has arced to the region of the waist; before that the fist should not be closed.

2. Error: the upper body does not lean slightly forward but instead drops the head and bends forward at the waist. The main cause is inattention to keeping the coccyx centred; this is a defect of the body method. Correction: although the body leans slightly forward, "the hundred meetings and the central pole, one breath running through" is required, forming a straight line from the crown of the head to the perineum.

3. Error: the two hands' movement pauses, especially as the right foot descends. The main cause is that the left leg has not sunk and settled firm; in order to keep the body balanced the hand movement is therefore stopped, causing upper and lower to be disconnected. Correction: settle the left leg firm, and let the two hands move in an arc with the turning of the waist.

VI. Teaching and practice methods 1. In this movement the linking movement must first be done well: repeatedly coach the sinking and slight bending of the left leg as the right leg descends, to lay a good foundation for the movements that follow.

2. Explain clearly that the upper body stays upright, and that as the right fist…

图 449A
Step Forward and Point at the Groin with the Fist in transition: the right palm arcs right, back and forward and is drawn in beside the right waist and closed into a fist, while the left palm brushes downward in an arc from front to right and then left.
图 449B
The left palm brushes to the side of the left knee, and the right fist is driven forward and down from beside the waist, the body folding slightly at the waist.
图 450
The settled Point at the Groin: the left bow stance, the left palm brushed to the side of the left knee, and the right fist driven forward and down at the height of the abdomen, the eyes looking straight ahead.

Striking forward, when the body turns into a slight forward lean, the head must not drop and the waist must not be curved — let the practitioner understand that a curved waist blocks the flow of qi and blood; explain and demonstrate this repeatedly.

3. The teacher must constantly correct the lateral distance of the stepping and the direction the foot points during practice, so that the hip-root and the limbs relate well to one another and the stance is consequently solid.

VII. Technical Analysis Advance Step and Strike Toward the Crotch has two movements: first, the parry of the left hand; second, the forward strike of the right hand — and two steps must be taken. This requires the movements to be continuous, upper and lower following one another. One must in particular train well the "calm mind and applied intent": before moving, dismiss all distracting thoughts, as if the ears heard nothing and the eyes saw nothing, so as to be in a state free of thought and worry. Once moving, concentrate the whole spirit on using intent to guide the performance of every movement. Therefore, in practising the form, mind comes first and body second, and one should use intent and not force, so that inner and outer become one.

Posture Seventy-Five — Step Up and Grasp the Bird's Tail

Posture Seventy-Five — Step Up and Grasp the Bird's Tail

Posture Seventy-Seven — Push Down

Posture Seventy-Seven — Push Down

The application, the course of movement and all the other sections are the same as Posture Fifty-Seven, Push Down: see the first figure on this page (the same as figure 349) and the second figure on this page (the same as figure 350).

Posture Seventy-Eight — Step Up to Seven Stars

I. Application Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent chops downward with the right hand from above, I immediately rise, turn the body slightly left, step forward and advance, both hands become fists and at once gather and cross to form the character "seven," the eye of the fists facing obliquely inward to ward off. Striking straight at the opponent's chest with the fist is also permissible.

Another application is this:

The opponent strikes up and down with the right hand; I perform Step Up to Seven Stars and block with both hands. The opponent then drives straight at my chest and abdomen with the left fist; I at once change step, separate both hands (left hand up, right hand down) and immediately strike straight out with the press.

II. Course of Movement 1. The waist and hips gradually turn left, the weight moves forward, the body gradually rises forward and turns left, the left toe swings outward, the left leg bends at the knee and bows forward, the right leg presses; the weight gradually shifts forward onto the left leg. The left palm, warding with the fingers, gradually scoops upward, and the right hand drops slightly (see the third figure on this page).

2. The weight continues to move forward, the left leg bends at the knee and the whole body weight is supported by the left leg; the upper body continues to turn gradually left, the right heel leaves the ground first, the foot lifts forward past the inner side of the left ankle, and at the same time the left palm scoops up to before the chest while the right hand follows the right leg lifting forward and moves from back to front to before the waist (see the fourth figure on this page).

3. The right leg steps forward half a step and touches the ground with the ball of the foot, forming a right empty stance; at the same time the left palm continues to move forward, and as the two fists are about to meet they close. The right fist crosses forward below the left fist, and both ward off forward and up together. The two fists form the character "seven," level with the forehead, the eyes of the fists facing obliquely up. The eyes look level to the front, the gaze attending to the forward ward-off of the crossed fists (see the fifth figure on this page).

图 468
Push Down: from the final position of Single Whip the body sinks, the right leg bends at the knee and sinks, the left leg straightens into a drop stance, the left palm extends forward and presses down.
图 469
Push Down, transition: the weight descends, the left palm extends along the inner side of the left leg and threads out, the eyes look at the forward hand.
图 470
Step Up to Seven Stars, opening: the weight gradually shifts onto the left leg, the left palm, warding with the fingers, scoops upward, the right hand drops slightly.

III. Key Points 1. In rising from the left drop stance, the movement must be led by the waist and hips: the left toe swings outward, the left leg gradually bends, the right leg gradually presses, the waist and hips relax, and the upper body moves level, forming a bow stance — do not rise by straightening both legs.

2. In passing from Push Down into the right empty stance, the body must not sway or lean forward; the upper body must stay upright and the waist and hips must be relaxed — do not stiffen the waist in order to keep balance.

3. When the two fists ward off forward and up, take care not to make it a forward flicking-up movement. The back of the fist follows the forearm; the whole back of the hand does not face outward.

4. When the two fists ward off forward, the shoulders must not rise or lock because the fists have crossed. The two arms must form an arc, attaining stored curvature and fullness.

5. One must be still altogether when still and move altogether when moving, and must change the inner force under the requirement of containing closure within opening and separation within closing; only thus can one train to the point of "touched, it turns freely, and never lacks power." The famous masters of Taijiquan in former times reached the technical state of "wherever it is leaned upon, there strike."

IV. Requirements 1. In passing from Push Down into this posture's right empty stance, each posture must carry through from the one before. When Push Down connects to Step Up to Seven Stars, the Push Down must not come to a dead stop — there must be "force broken but intent unbroken," "broken and then rejoined"; that is, the Push Down appears to pause, but in fact the intent is still focused and the inner force is still turning. Hence the requirement that the link and the transfer be nimble.

2. Rising from Push Down into the right empty stance of Step Up to Seven Stars, empty and full must be clearly distinguished, the step must not drag, and the body must not sway.

3. In the right empty stance, the waist and crotch must sink and be full — round and yet empty; the crotch must not be pinched into a pointed "inverted V."

4. In changing both hands into fists, the fists must close as they change.

图 471
Step Up to Seven Stars, transition: the weight shifts onto the left leg, the right foot lifts past the inner side of the left ankle, the left palm scoops up to before the chest, the right hand moves forward.
图 472
Step Up to Seven Stars, final position: a right empty stance, the two fists crossed to form the character "seven," level with the forehead, the eyes look to the front.

V. Errors, Causes, Corrections 1. Error: the crossed fists are too close to the chest, too far, too high or too low. The main cause is insufficient clarity about the application. One must know that the opponent chops down from above with the right hand: if I close the fists too close, the head is easily attacked. Since the opponent's attacking hand has already reached my head, if the fists are too far the arms straighten and the force is insufficient. If too high, my chest and abdomen are too "empty" and exposed to the opponent and easily attacked. Correction: repeatedly check and practise, and the fists are slightly higher than the shoulders and the two arms form an arc.

2. Error: in the right empty stance the right foot presses down firmly, producing double weighting. The main cause is that both legs are weak and the right foot shares the body weight in the hope of lightening the load on the left foot. A further cause is failure to understand the martial meaning. If both feet stand firm, then in advancing or retreating two movements are needed — first shift the weight, and only then can the right foot advance or retreat — and thus the moment is lost and one is beaten while passive. Correction: let the left leg bear the whole body weight, and repeatedly move the right leg forward and back, to strengthen the leg and experience empty and full.

3. Error: the upper body leans forward on rising. The main cause is that the left leg is weak, so one wants to use the forward lean of the upper body to lift the rear right leg. Correction: on rising, bow the left leg forward so that the weight shifts forward onto the left leg. But the fundamental method still lies in training the muscular strength of the legs: practise more the rising movement that connects Push Down to Step Up to Seven Stars. If elderly or weak, one may take a higher frame — that is, a larger angle of bend in the left leg — which lowers the difficulty and makes the movement easy to complete.

4. Error: when the two fists gather and cross into the character "seven," the position of the fists is wrong — some have the eye of the fist facing inward, some facing up. The main cause is shallow experience of the application. The opponent chops down from above with the right hand; I ward off forward and up with the two fists, and so the backs of the fists must follow the forearms and the eyes of the fists must face slightly obliquely up. If the eyes of the fists face up or the centres of the fists face inward, the former has no ward-off force and the latter causes the elbows to lift, so that one cannot relax the shoulders and drop the elbows. Correction: the eyes of the fists should face slightly obliquely up.

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods 1. The teacher observes from different angles the lateral distance between the legs, and the position and direction of the two fists, at the final position.

2. The emphasis should be placed on the rising from Push Down into Step Up to Seven Stars, because at this point the leg muscles bear the heaviest load. Above all one must train shifting the weight forward.

3. Teach so that the movement is even. Sudden speeding up is especially easy on rising. The forward movement of the two arms is also apt to speed up; one must be neither slow nor hurried, and within a single movement the hands and feet must move evenly, and throughout the whole Taijiquan set every posture must be even.

4. Paired practice combining the application: A — takes the final position of Push Down. B — stands directly in front and chops down from above with the right hand. A — bows the left leg, makes the right empty stance, both hands change to fists forward and up, gathering and crossing to ward off outward in the character "seven." The two then exchange and repeat.

VII. Technical Analysis 1. In the complete Yang-style Taijiquan set there are two "Push Down" postures: one follows "Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg," the other precedes this movement, "Step Up to Seven Stars." When the weight moves forward, "the tailbone centred and upright" is required, which means the two hip joints must be set straight and upright, advancing and retreating together, or exchanging evenly, striving to be neither leaning nor tilted, aligned above with the two shoulder joints and moving in the same direction — conforming to the requirement that "shoulders and hips unite."

2. In passing from Push Down into Step Up to Seven Stars, as the weight moves forward and one bows the left knee and lifts the right leg to rise, the body's centre of gravity moves far from the support point; if the frame is low, the amount of exercise grows even greater. Beginners may therefore take a higher frame, bringing the centre of gravity nearer, which also lightens the load on the legs and makes rising easier.
