Posture Seventy-Nine — Retreat a Step and Ride the Tiger

Posture Seventy-Nine — Retreat a Step and Ride the Tiger

I. Application Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent presses in with both hands, I at once stick my two wrists to the inner sides of the opponent's two wrists; the left hand spreads open toward the lower left, the right hand sticks and rises past the upper right, and both my palms turn outward with it. The right foot then withdraws a step backward, comes down and sits firmly, the waist sinks and the force goes down, and the left foot lifts with it, the toe touching the ground, forming the ride-the-tiger shape, so that the whole strength of the opponent falls into emptiness. At this moment, fierce as a tiger though the opponent be, at the slightest turn he comes under my control.

II. Course of Movement 1. The waist turns right about 70° or more, the right foot withdraws a step to the right-rear, the weight gradually shifts onto the right leg; at the same time the two fists become palms and separate, both palms descending together, the right palm following the turn in an arc slightly downward and then, as the back of the hand turns outward, moving slightly upward to before the right chest, while the left palm follows the turn in an arc to a point near the crook of the right elbow (see the first figure on this page).

图 473
Retreat a Step and Ride the Tiger, opening: the waist turns right, the right foot withdraws a step to the right-rear, the two fists become palms and separate, the right palm arcs up to before the right chest, the left palm moves to the crook of the right elbow.

2. The waist turns back to the left, the body still faces forward (east); the left foot lifts slightly and comes down essentially in the same place, touching the ground with the toe, forming a left empty stance. At the same time both hands continue to separate left and right: the right palm, as the body turns right, goes from front to down, then as the body turns back to face forward rises and opens up to the upper right; as it lifts, the right arm rotates inward so that the palm faces front-right, the fingers obliquely up, slightly higher than the head, moving to the upper right of the body, while the left palm falls in an arc to the lower left beside the left hip, palm facing down, fingers pointing forward. The gaze first attends to the right palm and looks to the front-right past the right elbow, then, after attending to both palms lifting and tearing down, looks forward (see the second and third figures on this page).

III. Key Points 1. Turning the body and withdrawing the step, and separating the two hands, must be done at the same time. This is a process of neutralizing: the opponent presses in, I turn the waist and withdraw the step, so that the pressing force that came straight in falls into emptiness. The waist and crotch are the key to regulating the amount of movement and to strengthening the explosive force; hence the rotation of the waist is required to be relaxed and sinking, straight and upright, without swaying or swinging — otherwise the sticking and the tearing will lack force.

2. Do not separate the two hands too fast; at the start the separation is of small extent. While turning the waist and withdrawing the step, the left hand is still at the crook of the right elbow, and only when the opponent's pressing force begins to waver do I separate the two hands further — the left hand tearing down, the right hand sticking and lifting (the right upper arm essentially level with the shoulder, the right forearm slanting). Note that as the right hand pulls up, the waist must lower.

3. When withdrawing the step backward, note where the right foot lands — do not place it on the same line. The foot is the root of the stance and the stepping; if the root is unsteady, then at the slightest deviation the stance and the stepping must fall into disorder. Victory lies in advancing to seize position; freedom from defeat lies in retreating a step to avoid the point — so the correct placement of the foot when withdrawing is very important.

4. When the right foot retreats and sits firmly, the waist and hips must sink, for only thus can one seize the moment and the position and keep the lower body stable. On the basis of relaxation, attend to straightness and sinking — do not press down stiffly or pull up stiffly, which would impair the flexibility of the waist's rotation. Used properly, the power of the waist can concentrate the strength of the whole body at one point.

IV. Requirements 1. There must be "one movement and nothing unmoving": turning the waist, withdrawing the step and separating the hands move together, upper and lower following one another, neither first nor last.

图 474A
Retreat a Step and Ride the Tiger, transition: the waist turns back left, the left foot comes down in place into a left empty stance, the two hands separate left and right, the right hand lifts to the upper right, palm facing forward.
图 474B
Retreat a Step and Ride the Tiger, final position: a left empty stance, the right palm lifts slightly higher than the head, palm facing front-right, the left palm tears down and presses beside the left hip, the eyes look to the front.

2. The chest must not be thrust out; one must contain the chest and raise the back. Thrusting the chest causes qi to crowd the chest, making the upper heavy and the lower light, so that the heels float up easily.

3. In withdrawing the step and forming the left empty stance, the weight must not fluctuate up and down.

4. The forward left empty leg and the right side of the chest have a tendency to attract and connect, so that the empty leg does not float off to one side and the upper and lower, left and right, are symmetrical and coordinated.

V. Errors, Causes, Corrections 1. Error: on retreating the step, empty and full are unclear and the weight is unsteady. The main cause is tension in the waist and hips, and the left leg not sitting firmly. Correction: the step should change with the body. The conversion of empty and full in the stepping must, along with the conversion of the body method, make the waist alternately draw and exchange left and right waist-gaps during the movement so as to divide empty and full; there must be "the two legs following one another below." Therefore, when the right leg descends to the right-rear with the turning of the waist, the right waist-gap must be empty and relaxed, and as the waist and hips relax and sink slightly, the stability of the weight is helped; moreover the right leg may retreat only slowly, and only after the left leg has sat firmly.

2. Error: after retreating, the two feet stand on the same line, causing the body to sway and be unsteady. The main cause is that the right leg wrongly goes back and to the left, so that the two feet stand on one line; with a small base the body will sway. This is unreasonable in terms of application: the opponent presses, the force coming in is straight forward; only if I step out to the right-rear and turn the waist can I use the neutralizing method and change the direction of the opponent's force. If I retreat straight back, that forms a clash; not only is the stance unsteady, but I cannot change the opponent's straight-forward pressing force, and I put myself at a passive disadvantage. Correction: the right foot, retreating, should go slightly to the right-rear.

3. Error: the two hands separate too early. The main cause is shallow understanding of the application. If the opponent's straight-forward pressing force is met by my two hands forcibly separating up and down, there is difficulty. One should first turn the waist and retreat the step, and only after his force has shifted and dispersed do I tear down and stick and lift, so as to make the whole strength of the opponent fall into emptiness. Correction: on retreating, first bring the left hand near the crook of the right arm so that the two wrists stick to the inner sides of the opponent's two wrists, and only then separate.

4. Error: the path of the two hands' movement is wrong — just one big circle drawn up and down. The main cause is insufficient understanding of the application, producing "scattering." Correction: in the mind, use my two wrists stick to the opponent's two wrists, and as I turn the waist right and retreat the step backward, my two hands first sink slightly, then move right with the turning waist; then the left palm, palm facing down, tears to the lower left, while the back of the right hand faces outward and sticks and lifts to the upper right. In this way there is both a vertical circle and a horizontal circle — it is not an unconscious random drawing of circles.

5. Error: the two hands stay rather close to the body, at essentially the same distance as in White Crane Spreads Its Wings. The main cause is shallow understanding of the application. The opponent is using the press; if my two hands are a small distance apart vertically and close to the body, not only can I not make the opponent's whole strength fall into emptiness, but it is very easy for him to take advantage of my position to attack at will.

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods 1. Broken-down practice: (1) the movement of the hands — first right, then separate up and down. (2) the movement of the feet — sit firmly on the left leg, the right leg retreats to the right-rear. (3) the complete movement.

2. Paired practice combining the application: A — presses with both hands on B. B — retreats the step and turns the waist, both hands sticking to the inner sides of A's two wrists, drawing back and to the right (neutralizing), then separates the two hands up and down, tearing left and lifting right, so that A's two-handed press falls into emptiness. In the paired practice the two exchange and repeat, and must experience the meaning of turning the body and retreating the step.

Book page 236

Posture Eighty — Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus

Posture Eighty — Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus

I. Application Continuing from the previous posture. If there is an opponent in front, and another opponent strikes from behind me with the right hand, then in this emergency where both front and rear must be guarded, I at once spin the right foot in place, the left foot hangs up behind and revolves with the body, and at the same time I use both hands and the left foot in the manner of a whirlwind, sweeping hands and foot together at the opponent's upper and lower parts. After revolving one full circle I return to the original position, and immediately stick to the right elbow and wrist of the opponent in front; then, going around to the opponent's inner wrist-gate, I ward, carry and tear back to the left, and at the same time swiftly kick with the back of the right foot at the opponent's chest and ribs using crosswise force. Where the foot passes it is like a fierce wind swaying lotus leaves — the so-called supple waist folding a hundred times as if boneless, and sweeping away, the whole body is hands. The subtlety of this skill is not something a beginner can grasp at once. II. Course of Movement 1. The movement begins: the right leg sinks slightly, the waist turns slightly right, the right palm comes down in an arc slightly to the right from above and pushes out past the chest, the palm slanting forward, the fingers slanting; at the same time the waist turns slightly left to face the front, the left palm rises in an arc slightly to the left from beside the left hip and guards up to before the left forehead, the fingers passing slightly above the head, the palm facing forward, the fingers slanting up. The eyes attend to the movement of the two hands, then look level to the front (see the first figure on this page).

2. Pivoting on the ball of the right foot, begin to revolve to the right-rear; the body must first sink down, the waist and hips relax, the right leg sinks, and then the waist and hips turn right-rear, the left foot with it rising slightly by pressing the ground, the left leg opening out and swinging to the right-rear with the turn. During the turn both palms face down and the two arms form an arc, the left hand high and the right low; as the turn proceeds the right palm rises level with the nose and the left palm level with the chest, the left palm slightly lower than the right elbow, the left palm still facing down and the right palm slanting forward. Because the "sweep" is done with both hands and the left foot at the same time, hands and foot swing around together with the turning of the body (see the second figure on this page).

3. Turning the waist and swinging the leg, the left foot swings toward the rear-left (northwest) obliquely; the toe turns in and touches the ground, the left toe pointing east-northeast, the left toe a little behind the right heel, the right toe pointing east-southeast. The waist and hips sink down, the weight gradually shifts onto the left foot until the whole foot is firm, and the left leg sits firmly with the knee bent. The right foot then slowly lifts, the body continues to turn right, and both palms shift rightward with the turn, the face toward the east, the hands toward the southeast corner diagonally; the right palm moves to the front-right diagonal of the body, and the left palm moves to the left of the right elbow, slightly lower than the right elbow. The gaze shifts with the direction of the hands (see the third and fourth figures on this page).

4. The waist turns slightly left, the left leg rises a little, the right foot lifts and goes left, and then the waist turns; the right leg swings outward in an arc from left to right and upward, the knee naturally slightly bent, the foot need not rise above the shoulder (because the instep kicks crosswise at the opponent's chest and ribs), the instep facing slightly to the right. At the same time hand and foot respond to one another — hand welcoming foot, foot welcoming hand — and both palms strike from right to left against the face of the right foot, the left hand slightly first and the right slightly after. The body continues to turn right and both hands swing with the momentum to the front-left diagonal, facing north-by-west. The gaze attends to the meeting of the two palms and the instep, then looks level forward (see the fifth and sixth figures on this page).

III. Key Points 1. The left hand guarding the forehead is oblique, not horizontal, otherwise would form a carried shoulder and a raised elbow. The right hand pushing forward must also be slightly oblique — it must not be horizontal or straight — and the fingers on the body's centreline, so that the fingers of the upper and lower hands cross slightly.

2. The revolving movement of Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus is comparatively difficult: one must "stand like the beam of a steelyard, move like a wheel." In revolving, the waist must be set straight and upright like a great banner and vertical, steady and roundly turning like the steelyard weight — not swaying, not collapsing. The turning must pivot on the ball of the right foot, the left foot pressing the ground slightly; first turn the waist and hips, and then the left leg swings to the right-rear with the momentum; only thus can the turn be round and lively. Hence the centre of gravity in the revolution must always be on the ball of the right foot, and must not deviate. The waist must not be stiffly held up, nor must it "fall apart."

3. After revolving, the left toe turns in and comes down, and the right foot at once becomes empty and lifts — only thus can empty and full be clearly distinguished.

4. After revolving, when the two hands move to the southeast they should not pause, but should continuously coordinate with the movement of the right foot and shift gradually to the left.

5. "Body shape and waist support — how could they be absent?" Therefore when the left foot comes down one must gradually squat, and then, as the waist turns from left to right and the right foot lifts and swings from left to right and up, the body must not only avoid leaning forward or back but must also have the intent of pressing up and stretching out.

6. After revolving, the right foot shifts left and then swings out to the right in a kick. This circle should not be too large; if it is large the movement "scatters," and the speed of movement slows and the time lengthens, so that the chance of kicking the opponent is reduced and the requirement of the application is not met.

7. Hand and foot meeting in the strike should pat lightly — the sound need not be loud. One must be relaxed, quiet and natural, because the substance of the movement is the two hands tearing to the lower left and the right leg swinging crosswise from left to right; the pat is only a form, and if the pat is heavy it actually interrupts the movement.

8. The right leg's swing is crosswise force: the turning of the waist must lead the swing of the right leg, and at the same time the hands and the foot move in opposite directions yet echo one another, which makes the movement of the leg more powerful.

9. In revolving, the two hands are before the chest and the left foot opens out and swings with the waist's revolution; at this moment hands and foot sweep at the opponent's upper and lower parts, so there must be the manner of a whirlwind, and it must be fast. The right foot kicks out with crosswise force, and where the foot passes is like a fierce wind swaying lotus leaves — this too must be fast. The boxing treatise says: "When the movement is urgent, respond urgently;

图 478
Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus: the waist turns slightly left, the left leg rises a little, the right foot lifts and goes left, both palms strike from right to left.
图 479
Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus: the right leg swings outward in an arc from left to right and upward, the instep facing slightly to the right.
图 480
Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus, final position: both palms strike from right to left against the face of the right foot, the left hand slightly first and the right slightly after, the eyes look to the front.

when the movement is slow, follow slowly"; "use stillness to master motion, strike later but arrive first." It can be seen that the application of Taijiquan is not simply a requirement of slowness — it requires the ability both to be slow and to be fast. Chen Xin said: "In slowness, be slow enough that others cannot keep up with me; in speed, be fast enough that others cannot keep up with me." So Taijiquan trains lightness and agility precisely in order to attain a later heaviness and speed, and in order that "in movement nothing, however small, is not reached." Relaxation and quietness must be stressed; therefore in practising Taijiquan, apart from a few individual movements, one should not be fast — one should be slow, light, agile and even, especially as a beginner.

IV. Requirements 1. Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus: first the turning of the body, second the swinging kick. The turn must be turned steadily, the body not swaying; the kick must be kicked roundly, with turning power and force.

2. The turning of the body should be led by the waist, and the swinging kick should also be led by the waist; one must not move only the leg without moving the waist — the principle "the master is in the waist" must be embodied.

3. After the right leg has swung and kicked, the left foot must still stand steady; the two hands swing left, and the right leg hangs rather than quickly coming to the ground — it hangs light, agile, steady and firm.

4. The positions of the two feet must be stood accurately.

V. Errors, Causes, Corrections 1. Error: at the start of the movement one attends only to the movement of the hands (left hand raising to the frame, right hand pushing forward) without attending to turning the waist and sinking, and after the body revolves one does not attend to sinking when the left foot lands, nor to the turning of the waist and hips. The main cause is neglect of "upper and lower following one another." Grandmaster Yang Chengfu's orally transmitted Ten Essentials of Taijiquan says: "When the hand moves, the waist moves, the foot moves, the eyes move with them — only thus can it be called upper and lower following one another. If one thing does not move, it is scattered." In terms of training the body, when hands, waist and feet all move the qi and blood of the whole body circulate and more muscular and other bodily tissues take part in the activity; this is a method of practice that stresses wholeness. As for the sinking of the body: in terms of application, a lowered centre of gravity makes the revolution steadier and gives the tearing and other hand movements a firm root. Correction: the waist should be the key to the turning of the upper and lower limbs, and one should use sinking to bring out the force of the crotch and hips, so that issuing force does not become floating and powerless and the movements remain agile.

2. Error: when the body revolves, the two hands suddenly change height, causing interruption. The main cause is that attention is focused on a part — if on the hands, then only the hands move; if on the foot, then only the foot moves. This is the error beginners most easily commit, one of the errors beginners most easily commit. If during the revolution the two hands do not move and only the revolution is done, then when the revolution is finished the height of the hands is suddenly corrected. Correction: from the very start of the revolution the two hands change height, going from left hand high and right hand low gradually to right hand high and left hand low. In this way there is no sudden change but a gradual one, which also conforms to the principle "one movement and nothing unmoving."

3. Error: after the revolution the direction of the body is incorrect. The left foot swings around too far and lands beyond northeast, so that the direction of the swinging kick goes beyond southeast. In terms of application, when the left foot has landed it is already close to the opponent, and the right leg's swinging kick has lost its effect. In some cases the revolution is insufficient and the left foot lands at the southeast, so that the direction of the right leg's swing is northeast, and then the right leg's swing cannot possibly reach the opponent. The main cause lies in not understanding the application. In Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus the enemy is front and rear — one opponent in front, one behind — and after the revolution one must still face the front (east) to deal with the attacking enemy. Correction: there must be control in the revolution; the left foot lands in a northwesterly direction, the right foot in front and the left foot behind.

4. Error: the revolution is poor and the swaying unsteady. The main cause is that the method has not been mastered. Correction: begin the revolution with the weight on the right foot, the left toe helping to keep balance, until the waist has turned so that the face is about to turn westward — only then lightly tap the left toe, lift the left leg, and swing it with the waist's revolution. Then, with one more slight turn of the waist, the left leg can swing around and come down with the momentum; the time spent on one leg is not long, and the body will not topple east and west. Moreover, in terms of application, the line along which the swinging force acts must be long, and then the sweeping power is greater.

5. Error: there is a pause in the middle of the movement — for example at the start, when the left hand raises to the frame and the right hand pushes forward; when preparing to revolve; and when the left foot lands after the revolution. All of these cause brief pauses. The main cause is shallow experience of unbroken continuity. Taijiquan masters most avoid having beginnings and endings, breaks and continuations, because when the old force is exhausted and the new force has not yet been born, this is the moment when one is most easily taken advantage of. Correction: Taijiquan uses intent and not force, unbroken from beginning to end, cycling round and beginning again, endless. Every posture must attend to rising, bearing, turning and closing, and must also attend to continuity in every movement; in the transitions of direction, the spirit must be gathered together, and only then can the opportunity and momentum for the next posture arise. There must absolutely be no pause anywhere in the movement. One must also attend to inner and outer, upper and lower, left and right, front and rear being coordinated and unified, and achieve "inner and outer united," "one qi running through," "done in one breath." For example: the moment the left foot lands, the right foot must lift with the waist's turn to the left — only thus can there be no pause.

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods 1. Explain the application, the direction of movement, the key points and so on.

2. Whole and sectional demonstration (left frame and forward push, revolution, swinging kick).

3. Mnemonic: left frame, right push, the body sinks slightly; the right foot is the axis, the waist turns right; the two hands and the left foot sweep behind the body; sweeping away, the whole body is hands. Left falls and right rises, the two hands oblique; stick the wrist, carry and tear, draw back; the crosswise force swings and kicks, moving the waist's force; it goes like a fierce wind swaying lotus leaves.

4. The difficulty lies in the revolution; the teaching method for the revolution lies in maintaining the centre of gravity, obtaining the motive force of the turn, and controlling direction: (1) To train well the maintenance of the centre of gravity, first let the practitioner attempt a revolution supported on one leg, watching one another. Most people, after the left leg has swung out, shift the weight forward, so that the left leg comes down (This page also carries one unnumbered push-hands demonstration photograph.) to the ground and cannot complete a full revolution. Therefore one uses the method of gradually increasing the angle of revolution, so that the learner can master it. Begin with a 90° revolution, after which the left foot swings from east to south; the second step increases it to turn from east to west; and after that it is increased to swing from east to north (the face still toward the east), completing the whole movement. (2) As for the motive force of the revolution: turning the waist and hips, together with the left foot pressing the ground and swinging, naturally carries the left leg swiftly swinging backward. If one relied only on the leg's swing, not only would the body be unsteady but the swing would be powerless, and could not meet the requirement of the martial art. (3) Directional control also requires repeated practice to raise the functional stability of the position sense receptors, gradually strengthening one's sense of the body's position and posture in space and the movement of each part of the body.

5. Progressive method: (1) left frame and right push. (2) As above, plus the revolution. (3) As above, plus the left foot descending, the right foot lifting to the left, the two hands going right. (4) As above, plus hand and foot meeting in the strike. (5) The complete movement.

Learn one part of the movement, then learn a new part, then add it to the old part, increasing gradually — consolidate one section, add one section, until the whole movement is learned.

6. Paired practice combining the application: A — (the principal practitioner) takes the final position of Retreat a Step and Ride the Tiger. B — (the partner) stands in front of A and strikes with the left fist. C — (the partner) stands behind A and strikes A with the right hand. A — immediately revolves, sweeping with both hands and the left foot at C behind him; then immediately carries and tears B's left wrist with both hands toward his own lower left, and at the same time kicks at B's chest and ribs with the instep of the right foot.

The main point is to experience the application and understand the meaning of the movement; one must on no account actually kick or strike, and must guard against injuring others. The three may take turns practising.

VII. Technical Analysis 1. The application is characterized by enemies front and rear. The movement is characterized in that the whole movement comprises the combination of two detailed movements.

2. During the revolution the point of support is the right foot; after the revolution it is the left foot; the transfer must be light and agile.

3. The right foot's kick with crosswise force must be controlled, otherwise the body's revolution will be out of control. To maintain the balance of the left-foot support, the two hands should shift to the left.

4. After the revolution the left leg sits firmly, so that one stands steady. The two hands moving to the front-right diagonal is the preparation for the swinging tear.

5. As for hand and foot meeting in the strike: if the hand pats the foot and the foot waits to be patted, that shows the hand to be the master, and it loses the meaning of the lotus-swinging foot. If the foot strikes the hand and the hand waits to be struck, that shows the foot to be the master, and it loses the meaning of the two hands' swinging tear. Therefore it should be the foot striking the hand and the hand patting the foot, but with the foot as master.

6. In practising this movement one easily exposes hardness of force: the revolution sways unsteadily, the foot lands heavily, and the right foot kicks stiffly with a loud patting sound. The movements of Taijiquan must be both light and agile and yet steady and settled; from relaxation one enters suppleness, and then one trains steadiness and settledness. The Yang-style Taijiquan elder Chen Xin said: "When the work of movement has lasted long, then hardness is transformed into suppleness, and suppleness is trained into hardness; when hard and soft attain the mean, then yin and yang appear. Hence this boxing cannot be named by hardness, nor can it be named by softness; it is simply named by the nameless name, the Supreme Ultimate." "The Supreme Ultimate means the perfect attainment of both hardness and softness, blended so as to leave no trace. Its work is much, and therefore its accomplishment is difficult." Grandmaster Yang Chengfu said: "Taijiquan is the art of containing hardness within suppleness, of hiding a needle in cotton." Many people have put in a great deal of effort, yet still find success difficult. If the qi shows outwardly and the movements are fierce, that leans toward hardness; if the outward appearance is excessively soft and gentle, that leans toward softness. One should attain "where yin and yang abide, no trace can be sought."

Book page 243

Posture Eighty-One — Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger

Posture Eighty-One — Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger

I. Application Continuing from the previous posture. If the opponent withdraws his body, I at once follow my left and right hands sticking to the opponent's hands, and going around the opponent's wrists revolve to the right; both hands close into fists and strike from the left corner. The left hand at the same time sinks at the opponent's right elbow and strikes forward again, and the right hand draws back and strikes again at the opponent's chest; at the same time the right leg comes down to the right-front and sits firmly, all storing its momentum, the waist having sinking force, rather like a riding-horse crotch, the left foot becoming empty, as if forming the shape of a bended bow shooting a tiger.

图 481A
Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus, adjustment: the left leg sits firmly and stands steady, the two hands move to the front-right diagonal, prepared for the swinging tear.
图 481B
Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus: the foot strikes the hand and the hand pats the foot, with the foot as master, both palms meeting the face of the right foot.
图 482
Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger, opening: the body turns slightly left, the left leg gradually squats and sits firmly, the right foot comes down in place, the toe pointing obliquely southeast.

II. Course of Movement 1. The body turns slightly left with the swinging momentum, the left leg gradually squats and sits firmly, the right foot comes down in place, the toe pointing obliquely southeast, first with the heel touching the ground, and as the weight gradually shifts onto the right leg until the whole foot is firm; at the same time the upper body turns slightly right, the two palms shift right in an arc with the turn, the right palm rotating outward so that the palm turns to face up (the left palm still facing down). The gaze attends to the two palms shifting right (see the third figure on the previous page).

2. The body continues to turn right (facing south-southeast), bowing the right leg and pressing the left leg, forming a right bow stance. The two palms, with the turning of the body, go from left to down and, passing before the abdomen, arc up to the right; the left palm arcs from before the chest to the upper right, the right palm arcs up from the right shoulder, and as it goes the arm rotates inward so that the right palm slants downward. The body turns left to face northeast; the right fist passes the right side of the head, the left fist passes before the right chest, and both fists strike out together toward the front-left diagonal (northeast), the right fist placed beside the right forehead with the right arm forming an arc, the left fist level with the chest. The gaze first attends to the two hands arcing up to the right, and when the body turns left and the two fists are about to strike out toward the front-left diagonal, it turns to the front-left diagonal and looks level, attending to the left fist's strike (see the fourth and fifth figures on the previous page).

III. Key Points 1. The linking movements must be done well. Each posture has its own rising, bearing, turning and closing. The beginning of "Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger" must not pause after the end of "Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus" (the foot pat), but must be continuously unbroken, sinking and turning the waist, immediately performing "Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger."

2. The two hands must turn with the waist: "palm, wrist, elbow and shoulder, back, waist, crotch, knee and foot — nine joints above and below, joint by joint issued from the waist." Therefore the changes of the hands must rely on the waist: the waist turns right, the two hands go from up to down and, passing before the abdomen, to the right and up; when the right palm has moved to the right side of the head (becoming a fist) and the left palm has moved to before the right chest, the body turns left, and the two fists strike out toward the front-left diagonal with the waist's force.

3. The movement of the two hands must conform to the requirements of the application: when shifting right, the upper right hand must not be too far from the body so as to cause "scattering"; the left hand should be before the chest; and on the strike, the right fist need not rise above the head, nor the left fist above the shoulder.

4. At the instant of forming the final position, guard against the right elbow lifting, the shoulders rising, and the body leaning forward.

5. The front and rear feet are not on one line; the right foot is slightly forward.

6. The gaze must change with the fists, from southwest to northeast.

图 483A
Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger, transition: the body turns right into a right bow stance, the two palms go from left to down and arc up to the right past the abdomen, the right palm closes into a fist and moves to the right side of the head.
图 483B
Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger, final position: both fists strike out toward the front-left diagonal (northeast), the right fist beside the right forehead, the left fist level with the chest, the eyes look at the left fist.

IV. Requirements 1. Both the upper and lower limbs must carry force through: "the source supports the waist and spine, the force runs through to the four tips." The upper limbs carry force through by intent, filling the whole arm; there must be both steadiness and settledness and relaxed quietness, and the arm movements are also required to be agile and unimpeded.

2. It is required that intent arrive, the eyes arrive, the body arrive, the hands arrive and the step arrive: when moving, all move together; when arriving, all arrive together. Therefore when the two fists strike out together at the end, the right knee must bow in and the two fists must arrive.

3. The direction of movement must be accurate: the waist turns right and faces southwest, the waist turns left and faces northeast.

4. In practising Taijiquan one must always be "relaxed and quiet," the attention concentrated, and the movements guided by intent. The movements must be relaxed and supple, and one must not use clumsy force. Training intent together with training the body enables inner and outer to become one; therefore practising Taijiquan can prevent and treat chronic illness and can strengthen the constitution.

V. Errors, Causes, Corrections 1. Error: the direction is wrong — the right leg steps not in front of the body (southeast) but to the right side. The main cause is failure to understand the application. Because after "Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus," the opponent withdraws his body and I at once follow the enemy's hands with my left and right hands sticking to them; if I step to the right, then (This page also carries one unnumbered push-hands demonstration photograph.) one cannot speak of "following." If I step forward to the right, advancing can meet the requirement of following, and retreating allows a left carry; if I then step forward once more I can close the fists and strike from the right corner — the left hand striking his right elbow, the right hand striking his chest. Correction: on the basis of understanding the application, attend to where the right foot is placed after the lotus swing — it should be placed to the right-front.

2. Error: the shoulder is carried when the fist strikes out. The main cause is failure to attend to sinking the shoulder and dropping the elbow, whence the elbow rises, and from the raised elbow the shoulder is carried. A carried shoulder brings a whole series of problems, such as impairing "containing the chest and raising the back" and hindering "sinking the qi to the elixir field." Correction: begin from the word "relax," and through experiencing the conversion of empty and full, achieve the sinking of the shoulder.

3. Error: instead of turning the waist and hips one merely sways the body left and right, violating the principle "the master is in the waist." The main cause is that the waist and hips are not relaxed. The waist is the key to the turning of the upper and lower; only if the central axis is unbent and uns waying can it be agile; only by using the waist's power in the movement can the force reach the four limbs. Correction: the waist must be relaxed, sinking and straight, so that its rotation is agile, so that one uses the waist's power and concentrates the strength of the whole body at one point — only then can the fist strike with force.

4. Error: the body leans forward after the fist strikes out. The Boxing Treatise says: "Stand like the beam of a steelyard, move like a wheel." If my body leans forward, the centre of gravity must shift forward, and at a slight push from another I must fall. Moreover, though one advances, one cannot retreat; hence "seeking the far by giving up the near" is wrong. The main cause is that one does not use the waist's power to strike, but uses the erroneous method of bending the waist and leaning forward. Correction: stress that when the fist strikes out the force is led from the spine to set the four limbs in motion; therefore there can only be rotation of the waist, and no leaning forward of the body.

5. Error: the right foot comes down too fast, reducing the amount of exercise. The main cause is that the left leg is weak: at a slight squat one feels the single leg cannot support, and so one can only bring the right foot down a little faster. Another cause is that during the lotus swing the right leg's rightward swing goes out of control, causing the body to turn and dragging the left foot, which is the root, so that the body sways and the right foot comes down too fast. Correction: (1) strengthen the legs and do more single-leg-support squatting practice, the squat going gradually from shallow to deep. (2) Hand and foot meeting in the strike must be controlled and must not favour one side; in particular attend to the swing amplitude of the right leg; with a stable centre of gravity, the left leg can squat slowly, "sending" the right leg down and out lightly.

6. Error: the method of holding the fist is poor — some hold the fist too tightly, some have the direction wrong. The main cause of the former is failure to understand the form of the closed fist. Taijiquan must contain hardness within suppleness, but one must enter by way of relaxation and suppleness; therefore the fist should not be held too tightly, but must have the intent of gathering its qi together, so that it cannot be opened when separated nor scattered when struck. One should also note Chen Xin's saying: "When going out, the hand is open; on meeting a person, it becomes a fist." The latter is that the direction of the fist is wrong: some have both fists' eye facing up, some have both fists' centre facing down — neither is right. The cause lies in failure to understand the application. The left fist strikes straight forward, using the upright fist, so its eye faces up (slightly oblique); the right hand is before the head, and it is correct for its eye to face obliquely down — this is called the "reverse fist." Correction: the fist must be held with appropriate tightness; the left fist in front and the right fist behind, the left low and the right high, the eyes of the two fists facing each other at a distance.

VI. Teaching and Practice Methods 1. Mnemonic: squat lightly and set the right leg down; stick and turn, revolving to the right; the waist sinks with force and the right foot is firm; the eyes of the fists face one another as they go out obliquely.

2. The difficulty lies in the linking: after the lotus swing one must do well the squatting of the left leg and the "sending" of the right foot out obliquely, which is generally not easy to do with ease and roundness, so it should be attacked as a difficulty, with much practice and much thought. First train control to make the centre of gravity stable, and then let the left leg squat.

3. Clarify the direction: (1) the right foot is placed at the southeast corner. (2) The face first turns to the northwest, then to the southwest, and finally to the northeast.

4. Progressive method: (1) the left leg squats, the right leg hangs. (2) As above, extend the right leg toward the southeast. (3) As above, both hands shift right in an arc. (4) As above, both hands continue to shift right, bow the right leg. (5) As above, both fists strike out.

Practise one detail, then add another detail, and gradually learn the whole movement.

5. Yang-style Taijiquan, as a means of preventing and treating illness, uses natural breathing. In teaching, no requirement is placed on the breathing; the practitioner need not fuss over the breathing, and simply lets it be natural, gradually training to "abdomen relaxed, qi gathered; mind quiet, spirit at ease."

VII. Technical Analysis 1. When I am smooth and the other is contrary, that is called sticking. Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger sticks first and strikes after: sticking to the other with oneself, one must know the other, and only thus can one be neither after nor before. Therefore the first half of the movement must stress sticking — sticking so that the two fists each strike where they should — and only then stress striking. Sticking makes it easy to listen to force.

2. When the left leg squats after the lotus swing, normal breathing is often affected; hence the abdomen is required to be relaxed and quiet — "with the abdomen relaxed and quiet, the qi rises of itself" — which also makes the lower body steady.

3. Two movements, four corners: Turn the Body and Swing the Lotus goes first to the southeast corner and then to the northwest corner; Bend the Bow and Shoot the Tiger goes first to the southwest corner and then to the northeast corner.

4. In practising Taijiquan one must "seek quiet within movement," "use quiet to govern movement, so that though moving one is as if still." Hence "the slower the form is practised the better; being slow, the breathing becomes deep and long, the qi sinks to the elixir field, and naturally there is no fault of the blood vessels swelling." Therefore in practising Taijiquan one's thoughts must be concentrated, the mind and spirit single, the breathing natural, the intent stored in the elixir field, distracting thoughts dismissed — hearing and yet not hearing, seeing and yet not seeing — being in a state free of thought and worry. In practising the form one concentrates wholly on using intent to guide each movement, "using intent to move the qi, using the qi to move the body." Naturally, a beginner remembers this movement and forgets that one, attends to the movement of the hands and forgets the movement of the feet, and is in a flurry, unable to be in that high state free of thought and worry. But after long practice, once the set is familiar, one can gradually train to "intent moves, form follows," and can even train to "in quiet there is movement, yet though moving one is still." In this way it can certainly play a good role in improving health, preventing and treating illness, and prolonging life.

Posture Eighty-Two — Advance, Deflect, Parry and Punch

Posture Eighty-Five — Closing

I. Course of Movement 1. The two arms extend forward, and as they extend both arms rotate inward so that the two palms turn to face down, forming a rough cross with the right hand below and the left hand above — see the fifth figure on this page.

图 495
Cross Hands: both hands raise above the head, the two arms separate, the palms facing forward.
图 496
Cross Hands: both palms come down to left and right, palms facing outward, the fingertips slanting up.
图 497
Cross Hands: the two hands cross before the chest, the right hand outside and the left inside, forming Cross Hands.
图 498
Cross Hands, final position: the two hands cross and embrace before the chest, both legs bend slightly at the knee, the eyes look to the front (the same as figures 64 to 67).

2. The two arms continue to separate until the distance between the two hands is the same as the shoulder width. Then the two elbows sink, naturally carrying the two palms gradually downward to press to beside the hips, the fingers pointing forward, the palms still facing down. The eyes look level forward — see the sixth figure on this page to the sixth figure on this page (the same as figures 2 to 4, and figure 1).

3. Finally the fingers of both hands hang naturally.

II. Technical Analysis The Closing is also called "closing Taijiquan." This is the ending posture of a whole set and the practitioner must not neglect it. Closing Taijiquan — closing the two modes, the four images, the eight trigrams and the sixty-four hexagrams — yet still returning to the Supreme Ultimate. That is to say, one gathers in one's mind and breath, brings them wholly back to the elixir field, concentrates the spirit, quiets the breath, knows where to stop and is settled, and must not let them disperse or finish carelessly.

When a set of the form is finished, at the Closing one must still return to the original place (that is, wherever the opening posture was at the start, there the Closing must still be at the end); the direction must be correct and the standing position must be right.

图 501

图 502
Closing, final position: the two hands hang at the sides of the body, the body stands erect, the eyes look to the front.
图 503
Closing, gathering the work: the whole set is finished, returning to the original place of the opening, the direction correct, the standing position accurate.

Chapter Three — Push Hands Yang-style Taijiquan push hands has three traditional pushing methods; a brief introduction to them is given here in passing (with the five-form push hands added).

Book page 254

Section One — Fixed-Step Push Hands

Section One — Fixed-Step Push Hands

Fixed-hand push hands, also called the four cardinal push hands, is performed by two people in place using the four techniques of ward-off, roll-back, press and push against one another. Its movements are as follows:

1. A and B face one another and each steps out the right foot (for convenience of explanation the right foot is assumed for both; in practice the left and right feet may alternate in front). They each raise the left hand and join it (backs of the hands facing each other, wrists crossing), each holding ward-off force; then each raises the right hand and places it at the other's left elbow, becoming the double joining of hands with the left wrists crossed. B bends the right leg and bows forward, A bends the left leg and sits back; at the same time they turn left and press toward A with both hands; A receives the other's pressing with the left arm's ward-off, and at the same time A's upper body, following the momentum, begins to turn left (push-hands figure 504: the one in black is A, the one in white is B; A is warding off, B is pressing).

2. A, following the other's pressing momentum, turns the body left and, as he sits back, the left wrist still wards off the other's left-palm pressing force, while the right wrist sticks to the other's left elbow and wards out to the left; on warding off, the right arm rotates outward. B at once takes the right hand off the other's left elbow and moves it to the inner side of his own left elbow (push-hands figure 505: A in the ward-off form).

图 504
Four cardinal push hands: B presses toward A with both hands, A receives it with the left arm's ward-off, and the two right wrists cross.
图 505
Four cardinal push hands: A turns left and sits back, the left wrist wards off B's pressing force, and wards out to the right.

3. B, following the other's ward-off momentum, places the right palm on the inner side of his own left elbow and presses out toward A's chest, at the same time bowing the right leg; A, following B's pressing momentum, the waist turns right and both arms rotate inward (push-hands figure 506: B in the press form).

4. A, following the other's pressing momentum, continues to turn the waist right, turning the body until it squarely faces B; at the same time both arms continue to rotate inward, and the right hand presses down on B's right hand while the left hand sinks down to the other's forearm near the elbow; both hands press forward together, and the right leg bends and bows forward; B at once receives the other's pressing with the right arm's ward-off (push-hands figure 507: A presses, B wards off).

Then B turns the upper body right and sticks the left hand to A's right elbow to ward off to the right; A then places the left hand on the inner side of his own right elbow and presses forward; B at once changes to the pressing and A again receives it with the left arm's ward-off — and so they push against one another in this cycle. If the upper limbs revolve in the opposite direction (pushing against one another), the movement is as before, only the left and right directions are reversed.

Fixed-step push hands requires that when each has pressed fully it is exactly the moment the step has bowed fully, and when each has warded off fully it is exactly the moment of sitting back to the point (if one sits back when pressing and bows forward when warding off, both are wrong). Ward-off and press lie between the bow and the sit.

Beginners at push hands must on no account let the movements become rough, to prevent accidents and injury; at the same time the breathing must be free and the movements relaxed and open.

Book page 255

Section Two — Moving-Step Push Hands

Section Two — Moving-Step Push Hands

Moving-step push hands is a circular practice performed by two people using the four techniques of ward-off, roll-back, press and push, coordinated with the stepping of advancing and retreating. There are two kinds of stepping: joined stepping and interlocking stepping.

1. Joined stepping: assume that A and B both have the left foot forward and begin with the double joining of hands (moving-step push hands figure 508, A's starting point).

图 506
Four cardinal push hands: A turns the waist right, both arms rotate inward, the right arm presses forward; B in the press form.
图 507
Four cardinal push hands: A presses forward with both hands and bends the right leg to bow; B receives A's pressing with the right arm's ward-off.

Suppose A retreats and B advances. A slightly lifts the right foot forward and then still sets it back in the same place, and B at the same time slightly lifts the left foot back and then still sets it down in the same place. Then A retreats the left foot, B advances the right foot; A retreats the right foot again, B advances the left foot (stepping figure 508, A). It looks as though A retreats three steps and B advances three steps, but in fact the first step is only a slight lift and then a setting down in the same place.

Then it changes to B retreating and A advancing (stepping figure 508, B's starting point — that is, the final footfall of both A and B in figure 508, A). When A has retreated three steps he lifts the left foot back and sets it forward in the same place (turning to advance), and B, having advanced three steps, lifts the right foot forward and sets it back in the same place (turning to retreat). Then A advances and B retreats two steps each (stepping figure 508, B).

Then it changes back to A retreating and B advancing, and so on in a cycle of one advancing and one retreating.

2. Interlocking stepping: A and B stand facing one another one step apart (stepping figure 509, A's starting point).

Suppose A retreats and B advances. B steps the left foot forward and inserts it on the inner side of A's right foot, while A retreats the left foot one step; then B steps the right foot forward and sets it on the outer side of A's left foot, while A retreats the right foot one step; then B steps the left foot again and still inserts it on the inner side of A's right foot, while A retreats the left foot one step (stepping figure 509, A).

Then it changes to B retreating and A advancing (stepping figure 509, B's starting point — that is, the final footfall of both A and B in figure 509, A). When A has retreated three steps, the right foot then passes from the outer side of B's left foot to the inner side (turning to advance); B at the same time slightly lifts the right foot forward and sets it back in the same place (turning to retreat). Then A advances and B retreats two steps each (stepping figure 509, B).

Then it changes back to A retreating and B advancing, and so on in a cycle of one advancing and one retreating.

In moving-step push hands, whether joined stepping or interlocking stepping, the upper limbs still use the four techniques of ward-off, roll-back, press and push; but when the stepping begins, the one retreating is necessarily rolling back and the one advancing necessarily pressing. Then the one retreating, as he retreats, changes to ward-off, and when the ward-off has reached its end the step has exactly retreated three steps; the one advancing, as he advances, changes to press, and when the press is full it is exactly the moment when the forward step is complete. Then when the one retreating changes to advancing, his upper limbs also change from ward-off to press; and when the one advancing changes to retreating, his upper limbs also change from press to ward-off.

In this way they perform the circular practice in coordination with the stepping.

Section Three — Five-Form Push Hands

Section Three — Five-Form Push Hands

1. Push hands with moving steps in place A and B stand and join hands in the manner of fixed-step push hands, and the movements of the hands likewise follow the four forms of ward-off, roll-back, press and push, cycling round without interruption. The only difference is that when A wards off B, the rear leg rises slightly and then at once comes down in the same place. Conversely, when B wards off A, B also moves the rear leg, and when A presses B he also first moves the front leg. In short, when A and B change techniques, they must follow the momentum and lift the empty step, echoing one another. They may also change hands and change steps in pushing. But when changing steps they must first bring the feet together — without bringing the feet together one cannot achieve the left-right alternating push.

2. Push hands with alternating left and right steps The upper-limb movements are as in the previous form. The only difference is that when A first steps up the right foot (leg), the rear leg (the left foot) rises slightly and comes down in the same place, and then the right step is at once withdrawn to stand together with the left foot; then he changes to stepping up the left foot (leg), and at this time A's right leg (that is, the rear leg) also rises slightly and comes down in the same place, and then the left step is withdrawn to stand together with the right foot, after which he steps up the right foot again — and so they push in alternation, repeatedly. B cooperates with A as in the first form: when A steps up the right foot, B retreats the right foot; when A withdraws the right step to stand together with the left foot, B draws back the right foot to stand together with the left foot. If A steps up the left foot, B retreats the left foot; if A withdraws the left step, B also draws back the left step to stand together with the right foot. In short, A and B must cooperate closely; when stepping up and changing steps they need only refer to the previous form. What differs is that the previous forms add a bringing-together of the feet so that the left and right steps can alternate with one another in a cycle. Note further: when stepping up, the stepping foot must be inserted into the opponent's crotch. For example, when A steps up the right foot, A's right foot is inserted into B's crotch and must stand together with B's right foot. When stepping up the left foot, A's left step must stand together with B's left foot.

3. Push hands with one step forward and one step back The upper-limb movements are the same. The lower-limb movements refer to the first form: on stepping up the right foot, the left foot is lifted and at once comes down in the same place, and then the right step is drawn back one step in retreat; after pressing down firmly the left foot is lifted, the left foot is raised and comes down in the same place, and then the right foot steps forward again — and so it continues, with only one step forward and one step back. Note only that when A steps up the right foot, B must retreat the left step, and when A retreats the right step, B must step up the left foot. If a bringing-together of the feet is added, then one may change hands and change feet (steps) in pushing. If in this way the left and right limbs can obtain balanced exercise.

4. Push hands with a step up and crotch insertion The movements refer to the previous; the difference is that when A steps up the right foot, B must retreat the right foot, and then A withdraws the right step and B must step up the right foot. At the same time, when B steps up, the foot must be inserted into the opponent's crotch, as in the second form, and they push in this way continuously. A bringing-together may also be added to change hands and change steps in pushing.

5. Push hands with left and right leaning The stepping is as in the second form. The only difference is that when A steps up the right foot and inserts into the crotch, the right side of his body leans toward B's chest, the left palm pressed into the hollow of the right elbow, and B retreats the right step and presses it full. After A withdraws the right step, he instead inserts the left step into B's crotch and leans the left side of his body toward B's chest, the right palm pressed into the hollow of the left elbow, and B retreats the left step and presses it full. Pushing continuously in this way feels very lively and spirited. A and B may also exchange in practice, provided only that they bring the feet together and change hands.

Book page 259

Section Four — Great Roll-Back

Section Four — Great Roll-Back

Because the great roll-back is coordinated with stepping, the extent of the roll-back is greater than the roll-back in fixed-step push hands, and so it is called the great roll-back. And because the direction of the great roll-back's stepping is toward the four oblique corners (see the overall tendency of the schematic of the directions of the great roll-back stepping), it is also called the four-corner push-hands method. And because its main movements are roll-back and lean, and in each cycle the two together perform four roll-backs and four leans, it is also called four roll-backs and four leans. Because the changes of direction are many and the movements are of large extent, it is very much liked by students of the form.

1. The two stand facing north and south: suppose A faces south and B faces north, and the two form the double joining of hands with the right wrists crossed; suppose further that A rolls back and B leans, A retreating and B advancing. B changes to pressing A's right forearm with both hands, and A wards it with the right forearm (great roll-back figure 510; in the movement description this is the right form, in the diagram it is the left form). A retreats the right foot toward the northwest obliquely, the body turning right; at the same time he turns over the right hand and plucks (loosely grips) B's right wrist, and uses the left forearm (the ulnar side near the wrist) to stick to B's right upper arm (near the elbow joint) and roll back to the right. While A retreats, B strides the left foot across to the west (slightly north), follows A's plucking and rolling momentum, and steps the right foot forward to insert it into A's crotch; at the same time the left palm moves to rest on the inner side of the right elbow and he leans shoulder-first toward A's chest. (For the stepping see the schematic of the directions of the great roll-back stepping, 510A; for the posture see great roll-back figure 513. In the diagram Yang Chengfu is B.) There are five reference diagrams of the great roll-back postures, all traced from original photographs of Grandmaster Yang Chengfu; because there are no diagrams of the transitional movements they are hard to link up, but the postures of rolling back and leaning on both sides are all present, and so they are appended for reference.

2. A sinks the left forearm with the waist to dissolve B's leaning force, and flashes the right hand at B's face. (Great roll-back figure 512; Yang is A here. In this diagram B's posture has not leaned fully; the stance should be the same as Yang Chengfu's in great roll-back figure 513.)

3. B then receives A's right wrist with his own right wrist, and at the same time moves the left hand to stick above A's right elbow, and the two of them again return to the original double joining of hands with the right wrists crossed. While receiving A's right wrist, B steps up the left foot and, pivoting on the sole of the left foot, turns the body to the right and retreats the right foot, standing parallel with the left foot, turning to face east. A at the same time slightly lifts the left foot back, turns the toe in toward the south and sets the foot down, turns the body right, brings the right foot alongside, and turns to face west. (Great roll-back stepping figure 510B.)

Each cycle of the great roll-back requires walking four oblique corners. In the above — A retreating and B advancing, A rolling back and B leaning — they have walked one oblique corner and completed the first leaning movement. Then the second roll-back and lean is B retreating and A advancing, B rolling back and A leaning (the movement is as above, only A and B exchange; B's retreating direction is southwest — great roll-back stepping figure 511A); B turns to face south and A faces north (great roll-back stepping figure 511B). The third is again A retreating and B advancing, A rolling back and B leaning, then turning to face east (the movement as in the first, only the direction differs — great roll-back stepping figure 512A and B). The fourth is again B retreating and A advancing, B rolling back and A leaning, returning again to A facing south and B facing north (the movement as in the second — great roll-back stepping figure 513A and B). And so they practise in repeated cycles.

The above movements begin from the double joining of hands with the right wrists crossed; therefore, whether A or B, the roll-back and the lean walked are all right roll-back and right lean. If one wishes to walk left roll-back and left lean, one may change to beginning from the double joining of hands with the left wrists crossed, and follow the movements described above with left and right reversed (great roll-back figures 511 and 514). In practice the left and right may alternate.

图 510
Great Roll-Back: A retreats the step and turns the body aside, B steps up and inserts into the crotch, and leans shoulder-first toward A's chest.
图 511
Great Roll-Back: the second roll-back and lean — B retreats and A advances, B rolls back and A leans, the direction turning to the southwest.
图 512
Great Roll-Back: A sinks the left forearm with the waist to dissolve B's leaning force, and flashes the right hand at B's face (Yang is A here).

The techniques of the great roll-back are four: pluck, roll-back, elbow and lean. In practice the movements of pluck (together with roll-back) and of lean are very clearly displayed, while roll-back and elbow are not displayed, being used only in the variations.

The roll-back method — In Grandmaster Yang Chengfu's Complete Book of Taijiquan for Body and Use, in the explanation of the four-corner push hands of the great roll-back, "roll-back" is explained thus: "…taking hold of B's left wrist is plucking. If the right hand does not move, that is cutting off. As soon as it changes it becomes roll-back. Rolling back means sweeping aside B's left elbow, and striking obliquely at B's collar with the palm." This is explained in terms of A rolling back on the left and B leaning on the left. A plucks B's left wrist with the left hand, and at the same time uses the right forearm (the ulnar side near the wrist) to stick to B's left upper arm (slightly above the elbow joint) and roll back to the left; if "the right hand does not move," then the ulnar side "cuts off" B's left elbow joint; if "as soon as it changes it becomes roll-back," then the right hand "sweeps aside B's left elbow" and strikes obliquely at B's collar with the back of the hand on the thumb side. Hence the roll-back movement is not displayed in practice, and there is a roll-back movement only in the intent or in the variation. Thus the oblique strike with the back of the hand is taken as "roll-back." Besides this there are two other explanations: one takes the flash as the roll-back palm; the other takes it that, immediately after the left roll-back, the right elbow sinks and the right hand draws and dissolves B's leaning force — this being taken as the roll-back.

The elbow method — this too is an elbow movement in the intent or in the variation: when A rolls back on the left and cuts off B's left elbow with the right forearm, B then folds and stacks his left elbow onto the upper side of A's right forearm and drives the tip of the elbow toward the top of A's chest — this being the elbow movement. From the sentence in Complete Book of Taijiquan for Body and Use, "The plucking posture. A plucks on the left and changes to the flash. The right is still the cut-off. B blocks with the left elbow" (People's Sports Publishing House, first edition July 1957, p. 42), it appears that it is also the one being rolled back who uses the elbow method by bringing the elbow to bear. But there is another view that it is the one rolling back who uses the elbow method — namely, when A rolls back on the left and B leans on the left, A uses the right elbow sinking to dissolve B's leaning force, this movement being taken as the elbow movement. Although the great roll-back is said to have the four techniques of pluck, roll-back, elbow and lean, it actually also includes the techniques of ward-off, press and push. For ward-off, roll-back and push, see in detail the movement descriptions of the great roll-back above. The press, before the one being rolled back uses the lean, contains the intent of pressing. In the variations, moreover, the one pressing also uses the press method: after A's left roll-back he still sticks the right forearm to B's left upper arm, releases the left hand from the lower pluck and moves it to rest at the right wrist, and this becomes the press form.

图 513
Great Roll-Back: A rolls back on the left, and B folds and stacks the left elbow onto the upper side of A's right forearm and drives the tip of the elbow toward A's chest.
图 514
Great Roll-Back: the posture of left roll-back and left lean (as shown in the original photograph of Yang Chengfu).
