Chapter Four — Important Writings of Famous Taijiquan Masters

Book page 266

I. A Talk on the Practice of Taijiquan

I. A Talk on the Practice of Taijiquan

Orally related by Yang Chengfu Recorded by Zhang Hongkui Among the martial arts of China, though the schools are many and varied, one should know that all of them are techniques embodying philosophical principle. Throughout the ages there have been men of old who exhausted the energies of a whole lifetime and still could not exhaust the profundities — such cases are everywhere. If a student spends a single day's effort, he gains a single day's result; by daily accumulation and monthly increase, when the water arrives the channel is formed.

Taijiquan is the art of containing hardness within suppleness, of hiding a needle in cotton; in technique, in physiology and in mechanics it holds a considerable philosophical principle. Therefore one who studies this way must pass through a definite procedure and a considerable time. Though the guidance of a good teacher and the mutual sharpening of good friends are certainly indispensable, the most essential thing is daily training of oneself. Otherwise, though one talks all day and yearns for years, on the day one joins hands there is emptiness and nothing there, and one remains an outsider — for there is nothing but daily work. This is what the ancients meant by "vain thought all day is not as good as study." If one can be unremitting morning and evening, unmoved by cold and heat, and the moment a thought arises take up the form and train, then whether old or young, male or female, the success is one and the same.

Recently, students of Taijiquan have spread from north to south, and like-minded people increase day by day; one cannot but rejoice for the future of the martial art. Yet among these people, though there is certainly no lack of those who train hard with single-minded devotion and sincerely seek learning, whose future is immeasurable, the ordinary run cannot avoid falling into one of two paths. The first: a man is naturally gifted, of strong years and strength, who from one instance infers three, whose intelligence stands out from the crowd — but alas, at a slight success he is content, and at once stops halfway, unable to receive the greater. The second: he is hasty in seeking quick results, and attains his form by neglect; before a year is out he has already learned boxing, sword, broadsword and spear — yet though he copies the gourd's shape, in reality he has not got the secret flavour of it. Once one examines his directions and movements, upper and lower, inner and outer, none of them accord with measure; if he wishes to correct them, then every form must be revised, and what is corrected in the morning is already forgotten by evening. Hence one often hears it said: "Learning the form is easy; correcting the form is hard." This saying arises entirely from hastening to completion. Such people, passing error on as error, come to mislead themselves and mislead others, and are the greatest cause for anxiety about the future of the art.

In beginning Taijiquan, one first practises the form frame. What is called the form frame is this: following the names of the forms in the boxing manual, form by form is taught by the teacher, and the student, with whole heart and quiet spirit, silently memorises and studies it, and performs it accordingly — this is called practising the frame. At this time the student should attend to inner and outer, upper and lower. What belongs to the inner is the so-called "use intent and not force": below, the qi sinks to the elixir field; above, the crown is suspended from the top. What belongs to the

Book page 267

A Talk on the Practice of Taijiquan (continued)

A Talk on the Practice of Taijiquan (continued)

As for what shows outwardly: the whole body is light and nimble, and every joint is threaded through — from the feet to the legs, to the waist, letting the shoulders sink and the elbows bend. When first learning, take these few phrases and ponder them morning and evening, and taste them for yourself; for each posture and each hand, always examine carefully and probe. In moving and practising, strive above all for correctness. Once the practice has become pure, then take up the second posture, and in this way gradually work through to the end of the form; if you do so, there will be nothing to go back and correct, and in time you will no longer need to be reminded of the key points.

In practising and moving, all the joints of the whole body must be relaxed and natural. First, the mouth and abdomen must not hold the breath; second, the four limbs, waist and legs must not put forth stiff force. These two sentences — students of the internal martial arts can all recite them; yet the moment they make one movement, turn one body, or kick a leg and swing the waist, their breath gasps and their body sways, and the fault lies precisely in holding the breath and putting forth stiff force.

1. In practising, the head must not tilt to the side nor tip forward or back; this is what is meant by "suspending the crown of the head" — as though something were held up on top of the head. Above all, beware of stiffening it straight; this is the meaning of the word "suspend." Though the eyes look level ahead, at times they must follow the movement of the body, and though the line of sight is empty, it is nonetheless a movement of key importance within the changes, supplementing what the body method and the hand method lack. The mouth is as if open, yet not open; as if closed, yet not closed; breathe out through the mouth and in through the nose, letting it be natural. If moisture forms beneath the tongue, swallow it with the body and do not spit it away.

2. The trunk should be centred and upright, not leaning; the spine and the coccyx should be vertical and not off-centre. But when meeting with the changes of opening and closing, there is the activity of "hollowing the chest and rounding the back," "sinking the shoulders and turning the waist"; at the time of first learning one must take note of this, otherwise in time it will be difficult to change, and one will surely fall into rigidity and stagnation, so that however deep one's skill, it will be hard to gain benefit and put it to use.

3. All the joints of the two arms must be relaxed and open. The shoulders should hang down, the elbows should bend downward, the palms should stretch slightly, and the fingertips should curve slightly. Move the arms with intent and thread the fingers with qi; as days and months accumulate, the internal power becomes penetrating and numinous, and its marvel quietly arises of itself.

4. The two legs should distinguish substantial and insubstantial, rising and falling like the walk of a cat. When the weight shifts to the left, the left is substantial and the right leg is called insubstantial; when it shifts to the right, the right is substantial and the left is called insubstantial. What is called insubstantial is not empty — its momentum is still unbroken, and it retains a reserve of intent for lengthening, shortening and changing. What is called substantial is simply solid, and does not mean that excessive force or violent strength is used. Thus the leg is bent to vertical as the standard; beyond this it is called overreaching in force, the body plunges forward, and the centred and upright posture is lost.

5. The sole of the foot should distinguish two forms — the kick (the left and right separate-foot or left and right raise-foot in the form) and the heel-push. In the kick, attend to the toe; in the heel-push, attend to the whole sole. When the intent arrives, the qi arrives; when the qi arrives, the power arrives of itself. But the joints of the leg must all be relaxed and steady as it goes out. At this moment one most easily puts forth stiff force, the body lurches this way and that, and the leg is issued without power.

As for the sequence of Taijiquan: first practise the form (which belongs to the bare-hand work), such as the Taijiquan and the Taiji Long Fist; next, single-hand push, in-place push-hands, moving-step push-hands, the Great Roll-back, and free-hand sparring; after that come the weapons, such as the Taiji Sword, the Taiji Sabre, the Taiji Spear (the Thirteen-Spear), and so on.

As for practice times: twice each day after rising; if there is no time in the morning, then twice before sleeping. Within a single day one should practise seven or eight times, and at the very least once at dawn and once at dusk. But after drunkenness and after a full meal, both should be avoided.

As for the place of practice: a courtyard and a hall that can let air through and that has plenty of light are suitable. Avoid places with harsh wind blowing directly upon one and places with damp, mouldy air; for once the body is set in motion the breathing is sure to become deep and long, and so if harsh wind and mouldy air penetrate deep into the abdomen they harm the organs and easily bring on illness. As for the clothing for practice, a wide cut of Chinese short jacket and broad-toed cloth shoes are suitable. When practising over a long stretch, if you come to sweat, on no account wipe yourself with cold water, otherwise there is none who will not fall ill.

Book page 268

II. Ten Essentials of Taijiquan

II. Ten Essentials of Taijiquan

Orally related by Yang Chengfu Recorded by Chen Weiming 1. Suspend the crown and lift the energy to the top — "Lifting the energy to the top" means the head is held upright, with the spirit threaded to the crown of the head. One must not use force; if force is used the neck becomes stiff and the blood and qi cannot flow. There must be the sense of an empty, numinous naturalness. Without suspending the crown and lifting the energy to the top, the spirit cannot be raised.

2. Hollow the chest and round the back — "Hollowing the chest" means the chest is slightly drawn in, so that the qi sinks to the cinnabar field. The chest must not be thrust out; if thrust out, the qi crowds at the chest, the upper is heavy and the lower light, and the heels easily float up. "Rounding the back" means the qi clings to the back. If one can hollow the chest one can naturally round the back; if one can round the back, the power can issue from the spine, and there is nothing one faces that one cannot overcome.

3. Relax the waist — The waist is the sovereign of the whole body. Only if the waist can relax will the two feet have strength and the lower base be steady; all the changes of substantial and insubstantial come from the turning of the waist. Hence it is said: "The source of life and intent lies in the hollow of the waist." Whenever one cannot get power, one must seek it from the waist and legs.

4. Distinguish substantial and insubstantial — Taijiquan takes the distinguishing of substantial and insubstantial as its first essential meaning. If the whole body sits on the right leg, then the right leg is substantial and the left leg is insubstantial; if the whole body sits on the left leg, then the left leg is substantial and the right leg is insubstantial. If substantial and insubstantial can be distinguished, then turning is light and nimble, with no effort at all; if they cannot be distinguished, then stepping is heavy and sluggish, one stands unstably, and one is easily pulled about by another.

5. Sink the shoulders and drop the elbows — "Sinking the shoulders" means the shoulders loosen and hang down. If they cannot loosen and hang, the two shoulders rise up, and the qi follows them up with it, so that the whole body loses its power. "Dropping the elbows" means the sense of the elbows loosening and dropping downward; if the elbows are held suspended, the shoulders cannot sink, one cannot send a person far, and one comes near to the broken power of the external schools.

6. Use intent and not force — The Taijiquan Treatise says: this is entirely a matter of using intent and not force. In practising Taijiquan the whole body loosens and opens; not the slightest clumsy force is allowed to linger between the sinews, bones and blood vessels so as to bind oneself — only then can one be light, nimble and changing, turning round and freely as one wishes. Some may doubt: if one does not use force, how can force grow? Now, the body has its channels and collaterals as the earth has its ditches and channels: if the ditches and channels are not blocked the water flows, and if the channels and collaterals are not closed the qi passes through. If the whole body is full of stiff force throughout the channels and collaterals, then the blood and qi stagnate, turning is not nimble, and pulling one hair moves the whole body. But if one does not use force and uses intent instead, then where the intent arrives the qi arrives with it; and so the blood and qi flow and pour in, day by day infusing, circulating through the whole body with no moment of stagnation. Practise long and long, and one gains the true internal power — which is what the Taijiquan Treatise calls "supremely soft, and then supremely firm and hard." For one whose Taijiquan skill has ripened, the arm is like cotton wrapped around iron, and its weight is exceedingly heavy; whereas one who practises an external-school boxing shows force when he uses force, and when he does not use force he is very light and buoyant — from which one can see that his force is the outward, surface force of external power. To use force and not intent is what most easily stirs one into motion, and is not to be prized.

7. Upper and lower follow one another — This is what the Taijiquan Treatise says: "Its root is in the feet, it issues from the legs, it is governed by the waist, and it takes shape in the fingers; from the feet to the legs to the waist, there must always be one complete qi." The hand moves, the foot moves, the leg moves, and the gaze follows and moves with them; only thus can it be called upper and lower following one another. If one thing does not move, then it is scattered and disordered.

8. Inner and outer unite — What Taijiquan practises lies in the spirit; hence it is said: "The spirit is the commander-in-chief, the body is the one driven." If the spirit can be raised, then naturally the movement is light and nimble. The frame is nothing other than the opening and closing of substantial and insubstantial. What is called opening is not only the hands and feet opening — the mind and intent open along with them; what is called closing is not only the hands and feet closing — the mind and intent close along with them. If one can unite inner and outer into one qi, then all is one seamless whole.

Book page 269

II. Ten Essentials of Taijiquan (continued)

II. Ten Essentials of Taijiquan (continued)

9. Linked without interruption — In the external schools of boxing, the power is the acquired, clumsy power, and so it has a beginning and an ending, times of continuation and times of break: the old power is spent and the new power not yet born, and at such a moment one is most easily taken advantage of. Taijiquan uses intent and not force; from first to last it is unbroken and continuous, going round and beginning again, cycling without end. The original treatise's words "like the great Yangtze and the sea, rolling on without cease," and again "in movement like drawing silk," both speak of its being threaded through as one qi.

10. Seek stillness within movement — In the external schools of boxing, leaping and bounding are taken as the skill, and all one's strength is used up, so that after practice there is none who is not out of breath. Taijiquan governs movement with a still mind; though it moves, it is as if still — hence the slower one practises the frame, the better. When slow, the breathing is deep and long, the qi sinks to the cinnabar field, and there is naturally none of the fault of blood and pulse swelling. Students who taste this with care may perhaps grasp its meaning.

III. A Treatise on Taijiquan

Wang Zongyue Taijiquan is born of the Ultimateless, and is the mother of yin and yang. In movement they separate, in stillness they join; without excess and without shortfall, following the bend and yielding to the stretch. When the other is hard and I am soft, this is called "yielding"; when I am in accord and the other is contrary, this is called "sticking." If the other moves urgently I respond urgently; if the other moves slowly I follow slowly. Though the changes are of ten thousand kinds, the principle runs through as one. From familiarity with the postures one gradually awakens to understanding power; from understanding power one ascends step by step to the numinous. Yet without long practice of the work, one cannot break through with sudden insight. Suspend the crown and lift the energy to the top, sink the qi to the cinnabar field; do not lean and do not tilt; now hidden, now revealed. Where the left is heavy, then the left is insubstantial; where the right is heavy, then the right vanishes. Raise it and it grows higher; press it down and it grows deeper; advance it and it grows longer; retreat it and it grows more urgent. A single feather cannot be added; a fly or an insect cannot alight. The other does not know me, while I alone know the other — that the hero finds nothing he faces that he cannot overcome follows from this. This art has many side doors. Though the postures differ, they come to no more than the strong bullying the weak, the slow giving way to the fast, the powerless struck by the powerful, and the slow hand yielding to the fast hand. These are all innate natural capacities, not a matter of acquired learning and deliberate effort. Observe the phrase "four ounces deflect a thousand catties" — plainly it is not victory by force. See the form in which a man of eighty or ninety can hold off a crowd — what use is speed there? Stand like a balance scale, move like a wheel; if one side is heavy it follows, if it is double-heavy it stagnates. One constantly sees those of several years of pure practice who cannot transform, and are invariably taken in hand by others: they have not awakened to the fault of double-heaviness. To avoid this fault one must know yin and yang. Sticking is yielding, and yielding is sticking. Yang does not leave yin, yin does not leave yang. Only when yin and yang aid one another is there understanding of power. After understanding power, the more one practises the finer one becomes. Silently and wordlessly pondering, one gradually arrives at doing as one's heart desires. This is at root "giving up oneself and following the other"; many go wrong by giving up the near and seeking the far. As it is said, "a hair's breadth of difference, and the error is a thousand miles." Students must not fail to distinguish this most carefully — this is the treatise.

As for the Long Fist: it is like the great Yangtze and the sea, rolling on without cease. Ward-off, roll-back, press and push, pluck, split, elbow and shoulder — these are the eight trigrams. Advancing step, retreating step, looking left, gazing right, and central equilibrium — these are the five elements. Ward-off, roll-back, press and push are the four cardinal directions, Qian, Kun, Kan and Li. Pluck, split, elbow and shoulder are Xun, Zhen, Dui and Gen, the four diagonal corners. Advance, retreat, look, gaze and equilibrium are metal, wood, water, fire and earth. Joined together they make the thirteen postures.

Book page 270

IV. Song of the Thirteen Postures

IV. Song of the Thirteen Postures

(Author unknown)

The thirteen overall postures are not to be made light of; the source of life and intent lies in the hollow of the waist; in changing and turning, substantial and insubstantial, one must take care, and the qi must spread through the body without the least stagnation. Struck within stillness, moving yet still; showing the marvellous according to the enemy's changes. Posture by posture keep it in mind and weigh its intent; what you gain, you will not feel to have cost you effort. Moment by moment keep your mind on the waist; within the belly, loose and still, the qi rises. The coccyx is centred and the spirit threads to the crown; the whole body is light and agile, the crown of the head suspended. Carefully keep your mind on pushing and seeking; in bending and stretching, opening and closing, let it be free. To enter the gate and be led on the way, one must be taught by word of mouth; the work never ceases, and the method one cultivates oneself. If you ask what is the standard for substance and function — intent and qi are the ruler, bone and flesh the minister; think: what after all is the aim of this intent? To lengthen life and prolong the years, an unaging spring. Sing it, sing it — the hundred and forty; every word is true and its meaning loses nothing. If you do not push and seek in this direction, you waste your effort and are left with sighs.

V. Heart of the Practice of the Thirteen Postures

Wu Yuxiang Use the mind to move the qi, and be sure to make it calm and settled. Only then can it gather and enter the bones, and use the qi to move the body. Be sure to make it smooth and compliant; only then can it be easy and follow the mind. If the spirit can be raised, there is no fear of sluggishness and heaviness — this is what is meant by "suspending the crown of the head." Intent and qi must be changed with agility; only then is there the delight of roundness and liveliness — this is what is meant by "changing and turning, substantial and insubstantial." In issuing power one must be calm, loose and clean, concentrating on one direction. In standing the body one must be centred, upright, at ease and comfortable, bracing in eight directions. Moving the qi is like a pearl of nine turnings, going everywhere without obstruction (this means the qi spreads through the body). Moving is like steel tempered a hundred times, crushing everything hard. In form like a falcon striking a rabbit, in spirit like a cat catching a mouse. Still as a mountain peak, moving as rivers and streams. Storing power like drawing a bow, issuing power like loosing an arrow. Seek the straight within the curved, store and then issue. Power issues from the spine, the step changes with the body. Gathering is issuing, broken and again joined. In going and returning there must be folding; in advancing and retreating there must be turning and exchange. Supremely soft, and then supremely firm and hard. Able to breathe, and then able to be nimble. The qi is nourished by straightness and takes no harm; the power is stored by curving and has surplus. The mind is the command, the qi is the banner; the waist is the great standard. First seek expansion, then seek compactness — only then can one attain to fine exactness.

It is also said: if the other does not move, I do not move; if the other moves slightly, I move first. The power is as if loose yet not loose, about to extend yet not extended. The power breaks but the intent does not break. It is also said: the mind comes first, the body after. The belly is loose, the qi gathers into the bones; the spirit is at ease, the body is still. Moment by moment keep it in mind. Remember firmly: if one thing moves, nothing does not move; if one thing is still, nothing is not still. Drawing and sending to and fro, the qi clings to the back and gathers into the spine. Within, solidify the spirit; without, show ease and calm. Step like the walk of a cat, move the power like drawing silk. The whole body's intent is in the spirit, not in the qi — if it is in the qi, then it stagnates. One who has qi has no power; one who has no qi is purely firm. The qi is like a cartwheel, the waist like the axle.

Book page 271

VI. A Treatise on Taijiquan

VI. A Treatise on Taijiquan

Wu Yuxiang In every movement the whole body must be light and nimble, and above all threaded through. The qi should be roused and stirred, the spirit should be gathered within. Let there be no place of deficiency, no place of concavity or convexity, no place of break or interruption. Its root is in the feet and it issues from the legs; it is governed by the waist and takes shape in the fingers. From the feet to the legs to the waist, there must always be one complete qi. Only then, advancing and retreating, can one gain the moment and gain the position. Where one fails to gain the moment and the position, the body becomes scattered and disordered, and the fault must be sought in the waist and legs — this holds for above and below, front and back, left and right. All of this is intent, and is not on the outside. Where there is above there is below; where there is front there is back; where there is left there is right. If the intent wants to go up, it lodges a downward intent. If you lift a thing up and add to it the force of a check, then its root breaks of itself — there is no doubt that this destroys it quickly. Substantial and insubstantial should be clearly distinguished: every place has its own substantial and insubstantial. Everywhere it is always this one substantial and insubstantial, and the whole body is threaded through joint by joint. Do not let there be the least interruption.

VII. Song of Striking Hands

Revised by Wang Zongyue Ward-off, roll-back, press and push must be done in earnest; upper and lower following one another, the opponent finds it hard to enter. Let him come at me with giant force — drawing him out, four ounces deflect a thousand catties. Lure him in, let him fall into emptiness, join and issue; stick, connect, adhere and follow, neither letting go nor resisting.

VIII. A Brief Talk on Practising Taijiquan

Fu Zhongwen In recent years Taijiquan has become a sport loved by the broad masses of the people. And the theory of Taijiquan has developed from a purely technical standpoint into an exploration grounded in science. This is something to be glad about.

I loved Taijiquan from the time I was a boy. Under the enlightenment and teaching of my teacher Yang Chengfu, I would not presume to say how much I have understood — only that in seventy years I have never once broken off. Precisely because I have persevered without slackening and practised Taijiquan earnestly, my constitution has been strengthened.

Taijiquan possesses a high degree of artistry and scientific content: it is subtle and fine, and its theory is profound. If one can, in accordance with the theory

Book page 272

VIII. A Brief Talk on Practising Taijiquan (continued)

VIII. A Brief Talk on Practising Taijiquan (continued)

…to train, then once one has real skill one can better grasp the inner delight of Taijiquan. To practise Taijiquan well, besides following the theoretical guidance of the sages of old and the pointers to the essentials, I hold that one must attend to several aspects.

First, one must grasp the meaning of "power" (jin). When one has practised Taijiquan earnestly to the appropriate stage, one will develop power. This power is a kind of "undifferentiated power," and it is the foundation of entry into Taijiquan. Hence it is said, "after understanding power, the more one practises the finer one becomes." By my own experience, this power is like a whole stretch of autumn reeds by a lake, blown down by a great wind and rising again — tough and not broken, supple yet with resilience. It is also like the rolling waves of the ocean: the substance of the water is soft, yet it holds a very deep and mighty force. Once the undifferentiated power has been developed, one goes on further, to develop from that undifferentiated power a "light and nimble power." The undifferentiated power is a deep, rich strength hidden and not displayed, so that one attains "firmness within softness." The light and nimble power means both possessing the feeling of lightness and nimbleness and being able to turn round and move with liveliness. Only by binding these two powers tightly together so that they serve one another can one reconcile firm and soft, and wrap a needle in cotton; and only when one can further transform and break them down into ward-off, roll-back, press and push, and can apply these powers with agility, can one reach the goal of thorough comprehension and doing as one's hands and heart desire, and so enter a realm of high artistry.

If one would develop power in Taijiquan, it cannot be done by mere brute courage and crude practice, without tasting its meaning and studying its frame. Beyond bitter practice of one's own, one must practise so that everything accords with the principles and requirements and squares with reality. This calls for attending to the following four points in daily practice.

One: the gaze is level, and must be concentrated and lively; when each posture changes, the line of sight must follow the movement of the body. Above all, avoid a wooden stare or looking wildly about.

Two: the waist is the sovereign of the whole body, and in practising one must "raise the waist." A mnemonic verse has it: "How can body shape and raised waist ever be absent?" In postures such as Cloud Hands, Brush Knee and Twist Step, the Diagonal Flying Posture, Needle at the Bottom of the Sea, and High Pat on Horse, the waist must be lifted and upright, like a pivot turning, and in the turning it never leaves the axis. It is also like a compass needle: the needle moves but the needle's axis does not leave its original position. What the martial artists call "holding the central earth" means precisely that the central earth does not leave its original position. To cite mechanics, this is the action of the centre of gravity. Therefore in practising one must study "the coccyx centred." The spirit threads to the crown; only when the coccyx is centred can one maintain the centre of gravity, without the faults of a tilted posture or a frame that overreaches or falls short. If, in practising, one lowers the head and hunches the shoulders, and the waist is not lifted, then the centre of gravity is lost — that is what is called a "sunken waist." As the saying goes, "head lowered, waist sunken, the skill is not high." For when the waist sinks the breathing is not free, the qi cannot sink, the crown cannot be empty and void, substantial and insubstantial are indistinct, and upper and lower cannot be threaded through as one qi — in the end one never practises to a high and luminous degree.

Three: the four limbs. On the movement of the four limbs in Taijiquan there is a saying: "arms like ruyi, legs like a winnowing basket rim." That is, both the arms and the legs must have a slight sense of bending and holding in reserve, and must not be stretched out too straight. "Power has surplus by holding in reserve" refers precisely to this. In postures such as Single Whip and Part the Wild Horse's Mane, the rear leg is slightly bent and rounded outward. Only so can one achieve the front bow and rear push, with the force issuing from the heel, like a tree rooted in the earth so that the whole body is steady — and not, instead, thrusting too straight backward. In general, the four limbs must be round and smooth, nimble and alive, steady and solid; above all, avoid stiff straightness.

Let me now set out the several joints one by one:

(1) One should sit the wrist and stand the palm upright, but the centre of the palm should be slightly concave and must not be flat — this is essential.

(2) The fingers should not be too straight, and the gaps between the fingers should not be closed tight; they should be as if open yet not open, and after long practice the power arises of itself.

(3) The shoulders must be loose, lively and sunken; one must not use stiff strength or have the sense of raising them up.

Book page 273

VIII. A Brief Talk on Practising Taijiquan (continued)

VIII. A Brief Talk on Practising Taijiquan (continued)

(4) The elbows must hang down. In a posture such as White Crane Spreads Its Wings, though the arms are lifted upward, the tip of the elbow must have a downward intent.

(5) The shoulder should lead the elbow, and the elbow should lead the wrist; and again, the fingers should lead the palm, and the palm should carry the arm while the elbow sinks and the shoulder relaxes. One should also use the intent of the waist and legs to match the hand, elbow and shoulder, so that upper and lower are linked through. Though there may be a slight order of before and after, the movement must be coordinated and threaded through joint by joint. One must not overreach in power; overreaching in power makes one stiff.

(6) In stepping, the heel must touch ground first, and then one settles it firmly, little by little — this is what is meant by "stepping like the walk of a cat." The image of a cat's walk is a marvellous one: the step is both light and nimble and steady and solid, while the body is lively. At the same time the knee follows forward, but in the bow stance one must not overreach in power (meaning that the knee should not pass beyond the toes), so that advancing and retreating can be nimble. The rear foot should hold a ward-off power, and must on no account be tilted over.

(7) The lifting and setting of the feet, as in the Cloud Hands posture: in the crossing step one must first lift the heel, and then lift the toes. After the crossing step, when the foot comes down, the toes must touch ground first, and then one settles it firmly, little by little. If one can do this, then left and right, substantial and insubstantial, are naturally clearly distinguished.

(8) One must hollow the chest. Hollowing the chest is not the same as a sunken waist or a caved-in chest; rather, all the joints of the two arms must be relaxed and open, the elbows hanging down, and the breathing natural.

(9) Open the crotch. Opening the crotch does not mean a wide step; it really means relaxing the hips — when the hips are relaxed, the crotch opens of itself.

(10) The crotch must be level, and when the crotch is level the lower base is steady. At the same time, on the basis of a level crotch the intent must also lift upward: lift the crotch and thread it to the crown. This must be done naturally, and then the head is naturally centred and upright, the breathing free and easy, the bearing calm and comfortable; and thereby one can have upper and lower following one another, every posture even, and can grasp for oneself the delight of a whole body light, nimble, round and lively.

IV. State of Mind

(1) The mind must be still while the spirit must be roused; avoid lowering the brows and downcast eyes, listless and dispirited, lacking vitality. But one must also avoid glaring with knitted brows and a thrust-out chest and bared teeth. The whole body must be threaded through joint by joint; do not let there be the least interruption.

(2) Value the experience accumulated by those who came before, and train earnestly in accordance with the classic frames. But one must practise so as to be natural, loose and clean, so that every movement makes the whole body light and nimble. One must "follow the rules, become familiar with the rules, transform the rules — yet never leave the rules." With this resolute spirit, only then can one practise to gaining the moment and gaining the position.

In sum, every frame in Taijiquan has its own essential meaning, and one must ponder it with all one's heart and grasp it with care. In raising the hand and setting the foot, one must not be too clumsy; if too clumsy, then the waist and legs do not follow and the whole body easily becomes stiff. The step must change with the body, and in advancing and retreating there must be folding. In posture one must first seek expansion, and afterwards seek compactness. Pay attention at all times, work on every posture, keep every posture clear and not vague; it must be linked through, completed in one breath. As days and months accumulate, when the work is complete it comes of itself.

IX. Theoretical Research in Taijiquan Is an Important Subject

Fu Zhongwen Our country's martial arts have a very early origin; examine the history and truly their source is distant and their stream long. From the relevant materials, masters of deep martial skill and transcendent art are also many, too many to enumerate. To speak of Yang-style Taijiquan alone,

Book page 274

IX. Theoretical Research in Taijiquan Is an Important Subject (continued)

IX. Theoretical Research in Taijiquan Is an Important Subject (continued)

The details cannot all be told at once; let me speak of what I know, and of my own experience.

I was born in my home town on South Street inside the city of Yongnian, a place that loved Taijiquan. From childhood I had my ears and eyes steeped in it, and quite naturally I came to love this boxing art as well.

Our founding master, Yang Lukchan, was a man of the South Gate of Yongnian. Because Taijiquan was then current in our county, many people studied the art under Lukchan, and students revered him as the founding master of Yang-style Taijiquan.

Yang-style Taijiquan, seen from its outward form, is soft and yielding as one practises the frame, and so in the north it is also called "cotton boxing." In fact the power within it is out of the ordinary: one must move as if drawing silk, continuous and unbroken, and yet must attain the requirement of "a needle wrapped in cotton"; and when one issues power, it is truly majestic and mighty indeed.

I hold that to practise this art of Taijiquan well one must put in bitter effort, for skill is produced by solid, honest practice. One must learn earnestly and practise assiduously. The masters of the older generations all produced their skill through long years and a tenacious, peerless will. When the skill is deep and the attainment high, reaching a certain realm, it is sublimated into theory; and so the sages of old summed up much precious experience. Works such as Wang Zongyue's Treatise on Taijiquan and Master Yang Chengfu's A Talk on Practising Taijiquan and others are all famous documents that set a model for later generations, so that those who come after have something to follow and take fewer crooked roads.

In the past there were also many relevant works on Taijiquan. Some authors wrote with great plausibility, but when you follow their talk round and round, most of it is copied back and forth from other writings, with little real skill behind it — truly a case of idle boasting. I myself have not practised hard enough either, so I can only speak of my own experience.

I hold that the skill of Taijiquan did not begin with theory; rather, the men of old practised over the long term, and through much time many masters gradually accumulated experience, and then deepened their understanding, put it into practice, and gradually produced a rich body of writing. This is the sublimation of skill, and also the guide to skill. Take calligraphy: at first people simply practised writing characters, and there was very little written exposition of method. Later, masters such as Wang Xizhi summed up the way to hold the brush and the requirements of writing, and thereafter many famous calligraphers appeared, and at the same time the content of the art of calligraphy was enriched. Practising Taijiquan is like the art of calligraphy: the frame must be practised until it is light, nimble and round, free and natural, yet upright and generous; the spirit must be full yet held within, and the bearing must be upright and lifted, avoiding listlessness. In the joining of one frame to the next, in the course of the movement, one must be like the calligrapher's "hiding the head and guarding the tail," turning round and smooth yet with reserve — and yet posture must be clear and not vague. Though there are fixed postures, one must not be wooden and stagnant; every posture must be linked through, moved with lightness and nimbleness. One must combine expansion with compactness, guarding against scattering and against stiffness. Know that "light and nimble" is not flightiness, and that calmness is not woodenness; one must make the practising of a whole set of frames turn round freely, every posture complete, finished in one breath. For the one practising, there is the sense of "the heart apprehending, the spirit understanding"; for the one watching, there is a feeling of peace and ease and comfort. Thus Taijiquan is indeed a method of exercise that can bring a person health and long life.

At present, judging by the momentum of Taijiquan's development, its prospects are indeed bright. But in order to carry forward and magnify this martial art, we must dig out the experience of the older generations, and take the profound and essential meanings within it, its true substance, and through practice and more practice advance our technique, so that the art of "a needle wrapped in cotton" may bloom in more brilliant flowers and bear more abundant fruit. And so, how to take the theory of those who came before and again put it in the service of those who come after — to study its essential spirit…

Book page 275

IX. Theoretical Research in Taijiquan Is an Important Subject (continued)

IX. Theoretical Research in Taijiquan Is an Important Subject (continued)

…its essential spirit, to advance the skill of Taijiquan and raise its artistic level — this is in truth a subject of the greatest importance.

X. The Essentials of Practising Taijiquan and What to Avoid

Fu Zhongwen Taijiquan is a precious martial-arts heritage of our country. Because it has a tremendous effect in promoting people's health and in casting off illness and prolonging life, it is deeply loved by the people.

I loved Taijiquan from childhood, and at the age of nine I became a student of Yang Chengfu of the Yang family gate of Taijiquan. Over seventy years I have kept up my practice without a single break; and though I have now reached a great age, I am still strong of body, clear of ear and eye, and whole in tooth. How should one practise to attain the best result, and what problems should one watch out for? Let me now speak of my own experience to my friends in the martial world.

Taijiquan divides into substantial and insubstantial (that is, yin and yang). In practising Taijiquan there is the insubstantial and the substantial, and firm and soft aid one another; hence the method of practising Taijiquan is required to accord with dialectics. In practising, one must first be still of mind — that is, concentrate one's thought and clear away distracting notions. Taijiquan requires stillness within movement: the mind must be still while the spirit must be roused; one must above all avoid lowering the brows and downcast eyes, listless and dispirited, lacking vitality. But one must also avoid glaring angrily with wide eyes and a thrust-out chest and bared teeth.

Second, the key to practising lies in correct posture, and it is required that every posture be even. Whether one's practice is correct can be seen from the practitioner's waist and body, because the waist is the sovereign of the whole body. In practising one must raise the waist — in postures such as Cloud Hands, Brush Knee and Twist Step, the Diagonal Flying Posture, Needle at the Bottom of the Sea, and High Pat on Horse, the waist must be lifted and upright, like a pivot turning, and in turning it never leaves the axis. It is also like a compass needle: the needle moves but the needle's axis does not leave its original position. If in practising the waist is not lifted and the centre of gravity is lost, that is what is called a "sunken waist." As the saying goes, "head lowered, waist sunken, the skill is not high." For when the waist sinks the breathing is not free, the qi cannot sink, the crown cannot be empty and void, substantial and insubstantial are indistinct, and upper and lower cannot be threaded through as one qi — in the end one cannot reach a high and luminous level. Many beginners are prone to the disease of impatience, hoping to finish learning the whole set of postures in a short time. In fact, "haste does not bring success." If at the start one does not demand correct posture, then later it will be hard to correct the frame. Incorrect posture will affect the efficacy of one's practice. In sum, one must "follow the rules, transform the rules, yet never leave the rules."

Again, in practising the gaze must be level, and must be concentrated and lively. As each posture of Taiji changes, the line of sight must follow the movement of the body; above all, avoid a wooden stare. In practising there are definite requirements for the movement of the four limbs. There is a saying: "arms like ruyi, legs like a winnowing basket rim." That is, the arms and legs must be slightly bent and must not be stretched too straight; both overreaching and falling short are improper. "Power has surplus by bending and storing" refers precisely to this. In postures such as Single Whip and Part the Wild Horse's Mane, with the right leg slightly bent and turned outward, one can achieve the front bow and the right push, with the force issuing from the heel. In general, the four limbs must be round and smooth, nimble and alive, steady and solid; above all, avoid stiff straightness.

In addition, in practising the shoulders must be loose, lively and sunken; one must not use stiff strength or have the intent of raising the shoulders, and the elbows must hang down. As in the White Crane…

Book page 276

X. The Essentials of Practising Taijiquan and What to Avoid (continued)

X. The Essentials of Practising Taijiquan and What to Avoid (continued)

…Spread Its Wings, though the arms are lifted upward, the tip of the elbow must have a downward intent. At the same time attend to hollowing the chest; all the joints of the two arms must be opened apart, and the breathing natural.

One who practises must also give attention to the way of nourishing life, and should achieve "diligence, constancy, courtesy and sincerity." Diligence means industriousness and frugality: in material life one should be tranquil and indifferent to fame or gain, and on no account give oneself up to pleasure. Constancy means a steady heart: practising the martial art and the boxing is not the work of a single day; it requires persistence — above all avoid one day of exposure and ten days of cold, and avoid stopping as soon as one has had a taste. Courtesy means politeness: in dealing with people and handling things one should be open and generous, tolerant and forbearing, and not haggle over small matters. Sincerity means being genuine: whether in practising the boxing or in conducting oneself, one must be open-hearted and aboveboard, whole-hearted and true, modest and prudent. As the saying goes, "when the heart is sincere, it works." Sincerity of heart is the foundation of success in every undertaking.

XI. On the Medical Efficacy of Taijiquan

Fu Zhongwen For the elderly to exercise the body there are many and various forms of movement — taking a walk, kicking the legs, bending the waist and so on — but the comparatively correct and comparatively systematic form of exercise is still the sport of Taijiquan.

I have taught Yang-style Taijiquan at Tongji University for more than ten years. Many comrades of weak health have, through practising Yang-style Taijiquan, gradually recovered their health. There was one teacher who had suffered from stomach trouble for many years, with more than ten major haemorrhages over three years, so that he could not even eat rice gruel. After a year of practising the boxing his condition improved, and he led students out to do fieldwork. Comrade Li Guohao, honorary president of Tongji University and chairman of the municipal Political Consultative Conference, also kept up his daily practice, and many times led the staff Taijiquan team to take part in the university's athletics meet, where they even won the team championship.

According to many years of scientific measurement at Tongji University, the sport of Taijiquan effectively improves the function of the cardiovascular system. It can lower cholesterol, triglycerides and free fatty acids, strengthen the activity of the anticoagulant system in the blood, and lower the level of uric acid in the blood, and thereby help resist platelet aggregation and prevent the formation of blood clots. This is of great benefit in preventing and treating cardiovascular disease in the elderly. The physiological functions of the elderly gradually decline with age; the cardiac output falls as age increases, and in addition the arteries readily harden, so that the blood supply to the internal organs is insufficient, and the heart, brain, kidneys and other important organs are especially liable to disease. But if one persists in practising Taijiquan, it can increase the blood circulation of the heart and raise the blood and oxygen supply to the organs of the whole body. It has been measured that after practising, both the systolic and diastolic blood pressure of the human body can fall by about ten millimetres of mercury. In addition it has good effects on the respiratory system, the bones, the joints, the muscles, and the metabolism of substances within the body.

After Liberation, the sport of Taijiquan was spread abroad, and in hospitals and sanatoria it has been listed as an important part of comprehensive therapy. That Taijiquan prevents illness, treats illness and prolongs life is already acknowledged by all.

Book page 277

XII. On the Method of Practising Yang-Style Taijiquan

XII. On the Method of Practising Yang-Style Taijiquan

Fu Shengyuan The movements of Taijiquan are movements of the whole body, not of a part; they are gentle movements, not violent movements. And its movement of the whole body and its gentle movement are precisely the Taiji movement that is continuous and unbroken, with firm and soft aiding one another: it is a spontaneous tendency, not something mysterious; it takes the natural movement of the body, with no forcing or contrivance anywhere in it. As for what Taiji means — using the principle of Taijiquan's movements to explain the meaning of the name "Taijiquan," without the least far-fetched attachment to mysterious talk, and without resorting to the fashionable jargon or mnemonic formulas of the boxing world for vague and impressionistic talk.

Consider the two characters "Tai Ji," which appear in the Xici commentary of the Zhouyi. The Xici says: "In the Yi there is the Supreme Ultimate, which gives birth to the two modes; the two modes give birth to the four images; the four images give birth to the eight trigrams." Let us explain this sentence in plain words: the two modes, the four images and the eight trigrams are all born of the Supreme Ultimate. The Supreme Ultimate is the primordial motive force of everything. The movement of the two modes, four images and eight trigrams is entirely the movement of the Supreme Ultimate. The cosmos is one Supreme Ultimate, and the human body is also one Supreme Ultimate. The belly of the human body (that is, the cinnabar field) is the Supreme Ultimate; the two flanks are the two modes; the two hands and two feet are the four images; and the two hands and two feet, each having two joints, make the eight trigrams.

The primordial motive force of the cosmos lies in the Supreme Ultimate; the primordial motive force of the human body also lies in the Supreme Ultimate. The movements of Taijiquan take the belly as their master. The belly is the most central place of the human body; when this place moves, there is nothing in the whole body that does not move. In the sport of Taijiquan, if one does not move, then nothing moves; but when one moves, the whole body moves. Hence a movement in which the whole body does not move is not Taiji. The belly is the most central place of the whole body; when the belly moves, the two flanks, the two hands and the two feet move swiftly without haste. The movements of Taijiquan take their origin from the belly (that is, the cinnabar field) as their master; without using violent force, there is no movement of the whole body that is not reached — outwardly exceedingly soft and gentle, inwardly a force continuous and unbroken, growing breath by breath.

In learning Taijiquan one must understand the importance of the three characters "loose," "solid" and "gathered." What is "loose"? The body must be loose. What is "solid"? The qi must be solid. What is "gathered"? The spirit must be gathered. Body loose, qi solid, spirit gathered — and one can gradually reach the realm of Taiji! But the reason why this is so can only be grasped by oneself once the student has practised to a certain degree.

(One) The body must be loose. The plain explanation of the character "loose" is simply not using force (not using stiff force), for as soon as one uses force, the movement cannot be natural. In the part where one deliberately applies force, the other parts are sure to be out of balance. Without using stiff force the movement is natural, spreading through the whole body, reaching everywhere without exception, and even and uniform throughout — and looseness is not the same as emptiness. To force the use of strength is hard: that is what is called clumsy force; and though clumsy force is great, it is the force of a part and does not hit the mark. Not using force is soft: that is what is called sinking power; and though sinking power is light and small, it is the force of the whole and can hit the mark.

(Two) The qi must be solid. The plain explanation of the character "solid" is simply not scattering, the body loose while the qi is solid. Though the body does not use force, the qi is nevertheless not scattered; if the qi is not scattered, then the movements can begin to be not scattered; if the movements are not scattered, then the whole body can begin to be one. How can one make the qi solid? Simply sink the qi into the belly and do not let it float on top. But this differs from deliberately deepening the breath and expanding the lungs to the utmost and pressing the diaphragm downward. In practising, the shoulders must hang, the elbows must drop, the waist must be settled down, and after a long time the qi naturally sinks — this is what is called the heart empty and the belly solid. When the belly is solid then the qi is solid, and the body has a centre of gravity; however the hands and feet move, the centre of gravity is always in the belly. Gaining that centre of gravity, the movements are as one wishes — hence it is said: when the qi is solid the body is steady of itself.

Book page 278

XII. On the Method of Practising Yang-Style Taijiquan (continued)

XII. On the Method of Practising Yang-Style Taijiquan (continued)

(Three) The spirit must be gathered. The plain explanation of the character "gathered" is simply that inner and outer unite, and so one can be gathered and settled. Though the body is loose and the qi solid, if inner and outer do not unite, one can in no way reach with the body wherever the mind goes. Only when inner and outer unite are body and mind one qi. Shoulder unites with hip, elbow unites with knee, hand unites with foot — this is called the outer three unities. Mind unites with intent, intent unites with qi, qi unites with power — this is called the inner three unities. These six unities are what is meant by inner and outer uniting; with the six unities the body is centred and upright, and when the body is centred and upright the spirit can be raised.

XIII. Key Points in Practising Yang-Style Taijiquan

Fu Shengyuan Nowadays there are many people practising Taijiquan, and not a few practising Yang-style Taijiquan; but what is regrettable is that many people, for various reasons, let their postures go out of shape in practice.

Some say that letting the postures go out of shape may even be a kind of innovation. I hold that this question is already stated most clearly in the prefatory notes to The Complete Book of Taijiquan: Substance and Function written by the Grand Master of Yang-style Taijiquan, my maternal great-grandfather Mr. Yang Chengfu. He said: "Taijiquan has only one school and no second method; one must not dazzle oneself with cleverness and recklessly add or subtract. As for the established methods of the former worthies, if there were anywhere to be altered — from the Yuan and Ming down to the present it is several hundred years, and if there were anything that could be changed, men of old would already have done it before us; why should they wait for our generation? May the students who come after not scramble only after the outward, but seek only the inward; if you would advance to purity and richness, the day may be awaited. In short, in the fine details of the boxing postures, do not seize upon outward form; one must seek the union of intent. I fear only that private notions will recklessly alter them, and error be passed on as error, so that the true transmission of substance and function is easily lost, and the original meaning of the former worthies buried." Therefore I hold that if one has not yet reached the point of practising Taijiquan without distortion, and has no deep attainment in the work, one had better not set about innovating the postures. And even if one wishes to innovate, one should not call it Yang-style Taijiquan, but should call it some other style of Taijiquan, so as to avoid misleading students and confusing people's eyes and ears.

Furthermore, I hold that in both learning and practising one must not be impatient; if one is in a hurry, I fear that haste defeats the purpose, and learning in front and forgetting behind is of no use. Taking Yang-style Taijiquan as the case: each set takes about twenty minutes to practise, and one should practise at least three sets a day, and further must practise according to the requirements. The frame one has learned must be corrected from time to time to raise one's own level; the longer one learns the higher the requirements, and the more one practises the more one feels it is not easy — only thus can there be progress.

In practising, one must gather one's spirit, and must not let one's thoughts wander; one must think about the movements, and imagine that an enemy is right beside one. Only thus can one use the postures freely, without appearing affected — this is what is called using intent and not force.

At the same time, in practising Taijiquan every lift of a hand and set of a foot must have spirit; Taijiquan is loose and not empty, and one must not practise it limp and yielding, going from looseness to emptiness.

Yang-style Taijiquan sets store by "sitting the wrist": the hand must sit the wrist, the wrist must have power, just as when tap water flows out of a rubber hose — with a little pressure the water's driving force is stronger and it shoots farther. But the fingers, the shoulder and elbow, and the arm must all be loose, and must not be stiff.

Book page 279

XIII. Key Points in Practising Yang-Style Taijiquan (continued)

XIII. Key Points in Practising Yang-Style Taijiquan (continued)

As for the breathing, it must certainly be natural; I hold that a person's breathing should be like a refrigerator, able to adjust itself automatically.

People often ask: "Why does the frame of Yang-style Taijiquan always turn about the root on the substantial foot?" I think this is a good question, because Yang-style Taijiquan's turning on the substantial foot is for the sake of the training, and is extremely rich in martial application. In the past this point was not made clear, and so in general, when practising, people used the insubstantial foot to turn the heel and shift the centre; this reduced the practice of Taijiquan to a mere general exercise and lowered its martial effectiveness. If one wants to restore the martial effectiveness of Taijiquan, then in practising one must take particular care to use the substantial foot to turn the root and shift the centre. For a frame that uses the insubstantial foot to change the centre of gravity has the foot only just set down when the centre is already shifting, and the foot is released the moment it takes the weight — so the training effect will not be as good as turning the root on the substantial foot. And the distinguishing feature of turning the root on the substantial foot is that the power is unbroken, and the power can keep on being carried forward unceasingly.

Some also worry whether turning the root on the substantial foot will break the power. I hold that so long as substantial and insubstantial are clearly distinguished, the root is not easily broken, because the substantial foot turning its root is a living pillar, and not a dead one.

In addition, one must also attend to this: turning the root must be coordinated with relaxing the hip, and in turning the toes must be slightly lifted, using the heel to turn. And in practising, from the Beginning Posture to the Closing Posture, the whole body must sink and must not float; only when loose can one sink, and the root must turn downward like turning a screw.

Of course, using the substantial foot to turn the root comes down from the old teaching method and is a little more difficult; the whole set of postures is one link clasping another. The number of repetitions should be set according to one's own physical strength; those in good health should train beyond their normal capacity — only then can they develop real skill.

I myself have followed my father Fu Zhongwen in practising from the age of nine. What I have said above is only some of my own experience over many years, and is not necessarily correct. I offer a brick to draw forth jade, and hope that the broad community of fellow practitioners will not stint their instruction.

Book page 280

Postscript One

Postscript One

Over more than twenty years I have read through in detail the works on Yang-style Taijiquan published at home and abroad, and have found that the fixed-posture photographs of the various schools are much alike, while the course of the movements differs considerably. During my travels away from home (to Chengdu, Harbin, Shenzhen and elsewhere), I saw that the Yang-style Taijiquan practised in different places was not quite the same either; and at international Taijiquan gatherings, the Yang-style Taijiquan demonstrated by the various well-known masters and by the delegates of different regions was again not entirely uniform. So then, what frame should one take as the standard? And which method of practice is the fitting one?

To be sure, the Yang-style Taijiquan most widely current today was given its definitive form by the Grand Master Yang Chengfu, the representative figure of the third generation of transmission. But we should further recognize that Master Yang's Taijiquan can be divided into two periods, earlier and later (conveniently taking about 1928 as the dividing line). This can be known from the two books Master Yang published in succession: namely The Art of Taijiquan, written in 1925 by Master Yang's disciple Mr. Chen Weiming, and The Complete Book of Taijiquan: Substance and Function, written in 1934 by Mr. Zheng Manqing. In them, Master Yang's photographs from before and after differ somewhat.

Furthermore, analysing a little the many books, periodicals, video recordings and demonstrations of Yang-style Taijiquan, one can also find this situation: the methods of Master Yang's earlier disciples, or of their disciples, are for the most part similar to one another, while the methods of his later disciples are again basically the same among themselves. Though the methods before and after differ, they were all transmitted directly or indirectly by Master Yang, and are all Yang-style Taijiquan; one cannot and should not say who is right and who is wrong. This is because Master Yang's Taijiquan was continually being improved (for example, in the earlier period the fixed posture of the left ward-off faced due south, while in the later period it was changed to face due west, and so on). Master Yang's Taijiquan differed before and after, so what a learner acquired was naturally different; add to this that each person's temperament differs and their comprehension differs, and one arrives at the present situation of divergent methods.

Then should we, in practising Yang-style Taijiquan, take the earlier or the later period as our standard? A study of Master Yang's photographs from the two periods shows that in the later period the body shape and the step shapes and so on are more regular and more reasonable than in the earlier. As Master Yang indeed points out in The Complete Book of Taijiquan: Substance and Function: "Reviewing the frames of my work of a dozen years past, they again do not come up to those of recent days." For a boxer, continually raising his art and improving his technique is an entirely normal phenomenon, and one that accords with the laws of the development of things. Therefore Yang-style Taijiquan should take Master Yang's frame of his later years as its standard.

That the fixed postures of the various forms of traditional Yang-style Taijiquan should take Master Yang Chengfu's photographs of his later years as their standard admits of no dispute. Yet as to the course of the movements, which method of practice is the fitting one?

Only by comparison can one discriminate. Surveying the photographs of the various schools of Yang-style Taijiquan that have been published, one does not find it hard to see that the photographs most resembling Master Yang's later ones are those of the late Master Fu Zhongwen. As the famous Taiji master, my uncle Master Chen Weiming, said, "Fu

Book page 281

Postscript One (continued)

Postscript One (continued)

Zhongwen was a junior relative of the Grand Master Yang Chengfu of Yongnian. He received the master's transmission, and in the rule and the plumb-line he was not off by a hair; hence people called him the orthodox line of Taijiquan." And again, the senior Yang Zhenji, a direct fourth-generation transmitter of Yang-style Taijiquan, said: "Fu Zhongwen loved the martial arts from childhood, and studied boxing with my father and elder brother. Under their meticulous teaching, through many years of hammering and whetting, he at last grasped the essence and profound purport of Yang-style Taijiquan, and became a Yang-style Taijiquan expert of weight at home and abroad." "'In the book Yang-Style Taijiquan, compiled and written by Mr. Fu Zhongwen, every posture in the book is compiled according to the frame the old gentleman taught in the past, and the fixed posture of each form has not been altered.'" Indeed, Teacher Fu studied boxing with Master Yang from childhood; and when Master Yang went south from Beijing in 1928 to teach boxing (in Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhu, Guangzhou and elsewhere), up until Master Yang's death from illness in Shanghai in 1936 (at the age of fifty-three), Teacher Fu stayed at his side throughout, together morning and evening, receiving Master Yang's strict and devoted guidance, and practising hard himself. Teacher Fu was thoroughly versed in Master Yang's frames of his later years, and was much valued; he often spoke on the spot in Master Yang's place, taught and demonstrated the boxing, and went out to compete, and thus deeply received Master Yang's true transmission. As Teacher Fu himself said with modesty: "Though my skill has not reached the point where the fire is purest blue, yet when it comes to the Yang family's Taijiquan, I dare assert that within the country there is no second person who understands it as clearly as I do." "Every one of my postures I learned from Master Yang, and I have not altered the least bit." And analysed again from the principles of boxing, Teacher Fu's manner of practice is comparatively scientific and reasonable — for example his emphasis on turning the body on the substantial foot, on sitting the leg and turning the waist, and on sitting the wrist; for this can not only raise the effect on health, but also make the lower base steady, the power unbroken, the body method nimble, rich in martial effectiveness, and conducive to developing real skill.

In sum, I hold that the frames (fixed postures) of traditional Yang-style Taijiquan must take as their standard the photographs of the Grand Master Yang Chengfu in his later period (published in 1934), while the course of its movements should follow the practice method of the late Master Fu Zhongwen.

This short piece is respectfully offered in place of a postscript.

Respectfully written as a postscript at Shanghai by Xi Guizhong

Book page 282

Postscript Two

Postscript Two

The book Yang-Style Taijiquan: Method of Teaching and Method of Practice, compiled and written by the great Teacher Fu Zhongwen and the Master Fu Shengyuan, had scarcely been published by Tongji University Press at the end of 1989 when it became so sought-after that paper grew dear in Luoyang and the printing was snapped up clean. Of all lovers of Taijiquan there was none who did not revere that book as a model.

The one small blemish on the book was that, owing to the paper and the printing, Teacher Fu Zhongwen's photographs in it were not clear, and the pictures were very small, so that there was no lover of Taijiquan who did not consider it a matter for regret. Everyone wished to strive to glimpse the splendour of Master Fu's boxing photographs, and to take them as the standard of the orthodox line.

Now The Directly Transmitted Yang-Style Taijiquan Coaching Method, after careful revision, is to be published anew — a matter of real significance. The boxing photographs have been replaced with photographs of Master Fu Zhongwen's beloved grandson, my senior fellow-disciple Fu Qingquan. Senior Fu Qingquan once won the championship of Taijiquan and Taiji Sword within China, and over the long term received the instruction of his grandfather and his father, deeply awakening to the essence of Yang-style Taijiquan.

The three generations — the great Teacher Fu Zhongwen, the Master Fu Shengyuan and senior Fu Qingquan — have all their lives done their utmost for the promotion of Yang-style Taijiquan, and have won the admiration and respect of the world.

In 1987 I had the good fortune, together with other senior and junior fellow-disciples, to study in Singapore the traditional eighty-five-form Yang-style Taijiquan under the Master Fu Shengyuan, and with my fellow-disciples I founded the Yongnian Taijiquan Society at Johor Bahru in Malaysia, to promote this eighty-five-form Yang-style Taijiquan given its definitive form by the famous Taijiquan master Yang Chengfu.

The founding master Yang Lukchan, who enjoyed the name "Yang the Invincible," had a martial art beyond compare, and the anecdotes handed down about him are exceedingly many, filling us with amazement and admiration; but regrettably, in those years the camera had not yet been invented, and we have no way to glimpse the frame and the spirit with which he practised.

The late Master Yang Chengfu is acclaimed as the one who gave Yang-style Taijiquan its definitive form. He fixed the positions of Yang-style Taijiquan, and left his later photographs as a model: settled and expansive, easy and generous, of great bearing and fine appearance, as a model for later generations.

The late great Teacher Fu Zhongwen, who stayed at the side of the late Master Yang Chengfu, fully inherited the frame given its definitive form in the late Master Yang Chengfu's later years; year in and year out, without the least carelessness, he trained, and in 1944 he founded the Yongnian Taijiquan Society in Shanghai. At that time the Grand Master Chen Weiming praised the great Teacher Fu's frame as the orthodox line of Taijiquan. This "orthodox line" refers to the frame given its definitive form by the late Master Yang Chengfu. The great Teacher Fu Zhongwen was the husband of the granddaughter of the sister of the late Taiji Master Yang Chengfu, and was one of the representative figures of contemporary Chinese Yang-style Taijiquan. From early childhood he followed at the side of the late Master Yang Chengfu, deeply probing and bitterly practising Taijiquan. At that time, if someone, admiring Master Yang's fame, offered to compare skills, Master Yang would always have the great Teacher Fu take the field, and there was none whom he did not bring to submission. Hence the great Teacher Fu enjoyed a lofty reputation in the martial world, of high virtue and great prestige.

Book page 283

Postscript Two (continued)

Postscript Two (continued)

The Master Fu Shengyuan practised the martial art with his father from childhood, was deeply influenced by his father, and, carrying on the family teaching, travelled north and south within China and overseas, invited to every part of the world to carry forward this traditional set of the orthodox Yang-style Taijiquan. He is humble as a valley, does not care for fame or gain, and teaches earnestly. Before retiring he taught at the Shanghai Mechanical and Electrical Workers' University and concurrently taught at Tongji University, the Shanghai Institute of Chemical Technology and the Shanghai Institute of Finance and Economics. In 1986 he carried his art south, and successively taught Taijiquan in Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and elsewhere. In recent years he has many times visited more than twenty countries in Europe and America to teach and to exchange, and is deeply welcomed by lovers of Taijiquan; he may be called the first to spread the orthodox Yang-style Taijiquan in the countries of Southeast Asia.

In Taijiquan, between one lift of the hand and one set of the foot there is substance and spirit; when one thing moves nothing does not move, when one thing is still nothing is not still; the whole set must have upper and lower following one another, continuous and unbroken — all of which embodies a serious pursuit of the frame. At the same time each stage has its different levels of requirement, and the most important of all is the training method of changing on the substantial foot, which fully carries through the spirit of the late Master Yang Chengfu's Ten Essentials of Taijiquan. In this book there are also special examples pointing out the errors easily committed in every posture and every form, the causes that produce them, and the methods of correcting them — to fellow students who love the sport of Taijiquan this is undoubtedly a reference book of great value.

We are deeply convinced that with the publication of this Directly Transmitted Yang-Style Taijiquan Coaching Method it will surely make its contribution in spreading and raising the art of Taijiquan, and in the sport of Taijiquan, where the schools are in confusion, it will clear the source and rectify the root for Yang-style Taijiquan.

What made me, a student, feel overwhelmed by the honour is that the Master Fu Shengyuan asked his student to write a short piece for this work, so that I, as his student, feel deeply the honour.

Finally, it is worth mentioning that in 1987, when the Master Fu Shengyuan came south to Singapore to teach boxing, he carried with him the draft manuscript of the Yang-Style Taijiquan: Method of Teaching and Method of Practice, which he had taken such pains to compile, and solemnly entrusted us to find a way to publish it in Malaysia. In the end, in 1993, after many twists and turns, we succeeded in publishing this book of his in Malaysia, under the title Yongnian Yang-Style Taijiquan. The boxing photographs in the book are of the Master Fu Shengyuan's own frame, and the photographs are clearly and beautifully printed.

I believe that with the publication of The Directly Transmitted Yang-Style Taijiquan Coaching Method, lovers of Taijiquan will have the chance to glimpse the frame style transmitted in a single line through three generations of the Fu family. This is a matter of great significance, for it keeps those who come after from straying into byways, enables them to distinguish what is the orthodox road of Yang-style Taijiquan, saves them from walking crooked roads, and lets them take directly the true marrow of Master Yang's Yang-style Taijiquan.

This is offered as a postscript.

Student: Huang Jiancheng The postscript writer is: Veteran journalist of the China Press of Malaysia Founder of the Yongnian Taijiquan Society of Johor Bahru, Malaysia President of the Malaysian Taijiquan Theory Research Association
